life-citizen-india.title: Citizen India: documents, rights and complaints
life-citizen-india.description: Get and protect your Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, passport, driving licence and DigiLocker; file an FIR, RTI or consumer complaint; vote and get your local government to act.

courses.title: Your documents: Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, passport, DL, DigiLocker
courses.summary: What each key Indian document is for, how to apply or update it through official portals, and how to keep it safe from misuse and fake websites.
outcomes: Learners can explain what Aadhaar is (and is not) and use masked Aadhaar and biometric lock
Learners can get a PAN and link it with Aadhaar
Learners can register as a voter and apply for a passport through official channels
Learners can go from learner’s licence to driving licence
Learners can store documents in DigiLocker and avoid fake agent sites

lessons.title: Aadhaar and PAN: identity and tax

scenes.text: Pooja, 18, in Patna gives full Aadhaar photocopies to a sim shop, a coaching centre and a hostel — without writing anything on them.
Months later she finds two mobile connections she never took, registered in her name.
Her uncle shows her how to check connections on Sanchar Saathi, download masked Aadhaar and lock biometrics on myAadhaar.
She also gets her PAN online in minutes for her first part-time job and links it with Aadhaar.

steps.title: Aadhaar: what it is (and isn’t)
steps.body:
- A **12-digit** identity number issued by **UIDAI**, linked to your demographic details (name, date of birth, address) and biometrics (fingerprints, iris, photo).
- Enrolment is **free**. Residents of India, including children, can enrol.
- It is **proof of identity** (and address as updated), but the Aadhaar Act says it is **not proof of citizenship or domicile**.
- Children’s biometrics must be updated at about **5 and 15 years** of age.
- Update address and some details online via the official **myAadhaar** portal; biometric changes need an Aadhaar centre.

steps.title: Keep Aadhaar safe
steps.body:
- Use **masked Aadhaar** (only last 4 digits visible) when someone needs a copy.
- On any photocopy, write the **purpose and date** (e.g., ‘For hostel admission only, 12/07’) across it.
- **Lock your biometrics** on myAadhaar or mAadhaar; unlock temporarily when needed.
- Check **Aadhaar authentication history** on myAadhaar for unknown use.
- Use an **offline Aadhaar QR / e-KYC** instead of photocopies where accepted.
- Never share Aadhaar OTPs.

steps.title: PAN: your tax identity
steps.body:
- **PAN** (Permanent Account Number) is a **10-character** alphanumeric ID issued by the **Income Tax Department** (e.g., ABCDE1234F format).
- Needed for filing income tax, opening many bank and investment accounts, and high-value transactions.
- Apply through the authorised portals (Protean/NSDL or UTIITSL) using Form 49A, or get a free **instant e-PAN** using Aadhaar on the income-tax e-filing portal.
- **Link PAN with Aadhaar** — an unlinked PAN can become inoperative.
- One person, **one PAN** only. Having more than one can attract a penalty; surrender extra PANs.

steps.title: Fake portals and agents
steps.body: Many websites look official and charge extra fees, or steal data. Always type the address yourself or start from the government’s official sites (they usually end in **.gov.in** — e.g., uidai.gov.in, incometax.gov.in). Ignore SMS links claiming ‘Aadhaar suspended’ or ‘PAN blocked — click to update’.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Log in to myAadhaar: download your masked Aadhaar, check authentication history, and lock biometrics. Check on the e-filing portal that your PAN-Aadhaar link status is ‘linked’.

activity.prompt: Match the document to its key fact.
pairs: 10-character tax ID from the Income Tax Department
Stops misuse of your fingerprints/iris for authentication
Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship

quiz.q: Aadhaar is issued by…
quiz.why: The answer is "UIDAI". Reason: Unique Identification Authority of India. The other choices, such as "RBI" and "Income Tax Department", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Is Aadhaar proof of citizenship?
options: No, it is proof of identity
quiz.why: The answer is "No, it is proof of identity". Reason: The Aadhaar Act clarifies this. The other choices, such as "Yes", do not fit the question. (Question: Is Aadhaar proof of citizenship?)

quiz.q: Safest way to share Aadhaar for a hostel?
options: Masked Aadhaar or a copy marked with purpose and date
quiz.why: The answer is "Masked Aadhaar or a copy marked with purpose and date". Reason: Limits misuse. The other choices, such as "Send OTP" and "Post on social media", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: If PAN is not linked to Aadhaar, it may become…
quiz.why: The answer is "Inoperative". Reason: Linking is mandatory for most individuals. The other choices, such as "A passport" and "Gold-plated", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: How many PANs can one person hold?
quiz.why: The answer is "One". Reason: Only one is allowed. The other choices, such as "Two" and "Five", do not fit the question. (Question: How many PANs can one person hold?)

lessons.title: Voter ID and passport

scenes.text: Imtiaz turns 18 in Srinagar. He assumes he’ll get a voter card automatically.
His teacher shows the class how to fill Form 6 on the Voter Helpline app. Imtiaz is added to the electoral roll and gets his EPIC.
A year later he gets a college exchange offer to Japan. He applies for a passport on the official Passport Seva portal.
After his appointment and police verification, the passport arrives by post. He avoided agents who wanted to charge him triple.

steps.title: Voter registration
steps.body:
- Any **Indian citizen aged 18** or more on the **qualifying date** can register in the constituency where they ordinarily live. There are now four qualifying dates a year (1 January, 1 April, 1 July, 1 October), and **17-year-olds can apply in advance**.
- Apply with **Form 6** on the official voters’ service portal or the **Voter Helpline app** of the Election Commission of India (ECI).
- You get an **EPIC** (Electors Photo Identity Card).
- **Form 8**: corrections, shifting residence, replacement EPIC. Your area’s **BLO** (Booth Level Officer) can help.
- What matters on polling day is that **your name is on the electoral roll**; if you lack your EPIC, ECI notifies other photo IDs you can show.

steps.title: Passport: the official route
steps.body:
1. Register on the official **Passport Seva** portal or mPassport Seva app (Ministry of External Affairs).
2. Fill the application (fresh/re-issue; normal or **Tatkaal** for urgent cases).
3. Pay the fee online and book an appointment at a **Passport Seva Kendra (PSK)** or **Post Office PSK**.
4. Visit with **original documents** (proof of date of birth, address, ID as listed on the portal).
5. **Police verification** (before or after issue depending on case).
6. Track status online; passport is sent by post.
An adult’s ordinary passport is generally valid for **10 years**; minors’ passports have shorter validity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using **look-alike passport websites** that charge extra ‘service fees’ — always use the official portal.
- Name or date-of-birth **mismatch** across documents (Aadhaar, school certificate, PAN). Fix mismatches first; they cause delays.
- Giving wrong address details — police verification fails.
- Forgetting to renew a passport before it has less than 6 months validity (many countries require 6 months).

steps.title: Keep a ‘document consistency’ sheet
steps.body: Write down exactly how your name, date of birth, father’s/mother’s name and address appear on each document. Use the **same spelling** everywhere. If you change your name (e.g., after marriage), plan the updates in order and keep the official proof (marriage certificate or gazette notification).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Search your name on the ECI electoral roll search service. If you’re 17+, find Form 6 on the Voter Helpline app.

activity.prompt: Put the passport steps in order.
items: Register on the official Passport Seva portal
Pay the fee and book an appointment

quiz.q: Which form is used for new voter registration?
quiz.why: The answer is "Form 6". Reason: Form 6 is for inclusion in the electoral roll. The other choices, such as "Form 49A" and "Form 8", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Can a 17-year-old apply in advance for voter registration?
quiz.why: Advance applications are allowed; name is added on reaching 18 by a qualifying date.

quiz.q: On polling day the most important thing is…
options: Your name on the electoral roll
quiz.why: The answer is "Your name on the electoral roll". Reason: Without your name on the roll you can’t vote. The other choices, such as "Your PAN" and "A passport", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Typical validity of an adult’s ordinary Indian passport?
quiz.why: The answer is "10 years". Reason: Generally 10 years. The other choices, such as "5 years" and "1 year", do not fit the question. (Question: Typical validity of an adult’s ordinary Indian passport?)

quiz.q: Biggest cause of passport delays?
quiz.why: Passport offices check your application against your other documents, so a name, date of birth or address that differs across them causes queries and delays. Booking appointments and using the official portal are the correct steps, not problems.

sources: Election Commission of India — voters’ services
Ministry of External Affairs — Passport Seva

lessons.title: Driving licence: from learner to licensed

scenes.text: Sunaina, 18, in Raipur has been riding her brother’s scooter ‘just around the colony’ without a licence.
A traffic check stops her. Her father has to pay a fine as the owner and is told it could have been much worse.
She applies for a learner’s licence on the official Sarathi Parivahan portal, takes the online road-rules test, and practises with her father for a month.
She passes the driving test at the RTO and downloads her DL into DigiLocker.

steps.title: Age rules
steps.body:
- **16 years**: learner’s licence for a **gearless motorcycle up to 50 cc**, with the consent of a parent/guardian.
- **18 years**: licence for other non-transport vehicles (motorcycles with gear, cars).
- Transport (commercial) vehicles have additional age and eligibility requirements.
Driving without a valid licence is an offence; under the amended Motor Vehicles Act, if a juvenile commits a traffic offence, the guardian or vehicle owner can be held responsible.

steps.title: Step by step
steps.body:
1. **Learner’s licence (LL)**: apply on the official **Sarathi Parivahan** portal (Ministry of Road Transport and Highways); upload documents, pay fee.
2. Take the **LL test** on road signs and rules — many states allow an online test with Aadhaar authentication; others at the RTO.
3. LL is valid for **6 months**. Practise only with a licensed driver beside you and ‘L’ plates displayed.
4. After at least **30 days** from the LL, apply for the **driving licence (DL)** and book a driving test slot.
5. Pass the practical test at the RTO (or as permitted in your state).
6. DL is issued; keep it in DigiLocker/mParivahan too.

steps.title: Prepare well
steps.body: Study the traffic signs (mandatory, cautionary, informatory), right of way, lane discipline and signals. For the practical test, practise slow-speed control, figure-of-8 (two-wheelers), reversing and parking (cars), mirror checks and indicators. Show calm, safe habits — examiners look for them.

steps.title: Avoid touts and fakes
steps.body: Pay only the official fees on the portal. ‘Licence without test’ offers are illegal and dangerous. Renew your DL before it expires (renewal can be applied online). Update the address on your DL when you move.

steps.title: Other countries
steps.body: Indian licences may be used abroad in some places with an **International Driving Permit (IDP)**, issued by the RTO. Rules vary by country — check the destination country’s official guidance before driving there.

activity.prompt: Fill in the blanks about licences in India.
activity.text: A learner’s licence is valid for ___ months. You can apply for a driving licence at least ___ days after getting the learner’s licence. A gearless scooter up to 50 cc can be licensed from age ___ with guardian consent.

quiz.q: The official portal for learner’s and driving licences is…
quiz.why: Sarathi Parivahan is the official portal for learner's and driving licences, run under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. Passport Seva is for passports and IRCTC for train tickets.

quiz.q: With a learner’s licence you should…
options: Practise with a licensed driver and display L plates
quiz.why: A learner's licence lets you practise only under conditions: a licensed driver must sit with you and L plates must be displayed. It does not allow paid passengers, heavy vehicles or riding alone.

quiz.q: Minimum age for a car licence (non-transport)?
quiz.why: The minimum age for a non-transport car licence is 18 years. A lower age is only allowed for certain low-powered gearless two-wheelers, and a higher age is not required for private cars.

quiz.q: ‘Licence without test, ₹5,000’ offer is…
quiz.why: A licence must be earned by the official process, including a driving test. Paying for a licence without a test is illegal and puts unqualified drivers on the road, endangering everyone.

lessons.title: DigiLocker, UMANG and keeping documents safe

scenes.text: When floods hit Chennai, the Raman family’s cupboard is soaked — marksheets, RC book and certificates ruined.
Their neighbour, Mr. Iyer, had linked his family’s Aadhaar to DigiLocker and pulled in their licences, marksheets and vehicle papers.
He uses the DigiLocker copies for insurance and bank work the following week.
The Ramans now keep digital copies, a waterproof pouch of originals and a list of document numbers.

steps.title: What DigiLocker is
steps.body: **DigiLocker** is the Government of India’s digital document wallet (under the Ministry of Electronics and IT). You sign up with your mobile number and Aadhaar, then **pull** documents directly from issuers: driving licence, vehicle RC, CBSE and many state-board marksheets, Aadhaar, PAN, insurance policies and more. Under the IT Act rules for digital lockers, documents **issued** into DigiLocker by the issuing authority are treated as equivalent to the original physical documents. (Your own uploaded scans are just copies.)

steps.title: UMANG and other official apps
steps.body:
- **UMANG**: one app for many central and state services (EPF passbook, some utility payments, scheme information).
- **mParivahan**: virtual DL and RC.
- **mAadhaar**: Aadhaar services.
- **Voter Helpline**: electoral services.
Download only from official app stores, checking the developer (e.g., the ministry or NIC/NeGD).

steps.title: A family document system
steps.body:
1. **Originals** in one waterproof, fire-resistant folder (birth certificates, property papers, marksheets, passports, policy documents).
2. **Digital**: DigiLocker for issued documents + encrypted scans of the rest.
3. **A master list** (paper and digital): document name, number, issue date, expiry date, where kept.
4. **Expiry reminders**: passport, DL, insurance, PUC.
5. Tell a trusted family member where things are.

steps.title: Privacy matters
steps.body: Never share DigiLocker login or OTP. Share documents only with trusted organisations and for a specific purpose. Don’t keep photos of all your IDs in your phone gallery or chat apps where they can be leaked.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: Procedures and portals change from time to time. Always follow the latest instructions on the official .gov.in website. This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Set up your document safety system
items: Pulled DL/RC, marksheets or PAN into DigiLocker
Made a master list of document numbers and expiry dates
Put originals in a waterproof folder
Told a trusted family member where documents are kept

quiz.q: DigiLocker is run by…
quiz.why: DigiLocker is an official government platform run by the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY). It is not a private social network, telecom company or bank service.

quiz.q: Which DigiLocker documents are treated like originals?
options: Documents issued into DigiLocker by the issuing authority
quiz.why: Documents pushed into DigiLocker by the issuing authority come straight from the source, so they are treated like originals. Your own scans, screenshots or forwards can be altered, so they carry no such status.

quiz.q: mParivahan provides…
quiz.why: mParivahan is the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways app that holds virtual driving licence (DL) and registration certificate (RC) details. Train tickets, Aadhaar enrolment and passports are handled elsewhere.

quiz.q: Best place to keep originals?
options: A waterproof, fire-resistant folder known to a trusted family member
quiz.why: Originals can be lost to floods, fire or theft, so use a waterproof, fire-resistant folder and tell a trusted family member where it is. A loose drawer, car dashboard or phone gallery gives little protection.

sources: IT (Preservation and Retention of Information by Intermediaries Providing Digital Locker Facilities) Rules 2016

questions.q: Aadhaar number has how many digits?
questions.why: An Aadhaar number has 12 digits. It is a unique identity number issued by UIDAI; 8, 10 or 16 digits is not the format.

questions.q: Official government websites in India usually end in…
questions.why: Official Indian government sites usually end in .gov.in (or .nic.in). Domains like .shop, .top or .xyz are cheap and open to anyone, so they are common in fake sites.

questions.q: Voter ID card is officially called…
questions.why: The voter ID card is officially the EPIC, the Electors Photo Identity Card. RC is a vehicle registration certificate, PAN is a tax number and UAN is a provident fund number.

questions.q: PAN is issued by…
questions.why: PAN (Permanent Account Number) is a tax identity issued by the Income Tax Department. ECI handles elections, UIDAI handles Aadhaar and the RTO handles vehicles and licences.

questions.q: Learner’s licence validity?
questions.why: A learner's licence is valid for 6 months, so you must complete the driving test and apply for a full licence within that time. It is not lifetime or only 1 month.

questions.q: Where do you apply for a passport?
questions.why: Passports are applied for on the Passport Seva portal run by the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). Travel agents, banks and social media are not official channels and risk fraud.

questions.q: Biometric lock on Aadhaar helps…
options: Prevent misuse of fingerprints for authentication
questions.why: Locking Aadhaar biometrics blocks fingerprint and iris authentication until you unlock it, so nobody can misuse your biometrics. It does not give loans, change addresses or let you vote.

questions.q: You moved to another city. To update your voter registration use…
questions.why: Form 8 is used by registered voters for shifting residence and correcting entries. Form 6 is for new registration and Form 16 and Form 49A relate to tax and PAN, not voting.

questions.q: Earliest you can apply for a DL after getting an LL?
questions.why: After getting a learner's licence you must wait at least 30 days before applying for the permanent driving licence. Applying the same day is not allowed, and you need not wait a year.

questions.q: Which statement about DigiLocker is correct?
options: Requires paying a fee per document
Any uploaded scan equals an original
Issuer-pushed documents are treated as equivalent to originals
It is a private bank app
questions.why: Documents pushed into DigiLocker by their issuers are treated as equivalent to originals under the IT rules for digital lockers. Your own uploaded scans are not, and DigiLocker is a government platform, not a bank app.

questions.q: You find mobile connections in your name you never took. Steps?
options: Report them via Sanchar Saathi, check Aadhaar authentication history, lock biometrics
questions.why: If connections exist in your name that you never took, report them through Sanchar Saathi, check your Aadhaar authentication history and lock biometrics. This finds and blocks misuse; a new SIM or PAN change does not.

questions.q: Name spelt differently on Aadhaar and school certificate before a passport application. Best plan?
options: Correct the mismatch first using official update processes, then apply
questions.why: A name mismatch between Aadhaar and a school certificate can lead to rejection or delay. Fix it through official update processes first, then apply. Nicknames and agents who 'adjust' records are unreliable or illegal.

questions.q: A 16-year-old wants to ride a 110 cc geared motorcycle legally. Can they?
options: Yes if a parent rides pillion
No — at 16, only gearless up to 50 cc with consent; geared needs 18
questions.why: Under the Motor Vehicles Act age rules, a 16-year-old may ride only a gearless two-wheeler up to 50 cc, with guardian consent. A 110 cc geared motorcycle needs a licence holder aged 18, whatever the day or pillion.

questions.q: Which is the strongest protection of Aadhaar when giving KYC to a new hostel?
options: Email a photo of the card
Masked Aadhaar or offline e-KYC/QR, copy marked with purpose/date, biometrics locked
questions.why: The safest way is layers of data minimisation: a masked Aadhaar or offline e-KYC/QR, a copy marked with purpose and date, and locked biometrics. Sharing logins, OTPs or full photocopies exposes you to misuse.

courses.title: Getting justice: FIR, RTI and consumer complaints
courses.summary: How to file an FIR (including Zero FIR and e-FIR) under the BNSS, what to do if police refuse, how to use the RTI Act, and how to win a consumer complaint — with India’s grievance portals.
outcomes: Learners can file an FIR and know their rights under the BNSS
Learners know the steps if police refuse to register an FIR
Learners can draft and appeal an RTI application
Learners can resolve a consumer dispute via 1915 and the consumer commissions
Learners can choose the right grievance channel (bank, insurance, government)
courses.guardianNote: Explains, in a factual and non-graphic way, how ordinary citizens report crimes and complaints to police, government and consumer bodies. It mentions crime only in general terms. Knowing these rights helps young people and their families act safely and lawfully.

lessons.title: Filing an FIR: your rights at the police station

scenes.text: Anil’s motorcycle is stolen outside a market in Meerut. At the police station, he is told to ‘come back tomorrow’ and that it’s ‘not our area’.
His cousin Farah, a law student, explains: theft is a cognizable offence; any police station must register at least a Zero FIR and transfer it.
Anil calmly asks for his statement to be recorded, reads it before signing, and receives a free copy of the FIR.
Farah also shows him that many states allow e-FIRs for vehicle theft online.

steps.title: Today’s laws
steps.body: Since **1 July 2024**, India’s criminal laws are the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** (offences), the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)** (procedure) and the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA)** (evidence). They replaced the IPC, CrPC and Indian Evidence Act. FIR rules are now in **Section 173 of the BNSS**.

steps.title: What an FIR is
steps.body:
An **FIR (First Information Report)** is the written record of information about a **cognizable offence** — a serious offence where police can arrest without a warrant and must investigate (e.g., theft, assault, robbery, cheating, kidnapping, sexual offences). Key points under BNSS Section 173:
- Information can be given **orally, in writing or electronically**. Oral information is written down and read over to you.
- An e-FIR/electronic information must be **signed by you within three days** to be taken on record.
- **Zero FIR**: you can report at **any police station**, regardless of where the crime happened; it is then transferred to the right station.
- You get a **free copy** of the FIR.
- For certain offences against women, statements are recorded by a woman officer, and special protections apply.

steps.title: What to say and check
steps.body:
Give: your name and contact, **what happened, when, where**, who was involved (names/descriptions), witnesses, property details (e.g., vehicle number, chassis/engine number, IMEI for phones), and any evidence (CCTV location, photos, messages).
Before signing: **read it fully**; make sure facts are correct and nothing is added that you didn’t say. Note the **FIR number, date and police station**. Keep calm and polite; ask for the officer’s name.

steps.title: If police refuse to register
steps.body:
1. Send the information in writing (by post/email) to the **Superintendent of Police / Commissioner** (BNSS Section 173(4)). Keep proof.
2. If still not registered, you may apply to the **Judicial Magistrate** (BNSS Section 175(3)), who can direct investigation.
3. For some offences punishable with 3–7 years’ imprisonment, BNSS allows police to do a **preliminary enquiry** (up to 14 days) before registering, with senior officer permission.
4. **Non-cognizable** offences (e.g., minor ones) are recorded differently; police need a magistrate’s order to investigate — they should still record your information and guide you.
For cyber fraud, call **1930** and file at **cybercrime.gov.in**.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For serious matters, contact a lawyer or free legal aid through Legal Services Authorities (NALSA helpline **15100**). In an emergency, call **112**.

a.text: Your phone was snatched near a bus stand in another police area. The nearest station officer says, ‘Not our jurisdiction, go there.’

choices.label: Politely ask them to register a Zero FIR and transfer it
choices.feedback: Correct — Zero FIR can be filed at any station.

choices.label: Give up and go home
choices.feedback: You lose evidence time and documentation needed for blocking and insurance.

choices.label: Send a written complaint to the Superintendent of Police, keeping proof, and use the state’s online e-FIR if available
choices.feedback: That’s the BNSS route (Section 173(4)).

choices.label: Argue loudly and threaten the officer
choices.feedback: Stay calm; use written legal routes.

meh.text: Restart calmly: file online if possible, or write to the SP. Also block the phone’s IMEI on Sanchar Saathi and inform your telecom provider.

good.text: Your FIR is registered and you have a free copy. You also blocked the phone via Sanchar Saathi.

quiz.q: Which law contains FIR rules today?
quiz.why: FIR rules are now in Section 173 of the BNSS 2023, which replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024. The IPC defines offences and the RTI Act deals with information, not FIR procedure.

quiz.q: A Zero FIR can be filed…
quiz.why: A Zero FIR can be registered at any police station regardless of where the crime happened, and is then transferred to the right station. It is not limited to lawyers or online filing.

quiz.q: Is the FIR copy free for the informant?
quiz.why: Yes. The informant is entitled to a free copy of the FIR. Charging for it is not allowed.

quiz.q: Police refuse to register an FIR for a cognizable offence. First escalation?
options: Write to the Superintendent of Police
quiz.why: If the police refuse to register an FIR for a cognizable offence, you can send the substance in writing to the Superintendent of Police under BNSS Section 173(4). Banks, social media or waiting do not compel registration.

quiz.q: An e-FIR must be signed by the informant within…
quiz.why: For an e-FIR, the informant must sign the information within 3 days under BNSS Section 173(1)(ii) so that it is formally recorded. Never signing or waiting a year would defeat that purpose.

sources: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023, Sections 173 and 175
Ministry of Home Affairs — new criminal laws

lessons.title: RTI: asking the government for information

story.title: Where did the road money go?

scenes.text: In a village in Rajasthan, a road was ‘completed’ on paper, but villagers still walk through mud.
Kamla Devi, a self-help-group leader, files an RTI asking for the sanctioned amount, contractor name, completion certificate and measurement book copies.
With no reply in 30 days, she files a first appeal. The documents arrive soon after.
The gram sabha discusses the gaps publicly; the work is redone. Information became power.

steps.title: The Right to Information Act 2005
steps.body:
Any **citizen of India** can request information from a **public authority** (government departments, local bodies, public sector bodies, and bodies substantially funded by government).
- Apply to the **Public Information Officer (PIO)** of that authority, in writing or online.
- **No need to give reasons** for asking.
- **Fee**: ₹10 for central government authorities (states set their own fees); **BPL** card holders are exempt.
- **Reply within 30 days**; within **48 hours** if it concerns someone’s **life or liberty**.
- Central ministries and many departments accept applications on the official **RTI Online** portal; many states have their own portals.

steps.title: Writing a good RTI
steps.body:
- Ask for **specific records**, not opinions: ‘Please provide certified copies of the work order, measurement book entries and completion certificate for the road from X to Y sanctioned in 2023–24’ — not ‘Why is the road bad?’
- Number your questions; keep them few and clear.
- Mention the period and location.
- Ask for inspection of files if useful.
- Keep copies of your application and fee proof.

steps.title: Appeals
steps.body:
- **First appeal**: if there’s no reply in 30 days or you’re unsatisfied, appeal to the **First Appellate Authority** (a senior officer in the same authority) within **30 days**.
- **Second appeal**: to the **Central or State Information Commission** within **90 days** of the first appeal decision (or the date it was due).
- Commissions can order disclosure and impose penalties on PIOs for unjustified delay or refusal.

steps.title: What can be refused
steps.body: Section 8 lists exemptions, such as information affecting national security or sovereignty, certain personal information with no public interest, information that would impede investigation, and cabinet papers before decisions. Even so, information that cannot be denied to Parliament or a State Legislature cannot be denied to a citizen. Private companies are not covered directly, but information about them held by a public authority (e.g., a regulator) may be.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Rules on fees and formats vary by state; check the relevant official portal.

activity.prompt: Good RTI question or poor RTI question?

items.text: Copies of attendance registers of the primary health centre for March 2025
Sanctioned amount and contractor name for ward 12 drain work, 2024–25
Status of my pension application no. 4567 with daily movement records
Tell me everything about the municipality

quiz.q: Time limit for an RTI reply normally?
quiz.why: An RTI reply is normally due within 30 days; where the information concerns life or liberty it is due within 48 hours. 7 days or 'no limit' is incorrect.

quiz.q: Fee for a central government RTI application?
quiz.why: The fee for a central government RTI application is ₹10, and people below the poverty line are exempt. It is not free for everyone and not ₹500 or ₹1,000.

quiz.q: Do you need to give reasons for an RTI request?
quiz.why: No. The RTI Act does not require you to give reasons for seeking information, so the authority cannot refuse for lack of a reason.

quiz.q: Second appeal goes to…
quiz.why: A second appeal under RTI goes to the Central or State Information Commission after the first appeal. Police and banks do not hear RTI appeals.

quiz.q: The best RTI asks for…
quiz.why: RTI gives access to records and information already held by a public authority, so the best request names specific records or documents. It cannot be used to ask for opinions, advice or predictions.

sources: Department of Personnel & Training — RTI guidance

lessons.title: Consumer complaints: from helpline to commission

scenes.text: Six weeks after buying a refrigerator in Jalandhar, Gurpreet’s compressor fails. The company keeps ‘escalating’ but never repairs it.
He registers a grievance with the National Consumer Helpline (1915). The company is contacted, but still no fix.
He files a complaint online with the District Consumer Commission, attaching the bill, warranty card and emails. No lawyer needed.
The commission orders replacement plus compensation for harassment and litigation costs.

steps.title: Your rights under the Consumer Protection Act 2019
steps.body: The Act protects anyone who buys goods or services for personal use (online or offline). Your rights include: **safety**, **information** (price, quality, quantity), **choice**, being **heard**, **redressal**, and **consumer education**. Problems covered include **defective goods**, **deficient services**, **unfair trade practices** (e.g., misleading claims), charging above MRP, and misleading advertisements. The Act also covers **e-commerce** and **product liability**.

steps.title: Step-by-step
steps.body:
1. **Complain to the seller/company in writing** (email, app, customer care) — keep ticket numbers.
2. Register with the **National Consumer Helpline: 1915**, the NCH app, or WhatsApp/website. NCH tries to resolve it with the company (a pre-litigation step).
3. If unresolved, send a **written notice** giving a deadline.
4. File a complaint with the **Consumer Commission** — online through the official e-Daakhil/e-Jagriti system or in person. You can file where **you live or work**, not only where the seller is.
5. Attach: bill/invoice, warranty, photos, emails, chat screenshots, and your requested relief (refund, replacement, compensation).

steps.title: Which commission?
steps.body:
Based on the **value of goods or services paid**:
- **District Commission**: up to ₹50 lakh
- **State Commission**: above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore
- **National Commission**: above ₹2 crore
Complaints generally must be filed within **2 years** of the problem arising. You can appear **yourself** — a lawyer isn’t required. Fees are small, and for low-value claims (up to ₹5 lakh) there is no fee.

steps.title: Other complaint channels
steps.body:
- **Banks/NBFCs/digital payments**: bank’s grievance cell, then **RBI Integrated Ombudsman** (online complaint management system).
- **Insurance**: insurer’s grievance cell, then IRDAI’s **Bima Bharosa** or the **Insurance Ombudsman**.
- **Investments**: SEBI **SCORES**.
- **Central government departments**: **CPGRAMS** (public grievance portal).
- **Telecom**: provider’s grievance and appellate channels.
Always keep reference numbers.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Limits and procedures may be updated; check the official consumer affairs portals.

activity.prompt: Match the problem to the right channel.
pairs: Bank wrongly charges fees and doesn’t reply

quiz.q: National Consumer Helpline number?
quiz.why: The National Consumer Helpline number is 1915. 100 is police, 1098 is Childline and 1930 is the cyber fraud helpline.

quiz.q: A ₹30,000 laptop dispute goes to the…
quiz.why: Under the 2019 Act, the District Commission handles claims up to ₹50 lakh, so a ₹30,000 laptop dispute goes there. State and National Commissions hear much larger claims.

quiz.q: Do you need a lawyer to file a consumer complaint?
quiz.why: No. Consumers may file and argue their own complaint without a lawyer, which keeps redress accessible.

quiz.q: Can you file in the district where you live?
options: No, only where the seller is
quiz.why: Yes. The 2019 Act lets you file where you reside or work, so you need not travel to where the seller is based.

quiz.q: General time limit for filing?
quiz.why: A consumer complaint must generally be filed within 2 years of the cause of action, though the Commission may excuse delay with sufficient reason. It is not unlimited or just one week.

sources: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District, State and National Commissions) Rules 2021

lessons.title: Free legal aid and writing an effective complaint

scenes.text: Shanta, a construction worker in Pune, hasn’t been paid for two months. She thinks lawyers are only for the rich.
A volunteer at a community centre tells her about free legal aid and the NALSA helpline 15100.
A paralegal helps her write a clear complaint with dates, amounts and witness names to the labour department.
The contractor is called for a hearing and pays her dues.

steps.title: Free legal aid in India
steps.body: Under the **Legal Services Authorities Act 1987**, free legal services are available through **NALSA** (national), **State**, **District** and **Taluk** Legal Services Authorities. Eligible groups include women and children, members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, persons with disabilities, victims of trafficking or disasters, industrial workmen, people in custody, and people below a set income limit. Services include advice, a lawyer, drafting and **Lok Adalats** (for settling disputes amicably). NALSA helpline: **15100**.

steps.title: The 5-part complaint letter
steps.body:
1. **To**: correct officer/authority and address.
2. **Subject**: one line (‘Complaint regarding non-payment of wages for May–June 2025’).
3. **Facts**: in date order — what, when, where, who, amounts.
4. **Evidence**: list attachments (bills, photos, messages, witness names).
5. **Request**: exactly what you want (payment, refund, action) and a reasonable deadline.
Sign, date, keep a copy, and get an acknowledgement (stamp, email reply or reference number).

steps.title: Tone and follow-up
steps.body: Be factual and polite; avoid insults or exaggeration — they weaken your case. Follow up on the date you mentioned. Escalate step by step: officer → senior officer → appellate/grievance authority → ombudsman/commission/court.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body:
- Paying ‘agents’ who promise quick results through contacts.
- Signing blank papers or documents you don’t understand.
- Missing deadlines (limitation periods).
- Sharing only on social media instead of official channels.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For your specific situation, contact your District Legal Services Authority or a lawyer.

activity.prompt: Arrange the parts of a strong complaint letter.

quiz.q: NALSA legal aid helpline number?
quiz.why: The NALSA legal aid helpline number is 15100. 1930 is for cyber fraud, 1915 for consumer issues and 181 for women's helpline.

quiz.q: Lok Adalats are for…
quiz.why: Lok Adalats settle disputes amicably through compromise, as an alternative dispute resolution forum under the Legal Services Authorities Act. They have nothing to do with passports, sports or elections.

quiz.q: Which makes a complaint stronger?
options: Facts in date order with evidence and a clear request
quiz.why: A strong complaint gives facts in date order, attaches evidence and makes a clear request. Insults, exaggeration or missing dates weaken it and make it easy to dismiss.

quiz.q: Which group is eligible for free legal aid?
quiz.why: Women and children are among the groups eligible for free legal aid, along with others such as people with low income and disabled persons. It is not limited to judges or companies.

questions.q: FIR stands for…
questions.why: FIR stands for First Information Report, the first written record of a cognizable offence given to the police. The other expansions are not real terms.

questions.q: Consumer helpline number?
questions.why: The National Consumer Helpline is 1915. 15100 is NALSA legal aid, 1098 is Childline and 112 is the emergency number.

questions.q: RTI lets citizens get…
questions.why: RTI lets citizens obtain information held by public authorities. It does not give money or passports, and it does not cover private company secrets.

questions.q: India’s new criminal procedure law (from 1 July 2024) is…
questions.why: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) replaced the CrPC as India's criminal procedure law from 1 July 2024. The IPC is the old penal code and RTI is an information law.

questions.q: Zero FIR means…
options: FIR filed at any police station regardless of jurisdiction, then transferred
questions.why: A Zero FIR is registered at any police station regardless of jurisdiction and then transferred to the proper station. It is not cancelled, online-only or valueless; its purpose is to stop jurisdiction excuses.

questions.q: RTI info about someone’s life or liberty must be given within…
questions.why: When RTI information concerns a person's life or liberty, it must be given within 48 hours, instead of the normal 30 days.

questions.q: Consumer dispute of ₹1.2 crore goes to…
questions.why: Under the 2019 Act, claims above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore go to the State Commission, so ₹1.2 crore falls there. District handles smaller claims and the National Commission larger ones.

questions.q: First RTI appeal is filed with…
options: First Appellate Authority in the same public authority
questions.why: The first RTI appeal goes to the First Appellate Authority, a senior officer in the same public authority, normally within 30 days. Consumer Commissions and police do not hear RTI appeals.

questions.q: For a bank’s unresolved complaint, escalate to…
questions.why: Banks are regulated by the RBI, so unresolved bank complaints go to the RBI Integrated Ombudsman. SEBI SCORES is for securities and IRDAI for insurance.

questions.q: Police refuse your FIR and the SP doesn’t act. Next legal step under BNSS?
questions.why: If the police and the SP do not act, you can approach the Judicial Magistrate under BNSS Section 175(3), who can order an investigation. An RTI alone cannot force registration, and giving up or bribing is wrong.

questions.q: Which RTI request is most likely to succeed?
options: ‘Certified copies of the hospital’s medicine stock register for June 2025’
questions.why: RTI works best when you ask for specific existing records, such as certified copies of a stock register for a given month. Questions asking 'why', private life or predictions are not information the authority holds.

questions.q: An e-commerce seller sold a fake branded watch for ₹8,000 and refuses refund. Best path?
options: Written complaint to platform → NCH 1915 → District Commission online with evidence
questions.why: Redress is graduated: complain to the platform in writing, call the National Consumer Helpline 1915, then file online with the District Commission with evidence. An RTI does not apply to a private seller.

questions.q: Which statement is legally accurate in 2026?
options: BNSS Section 173 governs FIRs, and e-FIR information must be signed within three days
questions.why: BNSS Section 173 governs FIRs now, and e-FIR information must be signed within three days. The IPC defines offences, not FIR procedure, and Zero FIR continues to exist.

questions.q: A daily-wage worker can’t afford a lawyer for a wage dispute. The best combined advice?
options: Contact District Legal Services Authority/NALSA 15100 for free aid, write a dated complaint to the labour department with evidence
questions.why: A worker who cannot afford a lawyer can get free aid from the District Legal Services Authority or NALSA (15100) and send a dated written complaint with evidence to the labour department. Agents or social media posts do not secure a remedy.

courses.title: Being an active citizen: vote, local government, rights and duties
courses.summary: How voting works (EVM, VVPAT, NOTA), how panchayats and municipalities work and how to get things fixed, your Fundamental Rights and Duties, and the helplines every Indian should know.
outcomes: Learners can describe the voting process and tools like VVPAT, NOTA and cVIGIL
Learners can explain the roles of gram sabha, panchayat and municipality
Learners can name the six groups of Fundamental Rights and some Fundamental Duties
Learners can raise a civic complaint effectively
Learners know India’s key helplines

lessons.title: How voting works

scenes.text: Rukmini Nani, 82, in Mysuru has voted in every election since she was young. This year she takes her grandson Kiran, voting for the first time.
At the booth, an officer checks Kiran’s name in the roll, marks his finger with indelible ink and he signs the register.
He presses the button next to his chosen candidate on the EVM and watches the VVPAT window show the slip for 7 seconds.
Outside, Nani says: ‘Your one vote counts exactly as much as a minister’s.’

steps.title: Before polling day
steps.body:
- Check your name in the **electoral roll** (ECI services portal or Voter Helpline app) and find your **polling station**.
- Learn about candidates: ECI publishes candidate **affidavits** (criminal cases, assets, education) — see the ‘Know Your Candidate’ information.
- The **Model Code of Conduct** applies from the announcement of elections; citizens can report violations (like distributing cash or liquor) through ECI’s **cVIGIL** app.

steps.title: At the polling booth
steps.body:
1. Stand in the queue (separate queues may exist; senior citizens and persons with disabilities get facilitation).
2. First polling officer checks your name and ID.
3. Second officer marks your **left forefinger with indelible ink**, you sign/thumb the register, and get a slip.
4. Third officer activates the **EVM** ballot unit.
5. Press the blue button next to your choice; a beep confirms.
6. The **VVPAT** shows a printed slip with the candidate’s serial number, name and symbol for about 7 seconds, then it drops into a sealed box.
Your vote is **secret**. Phones are generally not allowed inside the booth.

steps.title: NOTA
steps.body: **NOTA (None of the Above)** has been on EVMs since 2013 after a Supreme Court judgment. It lets you formally record that you reject all candidates. Under current rules, the candidate with the most votes still wins even if NOTA gets more votes; NOTA is a way to express your view while keeping your vote secret.

steps.title: Voting well
steps.body: Judge candidates on their record, promises you can check, and integrity — not on gifts, caste or religion appeals. Accepting money or gifts for votes is an electoral offence. Encourage first-time voters and help elders get to the booth.

activity.prompt: Put the polling-booth steps in order.
items: Officer checks your name in the roll and your ID
Indelible ink on your left forefinger and signature in the register
Press the button next to your choice
Check the VVPAT slip shown for about 7 seconds

quiz.q: VVPAT lets a voter…
options: See a printed slip confirming their choice
quiz.why: VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) shows a printed slip of your choice for a few seconds so you can check the machine recorded it correctly. You cannot take it home or change your vote.

quiz.q: NOTA means…
quiz.why: NOTA stands for None of the Above, giving voters the option to reject all candidates. The other expansions are not real.

quiz.q: Which app lets citizens report Model Code of Conduct violations?
quiz.why: cVIGIL is the Election Commission of India's app for citizens to report Model Code of Conduct violations with photos or videos. mAadhaar, BHIM and IRCTC serve other purposes.

quiz.q: Accepting money for your vote is…
quiz.why: Taking money for your vote is bribery, which is an electoral offence. It undermines free and fair elections.

sources: PUCL v. Union of India (2013) — NOTA

lessons.title: Local government: getting the streetlight fixed

scenes.text: In a ward of Bhopal, the lane to the bus stop has been dark for months. Girls avoid it after 7 pm.
College student Ayaan photographs the broken poles, notes their numbers and files a complaint on the municipal corporation’s app.
When nothing happens, he and neighbours attend the ward committee meeting with a signed letter and photos, and meet their councillor.
Two weeks later the lights are repaired. They keep the complaint number to report if it fails again.

steps.title: Three levels of government
steps.body:
- **Union** (central) government — defence, railways, currency, etc.
- **State** governments — police, health, agriculture, etc.
- **Local** governments — created as constitutional bodies by the **73rd (panchayats)** and **74th (municipalities) Amendments of 1992**.
Rural areas generally have a three-tier **Panchayati Raj** (gram panchayat, block/panchayat samiti, zila parishad). Urban areas have **municipal corporations**, **municipal councils** and **nagar panchayats**, divided into **wards** with elected councillors. Seats are reserved for women, SCs and STs (at least one-third for women; many states reserve 50%).

steps.title: Gram sabha and ward committees
steps.body: The **gram sabha** is all registered voters of a village panchayat area. It can discuss plans, approve beneficiary lists and conduct **social audits** of schemes like MGNREGA. In cities, **ward committees** and **area sabhas** (where states have created them) let residents raise issues. Attending these meetings is one of the most powerful things a citizen can do.

steps.title: Getting a civic problem fixed
steps.body:
1. **Identify** the responsible body (municipality for streetlights, garbage, drains; state electricity board for power supply; PWD for some roads).
2. **Document**: photos, exact location, pole numbers, dates.
3. **Complain** on the official app/helpline/portal; note the complaint number.
4. **Follow up** after the promised time; escalate to the ward officer or councillor.
5. **Organise**: a joint letter from residents carries weight.
6. **RTI** if needed to learn the status or budget.
7. For central government departments, use **CPGRAMS**.

steps.title: Be a constructive citizen
steps.body: Be specific and polite, propose solutions, and say thank you when things work. Combine complaints with your own action: segregate waste, don’t dump debris, report water leaks, plant and protect trees.

activity.prompt: Match the problem to who is usually responsible.
pairs: Garbage not collected in a city ward
Approving MGNREGA social audit in a village

quiz.q: Which amendment created constitutional status for panchayats?
quiz.why: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992) gave panchayats constitutional status. The 74th covers municipalities, the 42nd and 86th deal with other matters and the 101st is GST.

quiz.q: The gram sabha consists of…
options: All registered voters of the village panchayat area
quiz.why: The gram sabha is the village assembly made up of all registered voters in the village panchayat area. It is not just the sarpanch, MLAs or officers.

quiz.q: Best first step for a broken streetlight?
options: Complain on the official municipal app/helpline with photos and note the number
quiz.why: The best first step is to complain through the official municipal app or helpline with photos and keep the complaint number, so it can be tracked and escalated. Waiting, DIY wiring or only posting online will not get it fixed.

quiz.q: CPGRAMS is for grievances against…
quiz.why: CPGRAMS is the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System for complaints against central government departments. It does not handle neighbours or private shops.

sources: Constitution of India — Parts IX and IXA

lessons.title: Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties

scenes.text: Lakshmi, 13, from a fishing family in Kanyakumari, is told by a private school guard that ‘children like you don’t study here’.
Her civics teacher explains the right to equality and the Right to Education, including reserved seats in many private schools for children from weaker sections.
With help from a local NGO, her mother applies through the official admission process. Lakshmi gets a seat.
In class, Lakshmi reads the Fundamental Duties and volunteers for a beach clean-up — ‘rights and duties go together’.

steps.title: Six groups of Fundamental Rights (Part III)
steps.body:
1. **Right to Equality** (Articles 14–18): equality before law, no discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, equal opportunity in public jobs, abolition of untouchability.
2. **Right to Freedom** (19–22): speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession (with reasonable restrictions); **Article 21** — life and personal liberty; **21A** — free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14; protection in arrest.
3. **Right against Exploitation** (23–24): no trafficking or forced labour; no child labour in hazardous work.
4. **Right to Freedom of Religion** (25–28).
5. **Cultural and Educational Rights** (29–30).
6. **Right to Constitutional Remedies** (32): approach the Supreme Court for enforcement (High Courts under Article 226).

steps.title: Rights have limits
steps.body: Most rights have **reasonable restrictions** — for example, free speech doesn’t include defamation, incitement to violence or threats. Rights mostly protect you against the **State**; some, like the ban on untouchability and child labour, also apply to private persons. Courts have interpreted Article 21 widely to include rights like privacy, dignity, a clean environment and legal aid.

steps.title: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A)
steps.body: Added in 1976, with an 11th duty in 2002. They include: respect the Constitution, the National Flag and Anthem; uphold unity and integrity; promote harmony and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women; protect the environment and have compassion for living creatures; develop scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry; safeguard public property and abjure violence; strive towards excellence; and (for parents/guardians) provide opportunities for education to children aged 6–14.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. If your rights are violated, you can seek help from legal aid (NALSA 15100), human rights commissions, child rights commissions, or the courts.

activity.prompt: Fundamental Right or Fundamental Duty?

items.text: Approach the Supreme Court to enforce rights

quiz.q: Article 21 protects…
quiz.why: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, and courts have read it widely to include dignity and privacy. Property, taxes and voting are covered elsewhere.

quiz.q: Article 21A guarantees free education for ages…
quiz.why: Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years. Younger and older age groups are not covered by this article.

quiz.q: Fundamental Duties are in…
quiz.why: Fundamental Duties are listed in Article 51A, in Part IVA of the Constitution. Article 32 is about remedies and Article 370 was about Jammu and Kashmir.

quiz.q: Article 32 lets you…
options: Approach the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights
quiz.why: Article 32 gives the right to approach the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights. It is the right to constitutional remedies and has nothing to do with passports, voting or tax.

sources: Constitution of India — Parts III and IVA
NCERT Political Science — Indian Constitution at Work

lessons.title: Helplines every Indian should know

scenes.text: After a confusing night when her grandfather fell and the family didn’t know whom to call, Divya, 14, in Siliguri makes a list for the fridge.
She checks every number on official websites and adds what each is for.
Months later, her grandfather receives a ‘digital arrest’ call. He looks at the list and calls 1930 instead of paying.
Divya’s list now hangs in every flat on her floor.

steps.title: Emergencies
steps.body:
- **112**: single emergency number (police, fire, ambulance)
- **101**: fire · **108**: ambulance in many states · **102**: ambulance/maternal transport in many states
- **1906**: LPG emergency
- **1077 / 1070**: district / state disaster control rooms in many states

steps.title: Protection and support
steps.body:
- **1098**: Childline — children in need of care and protection
- **181**: Women helpline in many states
- **14567**: Elderline — national helpline for senior citizens
- **14416** (or 1-800-891-4416): **Tele-MANAS** — free mental health support, 24×7
- **15100**: NALSA free legal aid

steps.title: Money, consumer and cyber
steps.body:
- **1930**: National Cyber Crime Helpline (fraud) + cybercrime.gov.in
- **1915**: National Consumer Helpline
- Your bank’s official helpline (from the back of your card or the official app)
- **Chakshu** on Sanchar Saathi for reporting suspected fraud calls/messages

steps.title: Make your own list
steps.body: Add personal numbers: family doctor, nearest hospital, local police station, building security, a neighbour, and an out-of-town relative. Save them in your phone **and** on paper. Teach children to dial 112 and say their address.

activity.prompt: Match the helpline to its purpose.

quiz.q: A child is being abused at home. Which number?
quiz.why: Childline 1098 is the helpline for children in distress, including abuse; in immediate danger call 112. 1915 is consumer, 1906 is LPG and 15100 is legal aid.

quiz.q: An elderly neighbour needs advice on pension and abuse issues. Call…
quiz.why: 14567 is Elderline, which gives advice and support to senior citizens on pensions and abuse. 1906 is LPG, 101 is fire and 1930 is cyber fraud.

quiz.q: Someone feels overwhelmed and anxious for weeks. A free helpline is…
quiz.why: Tele-MANAS (14416) is the free national mental-health helpline for people feeling anxious or overwhelmed. Consumer, ambulance and disaster lines do not offer counselling.

quiz.q: Why also keep numbers on paper?
options: Phones can die or be lost
quiz.why: Phones can run out of charge, break or be lost, so numbers kept on paper are a backup in emergencies. Paper is not legally required.

sources: Ministry of Women and Child Development

questions.q: Minimum voting age in India?
questions.why: The minimum voting age in India is 18 years. 21 was the earlier age, lowered by the 61st Amendment in 1988.

questions.q: Single emergency number?
questions.why: 112 is India's single emergency number for police, fire and ambulance. 14416 is mental health, 1098 is Childline and 1915 is consumer help.

questions.q: Indelible ink is applied on…
questions.why: Indelible ink is applied on the left forefinger of the voter to show they have voted and prevent repeat voting.

questions.q: 74th Amendment relates to…
questions.why: The 74th Amendment deals with municipalities, meaning urban local bodies. The 73rd is the one about panchayats.

questions.q: VVPAT slip is visible for about…
questions.why: The VVPAT slip is visible through a glass window for about 7 seconds before it falls into a sealed box, so the voter can verify the choice.

questions.q: Right to Education is in Article…
questions.why: The Right to Education is in Article 21A. Article 32 is constitutional remedies, 51A is fundamental duties and 14 is equality before law.

questions.q: Which is a Fundamental Duty?
questions.why: Developing scientific temper is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(h). Property, movement and voting are rights, not duties.

questions.q: If NOTA gets the most votes, under current rules…
options: The candidate with most votes still wins
questions.why: Under current rules, NOTA votes are counted but do not decide the result; the candidate with the most votes among the actual candidates still wins. No fresh election is automatic.

questions.q: Social audits of MGNREGA are done in the…
questions.why: Social audits of MGNREGA works are carried out in the gram sabha, the village assembly, so villagers can review records and spending. The RBI, Supreme Court and Lok Sabha do not do this.

questions.q: Fundamental Rights are mainly enforceable against…
questions.why: Fundamental Rights are mainly enforceable against the State and its authorities, though some also apply against private persons. They are not enforceable against foreign governments.

questions.q: Best strategy for an unresolved ward problem after an app complaint failed?
options: Follow up with complaint number, escalate to ward officer/councillor, joint residents’ letter, RTI if needed
questions.why: After a failed app complaint, quote the complaint number, escalate to the ward officer or councillor, send a joint residents' letter and use RTI if needed. This documented, collective approach works; vandalism or giving up does not.

questions.q: Free speech in India includes…
options: Expression subject to reasonable restrictions such as defamation and incitement
questions.why: Free speech under Article 19(1)(a) is subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2), such as defamation and incitement to violence. It is neither absolute nor limited to praising the government.

questions.q: Which combination best describes active citizenship?
options: Informed voting, attending gram/area sabhas, using RTI/grievance systems, performing duties like protecting public property
questions.why: Active citizenship goes beyond voting: informed voting, attending gram or area sabhas, using RTI and grievance systems, and performing duties like protecting public property. Voting alone or only online complaining is not enough.

questions.q: A first-time voter sees cash being distributed the night before polling. Most effective action?
options: Report via cVIGIL with photo/video and location; don’t confront violently
questions.why: Report cash distribution through cVIGIL with photo or video and location, so the ECI can act quickly, and do not confront anyone violently. Taking the cash is an offence and rumours or ignoring it help nobody.

life-digital.title: Digital life, safely
life-digital.description: Passwords, two-factor authentication and device safety; scams, digital arrest frauds, deepfakes and sextortion; privacy, social media and your mental health.

courses.title: Lock it down: passwords, 2FA and devices
courses.summary: Make passwords that are strong and memorable, turn on two-factor authentication, secure your phone, and know exactly what to do if an account is hacked or a phone is lost.
outcomes: Learners can create long, unique passphrases and use a password manager
Learners can explain 2FA, OTPs, authenticator apps, backup codes and passkeys
Learners can secure a phone with updates, permissions, locks and backups
Learners can follow a step-by-step recovery plan after a hack or lost phone

lessons.title: Passwords that are strong and memorable

scenes.text: Aarav, 15, in Lucknow uses ‘Aarav@2010’ for his game account, email and Instagram.
A gaming site he once joined is hacked and its password list leaks online.
Within days, someone logs into his email and Instagram using the same password and starts messaging his friends for money.
His sister Mahi helps him reset everything with different long passphrases saved in a password manager.

steps.title: How passwords get stolen
steps.body:
- **Data breaches**: a website is hacked and its password list leaks. Attackers then try the same email + password on other sites (**credential stuffing**).
- **Guessing**: computers can try billions of combinations; short or common passwords (123456, name+birth year, ‘password’) fall in seconds.
- **Phishing**: fake login pages trick you into typing your password.
- **Shoulder surfing** or sharing with friends.

steps.title: Length beats complexity: the passphrase
steps.body:
A **passphrase** is several random words joined together, for example: **‘mango-river-bicycle-cloud-47’**. It is long (hard for computers), and easy to picture (easy for you).
- Use at least **4–5 random words** or **14+ characters**.
- Avoid song lyrics, famous quotes, names, birthdays, pet names, phone numbers.
- **‘P@ssw0rd!’** looks complex but is in every hacker’s list.

steps.title: One account, one password
steps.body:
Reusing a password means one breach unlocks everything. The most important accounts — **email** (it resets all others), **banking/UPI** and **phone/cloud account** — must have unique, strong passwords.
A **password manager** (a reputable app, or the one built into your phone or browser) creates and remembers a unique password for every site; you remember just one strong master passphrase. Some services let you check whether your email appeared in known breaches.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing passwords on a sticky note on the laptop.
- Saving passwords in a plain notes app or WhatsApp chat to yourself.
- Sharing passwords with a best friend or partner (relationships change).
- Logging in on shared/cyber-café computers and forgetting to log out.
- Changing ‘Password1’ to ‘Password2’.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick your email account. Create a new passphrase of 5 random words (open a book to random pages for words if you like), change it now, and turn on 2FA (next lesson).

activity.prompt: Strong or weak password?

items.text: A unique 20-character password made by a password manager

quiz.q: Which makes a password hardest to crack?
quiz.why: Length makes a password hard to crack because each extra character multiplies the possible combinations. Several random words are long and hard to guess, unlike pet names, birthdays or simple @ swaps.

quiz.q: Why is reusing passwords dangerous?
options: One breach unlocks all your accounts
quiz.why: If you reuse a password, one breach lets attackers try it on all your other accounts. Websites do not forbid reuse; the danger is real.

quiz.q: Which account needs the strongest unique password first?
quiz.why: Your email account needs the strongest, unique password first because it can be used to reset the passwords of all your other accounts. A recipe blog or quiz site holds little of value.

quiz.q: A password manager…
options: Creates and remembers unique passwords behind one master passphrase
Stores passwords in plain text for anyone
quiz.why: A password manager creates and remembers unique passwords for each account behind one strong master passphrase, so you need not reuse any. It does not store them in plain text or share them.

lessons.title: Two-factor authentication, OTPs and passkeys

scenes.text: Mrs. Fernandes, 64, in Goa gets a call: ‘Ma’am, I’m from your bank. To stop your card being blocked, read me the OTP we just sent.’
The SMS says: ‘OTP for transaction of ₹49,999… Do not share with anyone, including bank staff.’
She remembers her grandson’s rule: ‘An OTP is like a house key. Nobody genuine ever asks for it.’ She hangs up.
She calls the bank’s number from the back of her card. Her account was never at risk — the caller was a fraudster.

steps.title: What 2FA is
steps.body:
**Two-factor authentication (2FA)** — also called multi-factor (MFA) or two-step verification — asks for two different kinds of proof:
- **Something you know**: password or PIN
- **Something you have**: phone, OTP, security key
- **Something you are**: fingerprint, face
Even if a criminal steals your password, they can’t log in without the second factor. Turning on 2FA for email, social media, cloud and banking blocks most account takeovers.

steps.title: Types of second factor (weakest to strongest)
steps.body:
- **SMS OTP**: much better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM-swap fraud and to people tricking you into sharing it.
- **Authenticator app** (time-based codes that change every 30 seconds): stronger; works without network.
- **Push approval** in an app: convenient, but never approve a login you didn’t start (‘MFA fatigue’ attacks spam you with prompts).
- **Passkeys and hardware security keys**: strongest; they resist phishing because they only work on the real website. Many big services now support passkeys that use your phone’s fingerprint or face unlock.

steps.title: The OTP rule
steps.body: **An OTP is only for you to type into a website or app you opened yourself.** No bank, police, courier, telecom company, delivery person or ‘customer care’ will ever need it. If someone asks for an OTP, it’s a scam — 100% of the time. Also read OTP messages fully: they often say what the OTP will authorise (a payment, a login, a SIM change).

steps.title: Backup codes
steps.body: When you turn on 2FA, services usually give **backup/recovery codes**. Print or write them and keep them somewhere safe (not in the same phone). If you lose your phone, these let you back in. Also keep your recovery email and phone number up to date.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Open your email account’s security settings. Turn on 2-step verification, add an authenticator app or passkey if possible, and save backup codes on paper.

statements.s: A bank employee may ask for your OTP to stop your card being blocked.
statements.why: Banks never ask for OTPs. It is always a scam.

statements.s: With 2FA on, a stolen password alone is usually not enough to log in.
statements.why: The second factor stops the attacker.

statements.s: Authenticator apps are generally safer than SMS OTPs.
statements.why: They are not exposed to SIM-swap and SMS interception.

statements.s: If you get a login approval prompt you didn’t start, you should approve it to make it stop.
statements.why: Deny it and change your password — someone has it.

statements.s: Backup codes should be stored somewhere other than your phone.
statements.why: So you can recover if the phone is lost.

quiz.q: Which is ‘something you have’?
quiz.why: 'Something you have' is a possession factor, such as your phone receiving a code. A password, birthday or favourite colour is something you know.

quiz.q: Who can you share an OTP with?
options: Nobody — only type it into a site/app you opened
quiz.why: Never share an OTP with anyone; only type it into the site or app you opened yourself. Real banks, police and delivery staff do not need your OTP, and anyone asking is likely a scammer.

quiz.q: Which second factor resists phishing best?
quiz.why: A passkey or security key resists phishing because it works only on the genuine website. SMS codes, email links and security questions can be tricked out of you on a fake page.

quiz.q: You get 10 login approval prompts at midnight. You should…
options: Deny all, change password, check account activity
quiz.why: Many unexpected approval prompts mean someone already has your password and is pushing to get in. Deny them all, change your password and review account activity; approving one lets them in.

lessons.title: Securing your phone and laptop

scenes.text: Ritu, 20, in Indore downloads a ‘free movies’ APK file shared on a Telegram group.
It asks for permission to read SMS, access contacts and ‘display over other apps’. She taps Allow on everything.
Two days later, ₹12,000 is withdrawn using OTPs she never saw — the app was reading her SMS.
Her friend Danish shows her how to remove the app, check permissions and keep updates on. She reports the fraud at 1930 quickly.

steps.title: Five basic protections
steps.body:
1. **Updates**: install system and app updates promptly; they fix security holes.
2. **Screen lock**: PIN (6+ digits) or passphrase plus fingerprint/face. Avoid simple patterns.
3. **Official app stores only**: don’t install APK files from links, WhatsApp or Telegram; check developer name, reviews and downloads.
4. **Permissions**: give only what makes sense — a torch app doesn’t need contacts or SMS. Review permissions every few months.
5. **Find my device**: turn it on so you can locate, lock or erase a lost phone.

steps.title: Dangerous permissions to question
steps.body:
- **SMS** access (can read OTPs)
- **Accessibility** service (can see and tap on your screen)
- **Display over other apps** (can place fake screens over banking apps)
- **Device admin** (hard to uninstall)
- **Screen-sharing / remote-access** apps installed on a stranger’s instruction
If an app you don’t trust has these, uninstall it and change banking/email passwords from a safe device.

steps.title: Backups: the 3-2-1 idea
steps.body: Keep **3 copies** of important data (photos, documents), on **2 different types** of storage (phone + laptop/external drive), with **1 copy off-site** (cloud backup). If your phone is stolen, dropped in water or hit by ransomware, you lose nothing important.

steps.title: Public Wi-Fi and SIM safety
steps.body:
- On public Wi-Fi, avoid banking; use mobile data or a trusted VPN. Websites with HTTPS encrypt traffic, but fake hotspots exist.
- Set a **SIM PIN** so a stolen SIM can’t be used in another phone.
- If your phone suddenly loses network for a long time without reason and you get alerts about SIM change, contact your telecom provider immediately — it could be a **SIM-swap** attempt.
- The government’s **Sanchar Saathi** portal lets you check mobile connections registered in your name and request blocking of a lost/stolen phone.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Go to Settings → Apps → Permissions on your phone. Find which apps can read SMS and which have accessibility access. Remove any that don’t need it.

activity.prompt: Phone security check-up
items: System updated to the latest version
Screen lock set (6+ digit PIN or passphrase)
No apps installed from unknown links
Checked connections in my name on Sanchar Saathi

quiz.q: Why install updates promptly?
options: They fix security holes attackers use
quiz.why: Updates fix security holes that attackers use, so installing them promptly keeps your device protected. The other reasons given are not true.

quiz.q: A torch app asks for SMS access. You…
quiz.why: A torch app has no reason to read SMS, which suggests malware that could steal OTPs. Deny the permission and consider uninstalling it.

quiz.q: The 3-2-1 backup rule means…
quiz.why: The 3-2-1 rule means keeping 3 copies of data on 2 types of storage with 1 copy off-site. This redundancy protects against loss, theft or disaster.

quiz.q: Which government portal helps check mobile connections in your name and block lost phones?
quiz.why: Sanchar Saathi, run by the Department of Telecommunications, lets you check mobile connections in your name and block lost phones. DigiLocker stores documents and e-Daakhil is for consumer cases.

lessons.title: Hacked or lost phone: the recovery plan

scenes.text: Kunal, 19, a dance creator in Delhi with 20,000 followers, gets an email saying his account email was changed.
Minutes later, his account posts crypto ads and DMs his followers asking for money.
His friend Sara, who works in IT, walks him through a calm recovery: secure email first, use the platform’s official recovery, warn followers from another account.
In two days he has the account back, with 2FA and a passkey. He now checks ‘where you’re logged in’ monthly.

steps.title: Signs you may be hacked
steps.body:
- Emails about password or email changes you didn’t make
- Friends receive messages you didn’t send
- Unknown logins, devices or locations in security settings
- Unknown transactions
- Phone suddenly slow, hot, full of pop-ups, or new apps you didn’t install

steps.title: Step-by-step recovery
steps.body:
1. **From a clean device**, change the password of your **email first**, then the affected account.
2. Use **official recovery** pages only (not DMs offering ‘recovery services’ — those are scams).
3. **Sign out of all sessions/devices** in security settings.
4. Check and fix **recovery email/phone**, and remove unknown linked apps.
5. **Turn on 2FA** (authenticator or passkey).
6. **Warn contacts** that messages from you may be fake.
7. If money is involved: call **1930** and your bank immediately; report at **cybercrime.gov.in**.
8. Scan/clean your device; if it’s badly infected, back up data and factory reset.

steps.title: Lost or stolen phone
steps.body:
1. Use **find my device** to locate, lock or erase it.
2. Call your telecom provider to **block the SIM** and get a replacement SIM.
3. Ask your bank to block UPI/mobile banking if the phone was unlocked or you fear misuse.
4. File a police complaint (many states allow online lost-property reports).
5. Use **Sanchar Saathi (CEIR)** to request blocking of the phone’s IMEI so it can’t be used on Indian networks; it can be unblocked if recovered.
6. Change passwords of email and important apps.

steps.title: Avoid second scams
steps.body: After a hack, fake ‘recovery experts’ and ‘cyber police’ often contact victims promising to get money or accounts back for a fee. Genuine police don’t charge fees and official platforms don’t recover accounts through DMs. Report only through official portals and helplines.

steps.title: Prepare before it happens
steps.body: Keep backup codes on paper, know your IMEI (dial *#06#) and write it down, keep recovery email and phone updated, and save 1930 in your contacts.

a.text: You get an alert: ‘Your email recovery phone number was changed.’ You didn’t do it.

choices.label: Ignore it — probably a glitch
choices.feedback: Changes to recovery details are a classic first step in takeovers.

choices.label: Immediately log in from a trusted device, change password, restore your number, sign out other sessions
choices.feedback: Fast action stops the attacker.

b.text: You’re back in. A DM arrives: ‘I’m a certified hacker, I can secure your accounts for ₹2,000.’

choices.label: Pay — they sound professional
choices.feedback: These ‘recovery’ offers are scams.

choices.label: Ignore and block; turn on 2FA and check linked apps
choices.feedback: Correct.

bad.text: The attacker or scammer gains more control. Use official recovery pages, report at cybercrime.gov.in, and call 1930 if money is involved.

good.text: Account secured with 2FA. You also warned your contacts. Well handled.

quiz.q: Which account should you secure first after a hack?
quiz.why: Secure your email first after a hack, because it can reset the passwords of all your other accounts. Music, food and gaming accounts matter less.

quiz.q: How do you find your phone’s IMEI?
quiz.why: Dial *#06# on your phone to display its IMEI number. The IMEI is not your phone number and you should not ask a stranger or look at the charger.

quiz.q: A DM offers paid ‘account recovery’. This is…
quiz.why: A DM offering paid 'account recovery' is likely a scam. Recover accounts only through the platform's official channels, which do not charge you through random messages.

quiz.q: After money is stolen through a hacked account, call…
quiz.why: If money is stolen through a hacked account, call 1930 (the cyber fraud helpline) and your bank immediately, since quick reports help freeze funds. 101 is fire and 1906 is LPG.

questions.q: Which is the strongest password?
questions.why: A long, random passphrase like guitar-monsoon-lemon-rocket-19 is hardest to crack. Names with years, 12345678 and Password! are common guesses.

questions.q: Should you share an OTP with a bank official on the phone?
questions.why: No. Never share an OTP with anyone, even someone claiming to be a bank official; real banks never ask for it.

questions.q: Install apps from…
questions.why: Install apps only from official app stores, which check apps for malware. Random APK links, unknown websites and Telegram groups carry a much higher risk.

questions.q: 2FA protects because…
options: It needs a second proof beyond the password
questions.why: Two-factor authentication requires a second proof beyond the password, so a stolen password alone is not enough. It does not remove passwords or scan for viruses.
