questions.q: Credential stuffing is…
options: Trying leaked passwords on other sites
questions.why: Credential stuffing is when attackers try leaked passwords on other sites, which works if you reuse passwords. That is why each account needs a unique password.

questions.q: Which permission is most dangerous for an unknown app?
questions.why: Accessibility service is the most dangerous permission for an unknown app because it can read and control your screen. Vibration, camera for a camera app and internet for a browser are normal.

questions.q: A phone loses network unexpectedly for hours and you get a SIM-change alert. Likely risk?
questions.why: Sudden loss of network for hours plus a SIM-change alert points to SIM-swap fraud, where criminals take over your number to get OTPs. Contact your telecom provider immediately.

questions.q: 3-2-1 backup means 1 copy is…
questions.why: In the 3-2-1 rule, one copy is kept off-site, such as in the cloud, so theft, fire or damage at home does not destroy all your copies.

questions.q: Which is the best order after a hack?
options: Secure email → change affected password → sign out all sessions → enable 2FA → warn contacts
Post about it, then change password
questions.why: Secure your email first, then change the affected password, sign out all sessions, enable 2FA and warn contacts. Securing the root account first stops attackers from resetting everything else.

questions.q: Why are passkeys phishing-resistant?
options: They are bound to the genuine website and can’t be typed into a fake page
questions.why: Passkeys use cryptographic keys bound to the genuine website, so they cannot be typed into or used on a fake page. They are not SMS codes or longer passwords.

questions.q: ‘MFA fatigue’ attack means…
options: Spamming approval prompts hoping you tap Approve
questions.why: MFA fatigue is when attackers spam approval prompts hoping you tap Approve just to stop them. Never approve a prompt you did not start.

questions.q: Phone stolen, unlocked, UPI app on it. Most urgent pair of actions?
options: Block SIM with telecom and block UPI/mobile banking with bank; then IMEI block via CEIR and police report
questions.why: For a stolen unlocked phone, first cut access to money and OTPs: block the SIM with the telecom provider and UPI/mobile banking with the bank. Then block the IMEI through CEIR and file a police report.

questions.q: Which setup gives the best protection for a primary email account?
options: Same password as bank for easy memory
Unique long passphrase in a password manager + passkey/authenticator 2FA + backup codes on paper
questions.why: A unique long passphrase in a password manager, plus passkey or authenticator 2FA and paper backup codes, gives layered, phishing-resistant protection. Reused, short or SMS-only protection is weak.

courses.title: Scams, digital arrest, deepfakes & sextortion
courses.summary: How scammers hook people, India’s most common frauds (digital arrest, parcel, task/job, KYC), how to check deepfakes and voice clones, and what to do about online blackmail.
outcomes: Learners can name the psychological triggers scams use
Learners can recognise digital arrest, parcel, task and KYC frauds
Learners can verify a suspicious call or video using a second channel and a family code word
Learners know sextortion is never the victim’s fault and exactly how to report it
Learners can report fraud through 1930, cybercrime.gov.in and Chakshu
courses.guardianNote: Lesson 4 explains online blackmail (sextortion) in calm, non-explicit language: what it is, that it is never the victim’s fault, not to pay, how to keep evidence and where to report (1930, cybercrime.gov.in, 1098 for under-18s). No images or explicit descriptions. Teenagers are frequent targets, so knowing this protects them.

lessons.title: How scams hook you: the four triggers

scenes.text: Gopal, 58, a shopkeeper in Varanasi, gets an SMS: ‘Congratulations! You won ₹25 lakh in a lucky draw. Pay ₹4,999 processing fee.’
A ‘manager’ calls: ‘Pay within 2 hours or the prize goes to the next winner.’
His granddaughter Diya asks: ‘Dadaji, did you buy a ticket?’ He hadn’t.
They report the number via the Chakshu facility on Sanchar Saathi. Gopal now pauses before any ‘urgent’ money request.

steps.title: Scams work on emotions, not intelligence
steps.body:
Clever, educated people are scammed every day. Scammers use four triggers:
- **Urgency**: ‘in 30 minutes’, ‘today only’.
- **Authority**: pretending to be police, bank, CBI, courier, telecom, your boss.
- **Fear**: arrest, account block, power cut, a relative in trouble.
- **Greed or hope**: prize, job, high returns, cashback, romance.
When you feel a strong emotion plus pressure to act fast, that is your signal to **stop**.

steps.title: Spotting phishing links and messages
steps.body:
- Check the **sender**: banks use official short codes; random mobile numbers are a warning.
- Look carefully at **web addresses**: ‘sbi-kyc-update.xyz’ is not your bank. Look for misspellings and extra words.
- **Shortened links** hide destinations.
- Grammar errors, generic greetings (‘Dear customer’).
- Requests for OTP, PIN, CVV, passwords, remote-access apps or payment to ‘unlock’ something.
- Unexpected attachments (especially .apk files).

steps.title: The STOP–CHECK–CALL rule
steps.body:
1. **STOP**: don’t click, pay or share anything right now.
2. **CHECK**: search the official website/app yourself; ask a family member.
3. **CALL**: contact the organisation using the number from its official site, app or the back of your card — never the number in the message.
Genuine organisations will still be there in 10 minutes.

steps.title: Where to report
steps.body:
- **1930**: National Cyber Crime Helpline (financial fraud — call fast)
- **cybercrime.gov.in**: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal
- **Chakshu** on the Sanchar Saathi portal: report suspected fraud calls, SMS and WhatsApp messages (even if you didn’t lose money)
- Your bank’s official helpline for blocking cards/UPI

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Open your SMS inbox. Find one message that might be a scam. List which of the four triggers it uses and what clues give it away.

activity.prompt: Likely scam or likely genuine?

items.text: ‘Your KYC expires today. Click bit.ly/xyz to update or account blocked.’
Bank app notification of a payment you just made
‘You won a car! Pay ₹9,999 GST to claim.’
OTP SMS that arrives right after you log in to your own bank app
‘Electricity will be cut tonight. Call this mobile number now.’
‘Part-time job: like YouTube videos, earn ₹5,000 daily.’

quiz.q: Which is NOT a common scam trigger?
options: Patient explanation with time to verify
quiz.why: Scammers use urgency, fear and authority to rush you, while genuine organisations give you time to verify. A patient explanation with time to check is therefore not a scam trigger.

quiz.q: To verify a bank message, call…
options: The number on the bank’s official site/app or back of card
quiz.why: Call the number from the bank's official site, app or the back of your card, which you found independently. The number in a suspicious message may belong to the scammer.

quiz.q: Chakshu on Sanchar Saathi is for…
quiz.why: Chakshu on Sanchar Saathi lets you report suspected fraud calls and messages. It is not for payments, apps or train tickets.

quiz.q: Why are educated people also scammed?
options: Scams target emotions and pressure, not intelligence
quiz.why: Scams work by exploiting emotions and pressure, not intelligence, so anyone can be rushed into a mistake. Educated people are targeted too.

sources: I4C — National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

lessons.title: India’s top frauds: digital arrest, parcels, tasks and KYC

story.title: Six hours on a video call

scenes.text: Dr. Menon, a retired professor in Thiruvananthapuram, gets a call: ‘A parcel in your name with illegal drugs has been seized. Connecting you to the police.’
On a video call, a man in police uniform with an official-looking background says he is under ‘digital arrest’ and must not tell anyone.
He is told to transfer his savings to a ‘RBI verification account’ to prove innocence.
His daughter Leena walks in, sees the screen, ends the call and phones 1930. There is no such thing as a digital arrest.

steps.title: ‘Digital arrest’ is a scam — always
steps.body: **There is no ‘digital arrest’ in Indian law.** Police, CBI, ED, customs, RBI or courts do **not** arrest people over video calls, keep them on camera for hours, or ask them to transfer money to ‘verify’ or ‘safe’ accounts. Real legal processes involve written notices and in-person procedures. If anyone says you’re under digital arrest: **hang up, don’t pay, tell family, call 1930**. The government has run national awareness campaigns about this exact fraud.

steps.title: Other common frauds
steps.body:
- **Parcel/courier**: ‘Your parcel has drugs/passports’ — leads to digital-arrest style threats.
- **Task/job scam**: paid to like videos or rate hotels; small payouts first, then ‘pay to unlock bigger tasks’ — money vanishes.
- **KYC/account-block**: link or app to ‘update KYC’ steals banking details.
- **Fake customer care** numbers on search results.
- **‘Hi Mum/Dad, new number’**: a ‘child’ texts from an unknown number asking urgently for money.
- **Investment groups** promising high guaranteed returns.
- **Marketplace buyer/seller** (QR code to ‘receive’ money).
- **Sextortion** (covered in lesson 4).

steps.title: Why task scams feel real
steps.body: Day 1: you like 3 videos, get ₹150. Day 2: ₹300. Day 3: ‘Prepaid task: invest ₹1,000, get ₹1,300.’ It pays. Day 4: ‘Invest ₹10,000 for ₹14,000.’ Your dashboard shows profit, but withdrawal is ‘blocked until you complete the next task of ₹50,000’. The early small payouts were bait. **Any job that asks you to pay to earn is a scam.**

steps.title: Protect elders and family
steps.body: Talk to parents and grandparents about digital arrest and parcel scams — fraudsters target retired people with savings. Agree a rule: **‘No money transfer to anyone new, for any reason, without calling a family member first.’** Help them set transaction limits.

steps.title: Around the world
steps.body: Similar tricks exist everywhere: fake tax-office calls in the USA and UK, ‘police impersonation’ scams in China, ‘parcel stuck at customs’ texts in Europe. The pattern — authority + fear + secrecy + money transfer — is universal.

a.text: A caller says: ‘This is the cyber crime branch. Your Aadhaar is linked to money laundering. Stay on this video call; you are under digital arrest. Tell no one.’

choices.label: Stay on the call and follow instructions
choices.feedback: This is exactly how the scam works — isolation and fear.

choices.label: Hang up, tell a family member and call 1930
choices.feedback: Perfect. Digital arrest does not exist.

b.text: They show a fake arrest warrant with logos and ask you to transfer ₹3 lakh to a ‘secret supervision account’ to clear your name.

choices.label: Transfer the money
choices.feedback: The money goes straight to criminals.

choices.label: End the call now and report it
choices.feedback: It’s never too late to hang up.

bad.text: Call 1930 immediately and your bank; report on cybercrime.gov.in with all details. Speed can help freeze money.

good.text: You’re safe. Real police never arrest by video call or ask for money transfers.

quiz.q: ‘Digital arrest’ over video call is…
quiz.why: 'Digital arrest' by video call is always a scam because no such procedure exists in Indian law. Agencies like RBI and the police do not arrest or demand money over video calls.

quiz.q: A job asks you to pay ₹2,000 to ‘unlock’ higher-paying tasks. It is…
quiz.why: Asking you to pay to unlock higher-paying tasks is a task scam. Real jobs pay you and do not ask you to pay in order to earn.

quiz.q: A ‘new number’ message from your ‘son’ asks for urgent money. Best action?
options: Call your son on his old known number to verify
quiz.why: Verify by calling your son on his old known number before doing anything. Paying, sending an OTP or bank details to an unverified 'new number' is how these scams succeed.

quiz.q: Which do scammers often demand to keep you trapped?
options: That you visit a police station
quiz.why: Scammers demand secrecy, such as 'don't tell family', so you cannot get advice and notice the fraud. A real process lets you take time, visit police or call your bank.

sources: Ministry of Home Affairs public awareness campaigns

lessons.title: Deepfakes and voice clones: seeing is no longer believing

scenes.text: Simran, 21, in Chandigarh gets a call. It’s her father’s voice, crying: ‘Beta, I’ve had an accident, send ₹50,000 to this number, quickly!’
Something feels off — he calls her ‘beta’ but never says their family nickname.
She asks: ‘What’s our code word?’ The line goes silent and disconnects.
She calls her father’s own number — he’s safe at his office. The voice was cloned from his public videos.

steps.title: What deepfakes are
steps.body:
**Deepfakes** are fake videos, images or audio made with AI so that someone appears to say or do things they never did. **Voice cloning** can copy a voice from a few seconds of recording (from reels, voice notes or videos). They are used for:
- Fake emergency calls from ‘family’
- Fake celebrity or CEO videos promoting investments or apps
- Fake ‘boss’ calls asking staff to transfer money
- Harassment and fake intimate images
- Political misinformation

steps.title: Clues — but don’t rely on them alone
steps.body: Some deepfakes show odd blinking, blurry edges around face or hair, mismatched lip-sync, strange lighting, robotic tone or unnatural pauses. But the technology is improving quickly, so **don’t trust your eyes and ears alone**. The reliable defence is **verification through another channel**.

steps.title: Your verification toolkit
steps.body:
1. **Family code word**: agree a secret word or question with family that’s never posted online.
2. **Call back** on the number you already have saved — not the number calling you.
3. **Ask a personal question** only the real person would know.
4. **Slow down**: urgency + money = verify first.
5. For workplaces: any payment request by call/video must be confirmed through a second official channel.
6. For viral videos: check whether trusted news outlets or official accounts report the same thing; government claims can be checked with **PIB Fact Check**.

steps.title: Fake images of real people
steps.body: Creating or sharing fake intimate or defamatory images of a person without consent causes serious harm and can be a crime in India (for example under the IT Act provisions on privacy violation and cheating by personation, and under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita). Platforms must remove such content when reported. If it happens to you: save evidence (links, screenshots), report to the platform, report at cybercrime.gov.in, and tell someone you trust. **It is not your fault.**

steps.title: Reduce your exposure
steps.body: Keep social accounts private where possible, limit long public voice clips, and think before posting children’s photos publicly. You can’t remove all risk, but you can make yourself a harder target.

items.front: A video of a famous cricketer promoting a ‘guaranteed returns’ trading app
items.back: Very likely a deepfake ad. Celebrities’ faces and voices are often faked for investment scams. Don’t install; report the ad.

items.front: Your ‘boss’ on a video call asks you to urgently transfer company funds and keep it secret
items.back: Verify through a separate official channel (call their known number, email your finance team). Secrecy + urgency = red flag.

items.front: A crying ‘relative’ calls from an unknown number asking for money
items.back: Ask the family code word and call the relative back on their saved number.

items.front: A viral clip shows a minister announcing free money for everyone
items.back: Check official sources and PIB Fact Check before sharing.

items.front: Someone sends you a fake intimate image of a classmate
items.back: Don’t forward it. Report to the platform and cybercrime.gov.in, and support the person harmed.

quiz.q: The most reliable way to check a suspicious ‘family emergency’ call is…
options: Call the person back on their known number / use a code word
quiz.why: The most reliable check is to call the person back on their known number or use a family code word, a separate channel that a voice clone cannot fake. A convincing voice or sent money proves nothing.

quiz.q: Voice clones can be made from…
options: Short clips from social media or voice notes
quiz.why: Modern tools can clone a voice from short clips on social media or voice notes. Hours of studio audio are not needed.

quiz.q: Spotting visual glitches is…
options: Helpful but not reliable as deepfakes improve
quiz.why: Visual glitches can help spot a deepfake but are not reliable as the technology improves, so always verify through another channel.

quiz.q: You receive a fake intimate image of someone. You should…
options: Not share; report it and support the person
quiz.why: Do not share a fake intimate image; report it and support the person affected. Forwarding or posting it multiplies the harm and may be a crime.

lessons.title: Online blackmail (sextortion): not your fault, don’t pay, get help

scenes.text: Nikhil, 17, in Nagpur chats with a friendly ‘girl’ on Instagram who soon asks to video call. Later he gets a threat: a recording, edited to look embarrassing.
‘Pay ₹10,000 in one hour or I send this to your family and school.’ He feels sick and alone and thinks his life is over.
He finally tells his older cousin Raj. Raj says, ‘This is a crime against you. You did nothing that deserves this. We’ll handle it together.’
They stop replying, save evidence, report the account, file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in and call 1098. The threats stop.

steps.title: What sextortion is
steps.body: **Sextortion** is blackmail where someone threatens to share private or fake intimate images or videos unless the victim pays money, sends more images or does something else. Criminal gangs run it as a business, often with fake profiles. Teenagers and young men are frequent targets, but anyone can be. Images can be stolen, secretly recorded, or completely **fake (AI-made)**.

steps.title: The four rules
steps.body:
1. **It is not your fault.** The criminal is the one breaking the law.
2. **Don’t pay.** Paying usually leads to more demands, not deletion.
3. **Stop contact, but keep evidence**: screenshot chats, usernames, profile links, payment details. Don’t delete the account until evidence is saved; then block.
4. **Tell a trusted adult and report**: cybercrime.gov.in (it has a category for women- and child-related crimes), **1930**, or the local police. Under-18s and their families can call **Childline 1098**. Report the account on the platform.

steps.title: Getting images removed
steps.body:
- Report on the platform: major platforms remove non-consensual intimate content.
- **StopNCII.org** helps adults (18+) prevent intimate images from being shared on participating platforms by creating a digital fingerprint (‘hash’) — the image itself isn’t uploaded.
- **Take It Down** (run by NCMEC) does similar work for images taken when the person was under 18.
- Indian law treats creating or sharing sexual content involving anyone under 18 as a serious crime under the POCSO Act and the IT Act — that protects the child, who is the victim.

steps.title: If you’re feeling hopeless
steps.body: Blackmailers want you to feel there’s no way out. That feeling is temporary, and help works. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, tell someone now or call **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7) or **112** in an emergency. Families: respond with support, not anger — the child is the victim.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body:
- Be cautious with new online contacts who quickly become flirty or push for private video calls.
- Keep accounts private; don’t accept requests from strangers.
- Remember that anything sent can be saved and shared.
- Agree with friends: ‘If anyone ever threatens you, tell me — no judgement.’

activity.prompt: Questions people are too scared to ask

items.q: If I pay once, will they delete it?
items.a: Almost never. Payment shows you can pay, so demands usually increase. Don’t pay; report instead.

items.q: Will I get in trouble with the police for what was in the image?
items.a: If you are a victim of blackmail, police and Childline are there to help you. The blackmailer is the offender. Talk to a trusted adult and report.

items.q: Should I delete my chats right away?
items.a: Save screenshots and links first — they are evidence. Then block and report.

items.q: What if the image is fake?
items.a: AI-made fakes are also a crime to create and share for harassment. The same steps apply: don’t pay, save evidence, report.

items.q: I’m too ashamed to tell my parents.
items.a: Many people feel that. Choose any trusted adult — a cousin, teacher, counsellor — or call 1098 (Childline) or 14416 (Tele-MANAS). You don’t have to handle this alone.

quiz.q: First rule if someone blackmails you online?
options: Don’t pay; save evidence; tell someone; report
quiz.why: If blackmailed online, do not pay; save evidence, tell someone you trust and report it. Paying fuels more demands and deleting evidence makes action harder.

quiz.q: Whose fault is sextortion?
quiz.why: Sextortion is the blackmailer's fault. The criminal is responsible, not the victim, so victims should not feel shame in seeking help.

quiz.q: A child in India being blackmailed can call…
quiz.why: A child being blackmailed can call Childline 1098, which supports children in distress. 1906 is LPG, 101 is fire and 155260 is a cyber fraud reporting line.

quiz.q: StopNCII.org is for…
options: Adults’ intimate images, using a digital fingerprint
quiz.why: StopNCII.org helps adults stop their intimate images spreading, using a digital fingerprint (hash) so the image itself is never uploaded. It is not for shopping or downloads.

sources: I4C — National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

questions.q: National cyber fraud helpline number?
questions.why: 1930 is India's national cyber fraud helpline. 1098 is Childline, 101 fire and 108 ambulance.

questions.q: Digital arrest is…
questions.why: Digital arrest is always a scam; no such legal procedure exists, and it is not limited to foreigners or run by banks.

questions.q: Best response to a blackmail threat online?
options: Don’t pay, save evidence, report, tell someone
questions.why: If blackmailed online, do not pay, save the evidence, report it and tell someone you trust. Arguing, paying or deleting evidence makes things worse.

questions.q: Which trigger is ‘Act in 30 minutes or lose your account’?
questions.why: 'Act in 30 minutes or lose your account' is urgency, a time-pressure trigger scammers use so you do not stop and verify.

questions.q: ‘sbi-kyc-help.top’ is most likely…
questions.why: 'sbi-kyc-help.top' is most likely a phishing domain. Official bank sites use the bank's real domain, and odd names with extensions like .top signal a fake.

questions.q: A family code word helps against…
questions.why: A private family code word helps against voice-clone emergency calls, because a clone can copy a voice but cannot know the secret word.

questions.q: Task scams typically…
options: Pay small amounts first, then ask you to invest larger sums
questions.why: Task scams pay small amounts first to build trust, then ask you to invest larger sums that you lose. Real employers do not ask you to pay to work.

questions.q: Where can you report a suspected fraud call even if no money was lost?
questions.why: You can report a suspected fraud call on Chakshu on Sanchar Saathi even if no money was lost. It accepts reports of suspected fraud communications.

questions.q: Why shouldn’t you rely only on visual glitches to detect deepfakes?
options: Deepfakes are improving and may show no glitches
questions.why: Do not rely only on visual glitches because deepfakes keep improving and may show none. Verifying through another channel works better than trying to detect fakes by eye.

questions.q: Which tool helps under-18s remove intimate images taken when they were minors?
questions.why: Take It Down, run by NCMEC, helps under-18s remove intimate images taken when they were minors. DigiLocker, IRCTC and UMANG are unrelated services.

questions.q: A ‘CBI officer’ on video asks you to move savings to a ‘safe RBI account’ while keeping the call secret. Which features prove it’s fraud?
options: Video-call arrest, secrecy demand and money transfer to ‘verify’ — none are real procedures
questions.why: A video-call 'arrest', a demand for secrecy and a transfer of savings to 'verify' are all features of fraud, as none are real procedures of CBI or RBI. Uniforms and time of day prove nothing.

questions.q: Your company CFO appears on video asking you to wire ₹40 lakh urgently and confidentially. Best response?
options: Follow the company’s verification process via a separate known channel before any transfer
questions.why: Deepfake CEO/CFO fraud is real, so verify an urgent confidential transfer request through a separate known channel under your company's process before moving money. Asking for a selfie is easily faked.

questions.q: A teen is being sextorted and feels hopeless. The best combined response by an adult?
options: Reassure it’s not their fault, don’t pay, save evidence, report (cybercrime.gov.in/1930/1098), and connect to support such as Tele-MANAS 14416
Confiscate the phone and ignore it
questions.why: An adult should reassure the teen it is not their fault, not pay, save evidence, report (cybercrime.gov.in or 1930/1098) and connect them to support such as Tele-MANAS 14416. Scolding or paying makes things worse.

questions.q: Which statement about scams is most accurate?
options: Only uneducated people fall for them
They exploit emotions and pressure; verification habits protect everyone
questions.why: Scams exploit emotions and pressure, so verification habits protect everyone. Education does not make you immune, banks do not always refund and antivirus cannot stop you from being persuaded.

courses.title: Privacy, social media & your mind
courses.summary: Your digital footprint and privacy settings, how social media affects mood and sleep, building healthy screen habits, handling cyberbullying and checking misinformation.
outcomes: Learners can decide what is safe to share and set privacy controls
Learners can explain how feeds are designed to hold attention and how comparison affects mood
Learners can build a personal healthy-screen plan
Learners can respond to cyberbullying as a target or bystander
Learners can check a claim before sharing using simple steps
courses.guardianNote: Covers online privacy, social media and mental health, and cyberbullying in an age-appropriate, supportive way. Gives teens practical steps (block, save evidence, tell a trusted adult) and helplines (1098 Childline, 14416 Tele-MANAS). No graphic content.

lessons.title: Your digital footprint and privacy settings

scenes.text: Tanvi, 16, from Kochi posts an excited photo of her boarding pass: ‘Off to Singapore!’
A stranger uses the code on the pass to view and try to change her booking. Another notices from her stories that her home is empty.
Her old posts also show her school uniform and the route she walks every day.
Her aunt, a cybersecurity analyst, helps her clean up: private account, location off, and a new rule — post memories after, not during, trips.

steps.title: Your footprint lasts
steps.body: Your **digital footprint** is everything about you online: posts, comments, likes, photos, tags, and data apps collect. Deleting a post doesn’t delete screenshots others took. Colleges, employers and future partners may search your name. Ask before posting: **Would I be OK with my grandmother, a teacher and a stranger seeing this in five years?**

steps.title: Never post these publicly
steps.body:
- Aadhaar, PAN, passport or card photos (even partly)
- Boarding passes and tickets (barcodes contain booking details)
- Your exact home address, school uniform with name, daily routes
- Live location while you’re out (‘at the mall now’) or ‘house empty’ posts
- OTPs, bank screenshots, QR codes
- Photos of other people (especially children) without permission

steps.title: A 10-minute privacy check-up
steps.body:
1. Set accounts to **private**; review followers — remove strangers.
2. Turn off **location tagging** and remove location from photos.
3. Control **who can tag you, message you and see your friends list**.
4. Check **app permissions** (location, contacts, microphone).
5. Remove old apps and accounts you no longer use.
6. Search your own name and see what appears.
7. Use masked Aadhaar (shows only the last 4 digits) when a copy is needed.

steps.title: Your data rights in India
steps.body: The **Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023** sets rules for how organisations collect and use personal data. It is built around **consent** for specific purposes and gives individuals rights such as accessing information about their data, correction and erasure, and grievance redressal. For children’s data, organisations need verifiable parental consent. Its rules are being brought into force in phases, so check the current status.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do the 10-minute check-up on your most-used app now. Then scroll your own profile as if you were a stranger: what could you learn?

activity.prompt: Safe to share publicly, or think twice?

items.text: ‘Whole family away for a week!’ while travelling
Your school name and daily bus stop
Holiday photos posted after you return

quiz.q: Why avoid posting boarding passes?
options: Barcodes contain booking details that can be misused
quiz.why: A boarding pass barcode contains booking details that others could misuse, such as accessing your reservation. It is not about airline rules or looks.

quiz.q: Deleting a post means…
options: Others may already have screenshots or copies
quiz.why: Deleting a post does not guarantee it is gone, because others may already have screenshots or copies. Assume anything posted can persist.

quiz.q: Masked Aadhaar shows…
quiz.why: Masked Aadhaar hides the first 8 digits and shows only the last 4, which is safer when a copy is needed. It does not show your bank balance.

quiz.q: India’s 2023 data protection law is the…
quiz.why: India's 2023 data protection law is the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act. The Consumer Protection Act, Motor Vehicles Act and RTI Act cover other subjects.

lessons.title: Social media and your mind

scenes.text: Every night Riya, 15, in Ahmedabad scrolls until 1 am. Everyone seems prettier, richer and happier.
She feels tired at school, snaps at her brother and stops enjoying dance class.
Her school counsellor, Ms. Kapoor, explains how feeds are designed and how comparison works on the brain.
Riya moves her phone out of the bedroom at 10 pm and unfollows accounts that make her feel bad. After a few weeks she sleeps better and feels lighter.

steps.title: Feeds are designed to hold attention
steps.body: Most apps earn money from your attention. Features like **infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks, likes and unpredictable notifications** keep you coming back. Unpredictable rewards (sometimes a lot of likes, sometimes none) are especially habit-forming. Knowing this isn’t a reason to fear technology — it helps you **use it on purpose** instead of being used by it.

steps.title: Comparison and highlight reels
steps.body: People post their **best moments**, often edited or filtered. Comparing your everyday life with others’ highlight reels can make you feel inadequate. Research links **heavy** social media use with poorer sleep and, in some young people, higher anxiety and low mood, though effects differ from person to person and depend on how it’s used. Using it to connect with friends and learn tends to feel better than passive scrolling and comparison.

steps.title: Signs it’s hurting you
steps.body:
- Losing sleep to scroll; feeling tired every morning
- Feeling worse about your body, life or friends after using an app
- Anxiety when you can’t check your phone; checking dozens of times an hour
- Dropping hobbies, studies or in-person time
- Fear of missing out (FOMO) controlling your choices
If low mood, anxiety or hopelessness last for weeks, talk to a trusted adult or counsellor, or call **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

steps.title: Curate your feed
steps.body:
- **Unfollow or mute** accounts that make you feel bad.
- **Follow** accounts that teach, inspire or make you laugh.
- Remember filters and edits; real skin has texture, real lives have bad days.
- Notice how you feel after 10 minutes of an app — better or worse?

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For three days, write how you feel (1–10) before and after using your most-used app. Look for a pattern.

activity.label: Hours of recreational screen time on a school day

bands.text: Light use. Make sure the time you do spend is enjoyable and intentional.
Moderate. Check that sleep, study, exercise and in-person time aren’t being squeezed.
High. Many people at this level notice tiredness or less time for hobbies. Try app limits and phone-free hours.
Very high. This often crowds out sleep, movement and friendships. Make a plan with screen-time tools and a trusted adult; seek support if you feel unable to cut down.

quiz.q: Infinite scroll and autoplay are designed to…
options: Keep you using the app longer
quiz.why: Infinite scroll and autoplay remove natural stopping points, which keeps you using the app longer. They are built for engagement, not privacy, time-saving or sleep.

quiz.q: Comparing with others’ posts often makes people feel worse because…
options: Posts show edited highlights, not real everyday life
quiz.why: Posts usually show edited highlights, not real everyday life, so comparing yourself to them is unfair and can make you feel worse. Others are not always happier.

quiz.q: Which use of social media tends to feel better?
options: Actively connecting with friends and learning
quiz.why: Actively connecting with friends and learning tends to feel better, while passive late-night scrolling, body comparison and constant like-checking are linked with feeling worse.

quiz.q: Low mood lasting weeks — what should you do?
options: Talk to a trusted adult or counsellor, or call 14416
quiz.why: Low mood lasting weeks needs support: talk to a trusted adult or counsellor, or call Tele-MANAS 14416, which is free and confidential. Hiding it or scrolling more does not help.

sources: US Surgeon General Advisory on Social Media and Youth Mental Health (2023)

lessons.title: Healthy screen habits for every age

scenes.text: The Sharma family in Jaipur eats dinner in silence — four people, four phones. Even the 3-year-old watches cartoons.
Mrs. Sharma puts a basket on the table: all phones go in during meals and after 9:30 pm, including the parents’.
The first week is hard. By the third, they’re playing ludo, talking about school and the toddler is singing again.
Mr. Sharma admits he was the most addicted of all.

steps.title: Screen time for little children
steps.body: WHO guidance (2019) for under-5s: **no screen time for babies under 1 year**; for **2–4 year olds, no more than 1 hour a day of sedentary screen time — less is better**. Young children learn language and emotions mainly through face-to-face talk and play. Video calls with family are different from passive watching. When older children do use screens, co-watch and talk about what you see.

steps.title: A healthy screen plan (teens and adults)
steps.body:
1. **Phone-free zones**: meals and bedroom at night (use an alarm clock).
2. **Stop screens 30–60 minutes before sleep**; bright screens and exciting content delay sleep.
3. **Turn off non-essential notifications**; keep calls and important messages.
4. **App timers** with built-in tools (Digital Wellbeing / Screen Time).
5. **Grey-scale mode** makes apps less tempting.
6. **Replace, don’t just remove**: plan a walk, music, sport, reading, a hobby.
7. Teens generally need **8–10 hours of sleep**; adults about 7–9.

steps.title: For parents
steps.body: Children copy what adults do. Model the habits you want, agree family rules together, explain reasons, use parental controls appropriate to age, and keep devices in shared spaces for younger children. Focus on **what** they do online and **how they feel**, not just minutes.

steps.title: When it’s more than a habit
steps.body: If gaming or social media use leads to failing studies, skipping meals or sleep, angry outbursts when stopped, lying about use, or withdrawing from family for months, it may be a problem needing professional help. WHO recognises **gaming disorder** as a condition when such patterns are severe and persist (usually at least 12 months). Talk to a doctor, counsellor or Tele-MANAS (14416).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Check your phone’s screen-time report for last week. Choose one app to limit and one phone-free time to start today.

activity.prompt: My healthy screen plan
items: Phone out of the bedroom at night
No screens in the last 30–60 minutes before sleep
App timer set on my most-used app
One offline hobby planned this week

quiz.q: WHO recommends for babies under 1 year…
quiz.why: WHO recommends no screen time for babies under 1 year, because face-to-face interaction and movement matter most for development.

quiz.q: For 2–4-year-olds, sedentary screen time should be…
options: No more than 1 hour a day, less is better
quiz.why: WHO's 2019 guidance for 2–4-year-olds is no more than 1 hour of sedentary screen time a day, and less is better.

quiz.q: Why stop screens before bed?
quiz.why: Bright, stimulating content delays sleep, so screens should stop before bed. Light and excitement interfere with falling asleep.

quiz.q: Best way for parents to build healthy habits?
options: Model good habits and agree family rules together
quiz.why: Parents build healthy habits best by modelling them and agreeing family rules together, because children copy adults. Ignoring it or rules only for kids work poorly.

sources: WHO guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 (2019)

lessons.title: Cyberbullying and fake news: be the one who helps

scenes.text: In a Class 10 WhatsApp group in Kanpur, someone posts an edited meme mocking Arjun’s stammer. Everyone sends laughing emojis.
Arjun stops coming to school for three days.
His classmate Shreya writes in the group: ‘Not funny. Delete it.’ Two others agree. She also messages Arjun privately: ‘I’m with you.’
Shreya and Arjun show screenshots to the class teacher, who handles it with the students and parents. The bullying stops.

steps.title: What cyberbullying looks like
steps.body: Repeated, intentional harm online: insulting messages, embarrassing photos or memes, excluding someone from groups on purpose, spreading rumours, impersonation, threats, sharing private information (‘doxxing’). It follows people home and spreads fast, which is why it can hurt so much.

steps.title: If it’s happening to you
steps.body:
1. **Don’t retaliate** — it often escalates and can get you in trouble.
2. **Save evidence**: screenshots with dates, usernames, links.
3. **Block and report** the account on the platform.
4. **Tell a trusted adult**: parent, teacher, counsellor.
5. If there are threats, sexual content, or it doesn’t stop: report at **cybercrime.gov.in**, call **1098** (for under-18s) or **112** if in danger.
6. Look after yourself: spend time with people who care about you; talk to a counsellor or **Tele-MANAS 14416** if it’s affecting your mood or sleep.

steps.title: If you see it: the bystander’s power
steps.body:
Most bullying stops faster when bystanders act. You can:
- **Not join in** — no likes, shares or laughing emojis.
- **Speak up** if it feels safe (‘Not cool’).
- **Support the target** privately.
- **Report** the post and tell an adult.
If you’ve been the one doing it: stop, delete, apologise sincerely, and think about what made you do it — talking to a counsellor helps.

steps.title: Check before you share: a simple method
steps.body:
Misinformation spreads faster than corrections. Before forwarding:
- **Stop**: does it make you very angry or scared? That’s a sign to check.
- **Investigate the source**: who posted it first? Are they reliable?
- **Find better coverage**: do trusted news outlets or official sites report it?
- **Trace the original**: reverse-image search old photos; check dates.
For claims about the Government of India, check **PIB Fact Check**. Forwarding false medical ‘cures’ or communal rumours can cause real harm.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Words online have real-world effects. Spreading private images, threats or hateful content can be a criminal offence. When unsure, don’t post.

a.text: A classmate posts a mocking edited photo of a quiet student in your class group. Ten people react with 😂.

choices.label: Add a laughing emoji too — it’s just a joke
choices.feedback: Each reaction tells the bully the crowd approves.

choices.label: Don’t react; message the student privately and report the post
choices.feedback: Good — support and report.

b.text: The student says, ‘Please don’t tell anyone, it’ll get worse.’

choices.label: Respect that and do nothing more
choices.feedback: Their fear is real, but adults can often help safely.

choices.label: Offer to go with them to a trusted teacher or counsellor, with screenshots
choices.feedback: Going together reduces fear and gets help.

bad.text: The bullying grows. It’s never too late: delete your reaction, support the target and tell an adult.

meh.text: The posts continue. Check in again and gently encourage getting help together — you can also speak to a teacher yourself without naming them publicly.

good.text: The teacher handles it calmly. The student knows they’re not alone. You were the upstander.

quiz.q: If you are cyberbullied, first you should…
options: Save evidence, block, report and tell a trusted adult
quiz.why: If you are cyberbullied, save evidence, block, report and tell a trusted adult. Angry replies or retaliation can make things worse and weaken your case.

quiz.q: A bystander can help by…
options: Not joining in, supporting the target and reporting
quiz.why: A bystander can help by not joining in, supporting the target and reporting. Staying silent, forwarding or liking the post helps the bullying continue.

quiz.q: A forward makes you furious and says ‘share before it’s deleted!’ You should…
options: Add your own comments and share
Stop and check the source and trusted coverage first
quiz.why: Strong emotion plus urgency is a warning sign, so stop and check the source and trusted coverage before sharing. Sharing fast spreads possible misinformation.

quiz.q: Where can you check claims about the Government of India?
quiz.why: PIB Fact Check verifies claims related to the Government of India. Random groups and meme pages are not reliable sources.

quiz.q: Childline’s number in India is…
quiz.why: Childline's number in India is 1098, for children in need. 14567 is Elderline, 1930 is cyber fraud and 101 is fire.

questions.q: Is posting your Aadhaar card photo publicly safe?
questions.why: No. Posting your Aadhaar card publicly exposes identity details that can be misused for fraud.

questions.q: A good bedtime habit is…
questions.why: Keeping the phone out of the bedroom protects sleep. Scrolling in bed, loud notifications and late-night gaming disturb it.

questions.q: If cyberbullied, you should save…
questions.why: If cyberbullied, save screenshots as evidence, because they help schools, platforms or police take action. Do not delete everything or keep only the nice messages.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS mental-health helpline is…
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, India's free 24×7 mental-health helpline, is 14416. 1930 is cyber fraud, 1906 is LPG and 100 is police.

questions.q: ‘Highlight reel’ means…
options: Posts show people’s best, edited moments
questions.why: A 'highlight reel' means posts show people's best, edited moments, not their whole life, which distorts comparison.

questions.q: WHO screen guidance for a 3-year-old?
options: No more than 1 hour a day, less is better
questions.why: WHO's 2019 guidance for a 3-year-old is no more than 1 hour of sedentary screen time a day, with less being better.

questions.q: Which is the best privacy step?
options: Private account, location tagging off, review followers
questions.why: A private account, location tagging off and a review of followers limit who can see and track you. Accepting everyone, public tags or sharing passwords increase risk.

questions.q: Why are unpredictable likes and notifications habit-forming?
options: Variable rewards keep the brain checking
questions.why: Unpredictable likes and notifications are variable rewards, which keep the brain checking for the next one. This is why they are habit-forming.

questions.q: Before sharing a shocking photo, a smart check is…
options: Reverse-image search to see if it’s old or from elsewhere
questions.why: A reverse-image search shows whether a shocking photo is old or from elsewhere, because old pictures are often recycled as 'new'. Likes and captions do not prove truth.

questions.q: DPDP Act 2023 is built mainly around…
options: Consent for specific purposes and individuals’ rights over their data
questions.why: The DPDP Act 2023 is built mainly around consent for specific purposes and individuals' rights over their personal data. It is not about traffic, tax or rent.

questions.q: A friend’s gaming has caused failing grades, skipped meals and rage when stopped for over a year. Best advice?
options: Encourage professional help (doctor/counsellor/14416) and family support
questions.why: Failing grades, skipped meals and rage over a year suggest a persistent severe pattern that may be gaming disorder, so encourage help from a doctor or counsellor (or 14416) with family support. More gaming or ignoring it does not help.

questions.q: You bullied someone online last month and regret it. Most constructive step?
options: Delete the content, apologise sincerely, change behaviour, consider talking to a counsellor
questions.why: The constructive step is to delete the content, apologise sincerely, change your behaviour and consider talking to a counsellor. Distracting, hoping they forget or blaming others avoids responsibility.

questions.q: Which plan most effectively reduces late-night scrolling for a teen?
options: Phone charged outside the bedroom, app timers, notifications off, alternative wind-down routine
questions.why: Environment design beats willpower: charging the phone outside the bedroom, app timers, notifications off and a different wind-down routine reduce late-night scrolling. Caffeine and bright screens make sleep worse.

questions.q: A target asks you not to tell. Best balance of respect and safety?
options: Respect their feelings, offer to go together to a trusted adult, and seek help if there are threats or self-harm risk
questions.why: Respect their feelings but offer to go with them to a trusted adult, and seek help if there are threats or self-harm risk. Doing nothing, posting publicly or confronting violently is unsafe.

courses.title: Kitchen basics: cook safely, eat well, shop smart
courses.summary: Food hygiene and gas safety, your first everyday recipes (rice, dal, eggs, poha), planning meals and groceries, and building a balanced plate on a budget.

Learners can cook rice and dal safely in a pressure cooker
Learners can plan a weekly menu and grocery list
Learners can build a balanced plate from affordable foods

lessons.title: Kitchen safety and food hygiene

scenes.text: Kiran, 18, moves into a shared flat in Coimbatore. On day two he smells gas when he enters the kitchen.
His flatmate reaches for the light switch. Kiran shouts ‘Stop!’ — he remembers his mother saying a spark can ignite gas.
They open windows, turn off the cylinder regulator and call the gas distributor’s emergency line.
Later that week, a flatmate gets food poisoning from rice left out overnight. The flat writes ‘kitchen rules’ on the fridge.

steps.title: WHO’s five keys to safer food
steps.body:
1. **Keep clean**: wash hands with soap before cooking and after touching raw meat, eggs, the bin or the toilet. Clean surfaces and cloths.
2. **Separate raw and cooked**: use different boards/knives for raw meat or fish; store raw meat below cooked food in the fridge.
3. **Cook thoroughly**: especially meat, poultry, eggs and seafood; reheat leftovers until steaming hot.
4. **Keep food at safe temperatures**: don’t leave cooked food at room temperature for more than about 2 hours; refrigerate promptly. Bacteria grow fastest roughly between 5 °C and 60 °C.
5. **Use safe water and raw materials**: wash fruits and vegetables; check dates.

steps.title: If you smell gas (LPG)
steps.body:
- **Do not** switch any electrical switch on or off, light a match or use a lighter.
- Open all doors and windows.
- Turn the cylinder **regulator OFF** and close the stove knobs.
- Leave the area and call the distributor or the LPG emergency helpline **1906** from outside.
- Don’t restart until checked. Replace cracked rubber tubes (they have an expiry date) and never keep the cylinder lying down.

steps.title: Pan fires and burns
steps.body:
If oil in a pan catches fire: **turn off the heat and cover the pan with a lid or a damp (not dripping) cloth**. **Never pour water** on burning oil — it explodes into a fireball. Don’t carry the burning pan. If it spreads, get out and call **112** or fire services **101**.

For small burns, cool under cool running water for about 20 minutes (see the first-aid course). Turn pan handles inward, away from children.

steps.title: Knife and kitchen habits
steps.body:
- Cut on a stable board (put a damp cloth under it so it doesn’t slip); curl fingertips in.
- A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one (less force, fewer slips).
- Never leave knives in a sink full of water.
- Wipe spills immediately to prevent falls.
- Keep a small fire blanket or extinguisher if possible, and know where it is.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find your home’s gas regulator and practise turning it off. Check the date printed on the rubber tube. Write the LPG emergency number 1906 and your distributor’s number near the stove.

statements.s: If you smell gas, switch on the exhaust fan to clear it.
statements.why: Switching anything electrical can create a spark. Open windows instead.

statements.s: Pouring water on a burning oil pan is dangerous.
statements.why: Water turns to steam instantly and throws burning oil outward.

statements.s: Cooked rice left overnight at room temperature is always safe if reheated.
statements.why: Some bacteria make toxins that reheating doesn’t destroy. Refrigerate within about 2 hours.

statements.s: Raw chicken should be stored below cooked food in the fridge.
statements.why: So that drips from raw meat can’t contaminate ready-to-eat food.

statements.s: A blunt knife is safer than a sharp one.
statements.why: Blunt knives need more force and slip more easily.

quiz.q: First action when you enter a kitchen and smell gas?
options: Open windows and turn off the regulator without touching switches
quiz.why: With a gas smell, open windows and turn off the regulator without touching switches, as a spark could ignite the gas. Lighting a stove, switching on lights or an exhaust can cause an explosion.

quiz.q: A pan of oil catches fire. Best action?
options: Turn off heat and cover with a lid
quiz.why: For an oil fire, turn off the heat and cover the pan with a lid, which removes oxygen. Water makes burning oil flare up, and carrying the pan can spill it and burn you.

quiz.q: Cooked food should not stay at room temperature for more than about…
quiz.why: Cooked food should not stay at room temperature for more than about 2 hours because bacteria multiply quickly. Beyond that, it risks causing food poisoning.

quiz.q: Which is one of WHO’s five keys?
options: Wash meat in the sink near salad
Store raw meat on the top shelf
quiz.why: One of WHO's five keys to safer food is to separate raw and cooked food, which prevents cross-contamination. Washing meat near salad or tasting raw eggs spreads germs.

sources: WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
Oil marketing companies’ LPG safety guidance

lessons.title: Your first recipes: rice, dal, eggs and poha

scenes.text: Lena, an exchange student from Berlin, lives with Aditya’s family in Pune. She wants to learn ‘dal-chawal’.
Aditya admits he can’t cook either — his mother always did it.
His grandmother teaches both: wash, soak, measure water, count whistles, and finish with a tadka.
By the end of the week, both can make a full simple meal in 40 minutes.

steps.title: Rice (two ways)
steps.body:
**Measure**: about ½ cup (around 90–100 g) raw rice per adult per meal.
- **Absorption method (pot)**: wash rice 2–3 times until water is less cloudy. Use about **2 cups water per cup of rice** (varies by rice — basmati often a little less). Boil, lower heat, cover, cook ~15 minutes until water is absorbed, rest 5 minutes, fluff with a fork.
- **Pressure cooker**: rice + about 2 cups water per cup, 2 whistles on medium heat for many white rices, then let pressure drop naturally.
Common mistake: stirring often (makes it mushy) or too much water.

steps.title: Simple dal tadka
steps.body:
1. Wash ½ cup toor (arhar) dal; soak 20 minutes if time allows.
2. Pressure cook with about 1½ cups water, a pinch of turmeric and salt, ~3–4 whistles, until soft.
3. Release pressure fully before opening. Mash lightly; add water for the thickness you like.
4. **Tadka**: heat 1–2 tsp oil or ghee, add cumin (jeera) seeds; when they sizzle add chopped garlic/onion, then tomato, a pinch of chilli powder. Pour over dal.
5. Add lemon or coriander. Taste and adjust salt.

steps.title: Pressure cooker safety
steps.body:
- Don’t fill beyond about **two-thirds** (about **half** for dal, beans and rice that foam).
- Check that the gasket (rubber ring) and vent are clean before each use.
- **Never force the lid open**. Let pressure release naturally or as the manual says.
- If the safety valve hisses or leaks repeatedly, stop and get it checked.
- Keep the cooker off when you step away for long.

steps.title: Two 10-minute dishes
steps.body:
**Omelette**: beat 2 eggs with salt, chopped onion, chilli and coriander. Heat a little oil on medium, pour, let set, fold. Cook until no liquid egg remains.

**Poha**: rinse thick poha in a strainer (don’t soak long), add a little salt and turmeric. Heat oil, add mustard seeds, curry leaves, peanuts, onion; then potato cubes if using (cook till soft); add poha, mix gently, cover 2 minutes; finish with lemon and coriander.

steps.title: Cook like a pro
steps.body:
- **Mise en place**: chop and measure everything before you light the stove.
- **Taste as you go**; salt can be added, not removed.
- **Clean as you go** so the kitchen isn’t a disaster at the end.
- Cook a bigger batch of dal and refrigerate in a covered box for up to a day or two.

activity.prompt: Put the dal tadka steps in order.
items: Pressure cook with water, turmeric and salt
Let pressure release fully, then open
Heat oil or ghee and add cumin seeds
Pour the tadka over the dal and serve

quiz.q: About how much water for 1 cup of white rice using the absorption method?
quiz.why: About 2 cups of water per 1 cup of white rice is a common ratio for the absorption method; adjust by rice type. Half a cup is too little and 6 cups is far too much.

quiz.q: How full should a pressure cooker be for dal?
quiz.why: Fill a pressure cooker only about half for dal, because foaming foods need space or they can block the vent. Filling it to the brim is unsafe.

quiz.q: What is a tadka?
options: Spices tempered in hot oil or ghee poured over a dish
quiz.why: A tadka is spices tempered in hot oil or ghee and poured over a dish, which releases their flavour into the fat. It is not a salad, rice type or pot.

quiz.q: Before opening a pressure cooker you must…
options: Pour cold water on the lid while it whistles
quiz.why: Let the pressure release fully before opening a cooker, because opening it under pressure can cause severe burns. Forcing the lid or pouring cold water on it is dangerous.

lessons.title: Meal planning, groceries and reading food labels

scenes.text: Newly married Pooja and Sameer in Indore spend a lot on groceries and food delivery, yet half the vegetables rot.
They try a challenge: plan seven days of meals, shop once with a list, and buy fresh vegetables twice a week.
They store food correctly and cook leftovers into new dishes.
At the end of the month they spent much less and threw almost nothing away.

steps.title: Plan in 15 minutes a week
steps.body:
1. Check what you already have (fridge, shelves).
2. Plan breakfasts, lunches and dinners for 7 days; reuse ingredients across meals (e.g., one bunch of spinach → dal palak + paratha).
3. Write a list grouped by section: grains & pulses, vegetables, fruit, dairy, protein, spices, cleaning.
4. Shop once a week for staples and once or twice for fresh produce.
5. Keep one ‘flex’ night for leftovers or eating out.

steps.title: Reading Indian food labels
steps.body:
Packaged food labels must show the product name, ingredients, nutrition information, net quantity, MRP, date of manufacture/packing, best before or use by date, and the **FSSAI logo with licence number**. A **green mark** in a square means vegetarian; a **brown mark** means non-vegetarian.
- **Use by**: about safety — don’t eat after it.
- **Best before**: about quality — may still be safe if stored well, but quality falls.
Ingredients are listed in descending order by weight: if sugar is first or second, it’s a sugary product.

steps.title: Storage that prevents waste
steps.body:
- Leafy greens: wrap in a dry cloth or paper in the fridge.
- Onions and potatoes: cool, dry, dark place, **not together** (they spoil each other faster).
- Tomatoes and bananas ripen others — keep apart if you want slower ripening.
- Store grains and pulses in airtight jars; add a date label.
- **First in, first out**: move older items to the front.

steps.title: Leftover magic
steps.body:
- Leftover rice → lemon rice or curd rice (only if refrigerated properly).
- Leftover dal → dal paratha or thicker dal with fresh tadka.
- Leftover sabzi → wraps/frankie with roti.
- Overripe bananas → banana pancakes or shake.
Cool leftovers quickly, cover, refrigerate, and eat within a day or two.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a 7-day menu for your home and a grocery list from it. Then play the **Market Day** game to practise buying within a budget.

activity.prompt: Where should each item be stored?

quiz.q: ‘Use by’ date is mainly about…
quiz.why: 'Use by' is mainly about safety, so do not eat food after that date. 'Best before' is about quality.

quiz.q: On an Indian food pack, a green mark in a square means…
quiz.why: A green mark in a square on an Indian food pack means vegetarian; a brown mark means non-vegetarian. It does not mean sugar-free, organic or imported.

quiz.q: If sugar is the first ingredient listed, the product…
options: Has the most sugar by weight
quiz.why: Ingredients are listed in descending order by weight, so if sugar is first the product has more sugar than any other ingredient. It is not sugar-free.

quiz.q: Which habit most reduces food waste?
options: Buying the biggest pack of everything
Planning meals and using first in, first out
quiz.why: Planning meals and using first in, first out prevents spoilage and waste. Shopping without a list or buying the biggest packs leads to throwing food away.

lessons.title: A balanced plate on a budget

scenes.text: Mr. D’Souza, 66, in Goa, eats mostly white rice with a little curry. His doctor says he needs more protein and vegetables.
His granddaughter Tanya draws his plate as a pie: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains, a quarter protein.
They add affordable proteins: chana, rajma, eggs, fish, curd, peanuts.
Three months later he says he feels stronger walking to church.

steps.title: The half–quarter–quarter plate
steps.body:
A simple visual guide used by many health bodies:
- **Half the plate**: vegetables (and some fruit through the day) — different colours.
- **A quarter**: whole grains or millets (brown rice, whole-wheat roti, jowar, bajra, ragi).
- **A quarter**: protein (dal, beans, chana, eggs, fish, chicken, paneer, tofu, curd).
- Plus a little healthy fat (oil, nuts, seeds) and water.
India’s National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) publishes dietary guidelines with a similar balanced-plate idea.

steps.title: Cheap protein swaps
steps.body:
- Mix dal + rice or roti: grains and pulses together give a better protein mix.
- **Chana, rajma, moong, lobia**: buy dry, soak overnight, pressure cook — much cheaper than canned.
- **Sprouts**: soak moong for 8 hours, drain, keep covered 1–2 days; rinse daily.
- **Eggs**, **curd** and **peanuts** are affordable protein sources.
- **Seasonal vegetables** are cheaper and fresher than off-season ones.

steps.title: Common food mistakes
steps.body:
- Too much salt (pickles, papad, packaged snacks) — linked to high blood pressure.
- Sugary drinks counted as ‘just a drink’.
- Skipping breakfast then overeating at night.
- Deep-frying in reused oil repeatedly.
This is general education. People with diabetes, kidney disease, allergies, pregnancy or other conditions should follow advice from a doctor or registered dietitian.

steps.title: Small, lasting changes
steps.body: Change one thing a week: add a vegetable to breakfast; swap one white-rice meal for millet; keep roasted chana for snacks; drink water before reaching for a soft drink. Habits beat strict diets.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Photograph your next lunch. Is half the plate vegetables? Is there a protein? Plan one change for tomorrow.

activity.prompt: Match the food to its main role on the plate.

quiz.q: On a balanced plate, vegetables and fruit should be about…
quiz.why: A common guide for a balanced plate is about half vegetables and fruit, with the rest grains and protein. A tiny corner or the whole plate is unbalanced.

quiz.q: An affordable vegetarian protein is…
quiz.why: Chana (chickpeas) is an affordable vegetarian protein; pulses are protein-rich and cheap. Sugar, soft drinks and chips give little protein.

quiz.q: Why combine dal with rice or roti?
options: Grains and pulses complement each other’s proteins
quiz.why: Grains and pulses complement each other's proteins, so together they provide a better range of amino acids. It is nutrition, not just taste.

quiz.q: Who should get personalised diet advice from a professional?
options: People with conditions like diabetes or kidney disease
quiz.why: People with conditions like diabetes or kidney disease need individual guidance because the wrong diet can harm them. General advice may not fit their medical needs.

questions.q: Before cooking you should first…
questions.why: Wash your hands with soap before cooking, because clean hands prevent contamination of food. Tasting raw meat or leaving burners on is unsafe.

questions.q: The LPG emergency helpline number in India is…
questions.why: The LPG emergency helpline in India is 1906. 14416 is mental health, 1098 is Childline and 1930 is cyber fraud.

questions.q: Which is a whole grain or millet?
questions.why: Ragi (finger millet) is a whole grain millet. Maida biscuits are refined, and sugar and soft drinks are not grains.

questions.q: Burning oil in a pan — never use…
questions.why: Never use water on burning oil; it sinks, turns to steam and causes an explosive flare-up. Turning off the heat, using a lid or a damp cloth is safe.

questions.q: Raw meat should be stored…
questions.why: Raw meat should be stored below cooked food so its drips cannot fall on ready-to-eat items. Above or next to salad risks contamination.

questions.q: ‘Best before’ means…
questions.why: 'Best before' means the food has best quality until that date; it is a quality indicator, not a safety date like 'use by'. It is not the manufacture date.

questions.q: For a pressure cooker, the gasket should be…
questions.why: A pressure cooker gasket should be clean and in good condition, because a faulty one causes leaks and pressure problems. Never ignore or remove it.

questions.q: Ingredients: ‘sugar, wheat flour, palm oil…’. This product is…
questions.why: Ingredients are listed by weight, largest first, so a list starting with sugar means the product is mostly sugar by weight. It cannot be sugar-free or high protein.

questions.q: Why shouldn’t onions and potatoes be stored together?
questions.why: Onions and potatoes should be stored apart because moisture and gases from each speed up the other's spoilage.

questions.q: You cooked a big pot of rice at 1 pm. Safest plan for leftovers?
options: Freeze after 2 days at room temperature
Keep in a warm oven overnight
Cool and refrigerate within about 2 hours, reheat till steaming, eat within a day
questions.why: Cool and refrigerate rice within about 2 hours, reheat till steaming and eat within a day. Leaving rice out lets bacteria grow and produce toxins that reheating may not remove.

questions.q: Which weekly plan reduces cost AND waste most?
options: Buying all vegetables for a month
Menu → list → one staples trip + 1–2 fresh trips, reuse ingredients
questions.why: A menu, list, one staples trip and 1–2 fresh trips with reused ingredients match buying to use, cutting cost and waste. Bulk monthly vegetables spoil and random shopping or ordering costs more.

questions.q: A gas smell at night: correct sequence?
options: Don’t touch switches → open windows → regulator off → leave → call 1906/distributor from outside
questions.why: Do not touch switches, open windows, turn the regulator off, leave, then call 1906 or the distributor from outside. This avoids sparks, ventilates, isolates the gas and gets experts. Fans, candles and lights can ignite it.

questions.q: A family wants more protein without big cost. Best combined advice?
options: Add pulses/sprouts, eggs or curd daily, pair grains with dal, buy seasonal vegetables
questions.why: Add pulses or sprouts, eggs or curd daily, pair grains with dal and buy seasonal vegetables to raise protein cheaply within a balanced plate. Cutting vegetables, skipping meals or powder alone is not better.

courses.title: Cleaning, laundry, small repairs & waste
courses.summary: A cleaning routine that actually works, laundry without ruining clothes, safe small repairs (MCB, taps, drains), and segregating waste the right way.
outcomes: Learners can plan a daily/weekly/monthly cleaning routine
Learners know which cleaning chemicals must never be mixed
Learners can read care labels and treat common stains
Learners can safely reset a tripped MCB and fix simple leaks or clogs
Learners can segregate waste into wet, dry and hazardous

lessons.title: A cleaning routine that doesn’t take all weekend

story.title: The flat that never felt clean

scenes.text: Three flatmates in Noida — Ayesha, Neha and Ben from Canada — clean only when guests come. Every Sunday becomes a fight.
Ayesha makes a chart: 10 minutes daily each, one weekly zone each, monthly deep tasks rotating.
Ben once mixed bleach with a toilet cleaner and started coughing. They learn chemical safety the hard way.
Within a month the flat stays tidy and Sundays are free again.

steps.title: Two principles: top to bottom, dry to wet
steps.body: Dust falls down, so clean **high surfaces first** (fans, shelves) and floors **last**. Do **dry work first** (dusting, sweeping) and **wet work after** (wiping, mopping) — otherwise you turn dust into mud. Work from the far end of a room towards the door so you don’t walk on wet floors.

steps.title: A simple routine
steps.body:
**Daily (10–15 minutes)**: wash dishes, wipe kitchen counter and stove, sweep main areas, empty bins, put things back.
**Weekly**: mop floors, clean bathroom and toilet, change bed sheets, dust furniture, wipe fridge shelves, clean mirrors.
**Monthly**: fan blades, windows and grills, kitchen tiles and chimney filter, under furniture, throw out expired items.
Split by person or by day — fairness matters more than perfection.

steps.title: Never mix these
steps.body:
- **Bleach + acid-based cleaners** (many toilet cleaners, vinegar) → releases **chlorine gas**.
- **Bleach + ammonia** (some glass cleaners) → toxic **chloramine** gas.
- Don’t mix different drain cleaners.
Use one product at a time, rinse between, keep windows open, wear gloves, keep chemicals in original labelled bottles, out of children’s reach. If someone feels breathless after fumes, move them to fresh air and seek medical help.

steps.title: Cheap, effective basics
steps.body:
- Soap/detergent and water clean most things.
- Microfibre cloths trap dust better than old rags.
- Colour-code cloths: one for kitchen, a different one for bathroom.
- Wash and dry cloths and mops often — a damp smelly mop spreads germs.
- ‘One in, one out’: when something new comes in, something old goes out — less clutter, less cleaning.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Set a 10-minute timer and do the daily list now. Then write a weekly chart for your home with names against each task.

activity.prompt: How often should each task usually be done?

quiz.q: Which should you clean first in a room?
quiz.why: Clean top to bottom, starting with the ceiling fan and high shelves, because dust falls down onto surfaces below. Cleaning the floor first means redoing it.

quiz.q: Mixing bleach with an acidic toilet cleaner can release…
quiz.why: Bleach mixed with an acidic toilet cleaner can release toxic chlorine gas. This is a dangerous and common household accident, so never mix cleaners.

quiz.q: Why do dry tasks before wet ones?
options: Wet first turns dust into mud
Brooms work better on wet floors
quiz.why: Do dry tasks like sweeping and dusting before wet ones, because wetting dust first turns it into mud. Then wipe or mop.

quiz.q: Using the same cloth for toilet and kitchen…
quiz.why: Using the same cloth for toilet and kitchen spreads germs to food areas. Colour-code cloths to avoid cross-contamination.

sources: Poison-control and household chemical safety guidance

lessons.title: Laundry: labels, sorting and stains

scenes.text: Rohit, 19, washes his new red kurta with all his white school shirts in Ranchi.
Everything comes out pink. His favourite wool sweater, washed in hot water, has shrunk to a child’s size.
His neighbour Aunty Mary, who runs a tailoring shop, shows him the small care label inside every garment.
Now he sorts, reads labels and treats stains early. No more pink shirts.

steps.title: Read the care label
steps.body:
Care labels use symbols:
- **Tub with water**: washing; a number (30, 40, 60) is the maximum temperature in °C; a hand in the tub = hand wash; a cross = do not wash.
- **Triangle**: bleach (crossed out = no bleach).
- **Square with a circle**: tumble dry (dots = heat level).
- **Iron**: dots show heat (1 low, 3 high).
- **Circle**: dry clean only.
When in doubt: cold or lukewarm water, gentle cycle, dry in shade.

steps.title: Sorting and washing
steps.body:
1. **Sort** into whites/lights, darks/colours, delicates, and heavy items (towels, jeans).
2. **Test new coloured clothes** for colour bleeding: dab a wet white cloth on a hidden part; if colour transfers, wash separately.
3. Empty pockets (tissues, pens, coins).
4. Turn dark and printed clothes inside out to reduce fading.
5. Don’t overload the machine — clothes need room to move.
6. Use the detergent amount on the pack; more is **not** cleaner (leaves residue).

steps.title: Stain first aid
steps.body:
Act fast, **blot, don’t rub** (rubbing spreads and pushes the stain in).
- **Blood**: rinse in **cold** water (hot water sets it), then detergent.
- **Oil/grease**: sprinkle talc or apply a little dish-washing liquid, let sit, then wash.
- **Tea/coffee**: rinse quickly with cold water from the back of the stain, then wash.
- **Turmeric (haldi)**: wash with soap and dry in sunlight — sun often fades the yellow.
- **Ink**: test any remover on a hidden spot first.
Always check the stain is gone **before** drying with heat or ironing; heat makes stains permanent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hot water on wool or silk (shrinkage, damage).
- Leaving wet clothes in the machine for hours (smell, mould).
- Drying dark clothes in harsh sun for long (fading).
- Bleaching coloured clothes.
- Ironing on the highest heat for synthetic fabric (melting).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick five clothes from your cupboard and read their labels. Sort them into wash groups. Write down which needs cold water or hand wash.

activity.prompt: Match the stain or problem to the right first step.
pairs: Talc or dish-washing liquid, then wash
Soap wash and dry in sunlight
Test for colour bleeding; wash separately
Cold water, gentle or hand wash, dry flat
Clothes forgotten wet in the machine

quiz.q: A tub symbol with ‘30’ means…
quiz.why: The number in the wash tub symbol is the maximum wash temperature, so 30 means a maximum of 30 °C. It is not minutes or number of clothes.

quiz.q: Blood stains should be rinsed in…
quiz.why: Rinse blood stains in cold water, because hot water sets protein stains so they are hard to remove. Oil or tea will not help.

quiz.q: Using double detergent makes clothes…
options: Can leave residue and irritate skin
quiz.why: Using double detergent does not clean better; excess detergent does not rinse out well and can leave residue that irritates skin. It does not waterproof clothes.

quiz.q: Why blot instead of rubbing a stain?
options: Rubbing spreads it and pushes it deeper
quiz.why: Rubbing a stain spreads it and pushes it deeper into the fibres, while blotting lifts it without spreading it.

lessons.title: Small repairs you can do safely

scenes.text: Every time Mrs. Banerjee in Durgapur switches on her new electric kettle with the microwave, the lights go off.
She used to call an electrician each time and pay a visit fee.
Her son Arnav learns how the MCB board works, why it trips, and when it is a sign of real danger.
He also fixes a dripping tap and a slow drain — and knows when to stop and call a professional.

steps.title: A basic home toolkit
steps.body: Screwdrivers (flat and Phillips), a **tester screwdriver** (line tester), pliers, adjustable spanner, measuring tape, torch, insulating tape, plumber’s (PTFE/Teflon) tape, a plunger, spare tap washers, a few screws and wall plugs, super glue, and gloves. Keep them in one box that everyone knows.

steps.title: When the MCB trips
steps.body:
An **MCB** (miniature circuit breaker) switches off a circuit when too much current flows (overload or short circuit). An **RCCB/RCD** trips if current leaks, for example through a person — it protects against electric shock.
1. Switch off and unplug appliances on that circuit.
2. Push the MCB lever back up (ON).
3. Plug in appliances one by one. If one makes it trip, that appliance is faulty or you are overloading.
4. If it trips **immediately with nothing plugged in**, or you smell burning, see sparks or the switchboard is hot — **stop and call a licensed electrician**.

steps.title: Electrical safety rules
steps.body:
- Never work on wiring with wet hands or standing on a wet floor.
- Switch off the **main** before changing a switch, fitting or fan.
- Never replace an MCB with a bigger rating ‘to stop tripping’ or bypass an RCCB.
- Don’t overload a single socket with many adapters.
- If someone gets an electric shock: **don’t touch them** until power is off; switch off the main or move the source with a dry non-conducting object; then call **112** and give first aid.

steps.title: Dripping tap and slow drain
steps.body:
**Dripping tap** (screw-type): close the angle valve or the main water valve, open the tap to drain, unscrew the head, replace the worn rubber washer with the same size, reassemble with PTFE tape on threads where needed. Ceramic/quarter-turn taps use a cartridge instead.

**Slow drain**: remove hair and gunk from the grating; use a **plunger** (cover the overflow hole, plunge firmly 10–15 times); pour hot (not boiling, for plastic pipes) water. Avoid mixing chemical drain cleaners; never use them along with plunging. Prevent clogs with a mesh strainer and by never pouring cooking oil down the sink.

steps.title: Know when to call a pro
steps.body: Call a licensed professional for: new wiring, repeated tripping, burning smells, water leaking inside walls, gas lines, anything on a ladder you’re unsure about, and tall-building work. A good rule: if a mistake could cause a fire, flood, shock or fall, get help.

a.text: The kitchen lights go off when you switch on the kettle. The MCB board shows one lever down. What first?

choices.label: Unplug the kettle and other kitchen appliances, then switch the MCB back on
choices.feedback: Right — remove the load before resetting.

choices.label: Tape the lever up so it can’t trip again
choices.feedback: Never defeat a safety device. It can cause a fire.

b.text: The MCB stays on. You plug in the kettle alone and it trips again immediately.

choices.label: Stop using the kettle; get it checked or replaced
choices.feedback: The kettle is likely faulty (short or leakage).

choices.label: Open the kettle base with wet hands to look inside
choices.feedback: Wet hands + electrical device = shock risk.

bad.text: Dangerous choice. Safety devices trip for a reason. Switch off the main, and call a licensed electrician.

good.text: Well done — you found the faulty appliance safely and the home stays protected.

quiz.q: What does an MCB do?
options: Cuts power when a circuit is overloaded or shorted
quiz.why: An MCB (miniature circuit breaker) cuts power when a circuit is overloaded or shorted, protecting wiring. It does not store electricity or brighten lights.

quiz.q: Before replacing a tap washer you must…
quiz.why: Close the water valve before replacing a tap washer, otherwise water gushes out when you open the tap.

quiz.q: Someone is stuck to a live wire. First step?
options: Switch off power or push the source away with a dry non-conducting object
quiz.why: Switch off the power or push the source away with a dry non-conducting object. Touching the person with bare hands or using water can shock you too.

quiz.q: Which should you never pour down a kitchen sink?
quiz.why: Never pour cooking oil down the sink; it solidifies and clogs the pipes. Water, soapy water and rinse water are fine.

quiz.q: MCB trips even with nothing plugged in. You should…
quiz.why: An MCB that trips with nothing plugged in may mean a wiring fault, which is a fire risk, so call a licensed electrician. A bigger MCB or repeated resets hides the danger.

sources: Bureau of Indian Standards / Central Electricity Authority safety guidance

lessons.title: Waste segregation, composting and pests

scenes.text: In a housing society in Mysuru, all waste goes in one bag. The collection van often refuses it, and stray animals tear bags open.
Resident Mrs. Gowda starts a two-bin drive: green for wet, blue for dry, plus a box for hazardous items.
Wet waste becomes compost for the society garden. Dry waste goes to a recycler.
They also clear stagnant water from pots and coolers — dengue cases in the building drop.
