steps.title: Three streams (as per India’s Solid Waste Management Rules 2016)
steps.body:
Households should segregate waste into:
- **Wet / biodegradable**: vegetable and fruit peels, leftover food, tea leaves, eggshells, garden leaves.
- **Dry / non-biodegradable**: plastic, paper, cardboard, metal, glass, cloth, packaging (keep it clean and dry so it can be recycled).
- **Domestic hazardous**: batteries, expired medicines, paint cans, chemical containers, broken CFL/tubelights, used needles.
Sanitary waste (diapers, pads) should be wrapped securely in paper/newspaper and handed over as per local instructions. E-waste (old phones, chargers) goes to authorised e-waste collectors.

steps.title: Composting at home
steps.body:
A simple pot or bucket method:
1. Drill small holes in a bucket or use a terracotta compost pot.
2. Layer **greens** (wet kitchen waste) with **browns** (dry leaves, shredded paper, cocopeat) roughly 1:1 or more browns.
3. Keep it moist like a squeezed sponge; mix every few days.
4. No meat, dairy or oil in simple home bins (smell, pests).
5. In about 6–8 weeks you get dark, earthy compost.
Smelly? Add more browns. Too dry? Sprinkle water.

steps.title: Mosquitoes, rats and cockroaches
steps.body:
- **Aedes mosquitoes** (dengue, chikungunya) breed in **clean stagnant water** and bite mostly in the **daytime**. Empty water from flower-pot trays, coolers, tyres, buckets and water tanks at least **once a week**; cover tanks.
- Keep food covered; take out wet waste daily.
- Seal gaps around pipes; fix leaks (cockroaches love moisture).
- Use pesticides only as labelled, away from food and children; store them locked.

steps.title: Reduce before recycle
steps.body: Carry a cloth bag, a water bottle and a lunch box. Refuse what you don’t need, reuse what you can, repair before replacing, then recycle. The cleanest waste is the waste never created.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Label two bins at home (wet/dry) and one small box for hazardous items. Walk around your home and empty any standing water.

activity.prompt: Sort the waste into the right stream.

quiz.q: Which is domestic hazardous waste?
quiz.why: Used batteries are domestic hazardous waste because they contain chemicals and metals that harm the environment. Peels, newspaper and a steel spoon are not hazardous.

quiz.q: Dengue mosquitoes breed mainly in…
quiz.why: Aedes mosquitoes that spread dengue breed in clean stagnant water collected in containers. They do not breed in dry sand or fast running rivers.

quiz.q: Why keep dry waste clean?
quiz.why: Keep dry waste clean so it can be recycled, because food-soiled packaging often cannot be recycled.

quiz.q: Compost smells bad. Most likely fix?
options: Add more browns like dry leaves
quiz.why: A smelly compost usually has too much wet material, so add more 'browns' like dry leaves to balance it. Meat and oil worsen smell and sealing it airtight does too.

sources: National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control — dengue prevention

questions.q: Clean a room in which order?
questions.why: Clean a room from top to bottom, because dust falls downward and would dirty a floor already cleaned.

questions.q: Banana peels go in…
questions.why: Banana peels are biodegradable, so they go in wet waste, not e-waste, dry or hazardous waste.

questions.q: Which tool clears a blocked sink without chemicals?
questions.why: A plunger clears a blocked sink without chemicals by using pressure to dislodge the clog. An iron, hammer or ladder cannot.

questions.q: Never mix bleach with…
questions.why: Never mix bleach with acidic toilet cleaner or ammonia, because toxic gases form. Mixing it with water is normal dilution.

questions.q: A cross over a triangle on a label means…
questions.why: A triangle on a care label is the bleach symbol, and a cross over it means do not bleach. No ironing and dry cleaning have different symbols.

questions.q: Aedes mosquitoes mostly bite…
questions.why: Aedes mosquitoes, the dengue vectors, mostly bite during the day, so protection is needed in daytime too.

questions.q: Which device protects people against electric shock from leakage current?
questions.why: An RCCB/RCD detects leakage current to earth and cuts power to protect people from electric shock. An MCB protects against overload and short circuit, not leakage.

questions.q: Blood on a white shirt: what NOT to do?
questions.why: Do not wash blood in hot water first; hot water sets the stain. Blot, rinse in cold water and use detergent.

questions.q: Expired medicines should be…
options: Put in domestic hazardous waste / take-back as per local rules
questions.why: Expired medicines are hazardous waste, so put them in domestic hazardous waste or a take-back scheme per local rules. Do not flush, burn or give them to pets.

questions.q: MCB trips repeatedly with one specific iron plugged in. Most likely?
options: The iron is faulty or draws too much for that circuit
MCB too small, replace with bigger
questions.why: If the MCB trips only with one iron plugged in, that iron is faulty or draws too much for that circuit. Isolating appliances finds the fault; never replace the MCB with a bigger one.

questions.q: Flatmates keep arguing about cleaning. Most effective fix?
options: A written daily/weekly/monthly rota shared fairly
questions.why: A written, fairly shared daily, weekly and monthly rota makes duties clear and visible, so it reduces arguments. One person doing everything or cleaning only for guests causes conflict.

questions.q: A family member is dizzy after cleaning a bathroom with two products. Correct response?
options: Move to fresh air, ventilate, stop using the products, seek medical help if symptoms persist or are severe (call 112)
questions.why: Move the person to fresh air, ventilate, stop using the products and get medical help if symptoms persist or are severe (call 112). Mixed cleaners may release toxic fumes; air freshener or continuing makes it worse.

questions.q: Which combination best prevents dengue at home?
options: Weekly emptying of containers, covering tanks, using nets/repellents in the daytime
questions.why: Weekly emptying of containers, covering tanks and using nets or repellents in the daytime remove breeding sites and prevent bites. Removing breeding sites weekly is the key; fogging once a year or full coolers do not control dengue.

courses.title: Renting a flat: search, agreement, living, moving out
courses.summary: How to find a flat without being scammed, what a rent agreement must contain, registration and stamp duty basics, tenant verification, and how to get your deposit back.
outcomes: Learners can set a rent budget and inspect a flat with a checklist
Learners can list the essential clauses of a rent agreement
Learners can explain why many agreements are 11 months and what registration means
Learners can document a flat’s condition at move-in
Learners can handle deposit disputes calmly and in writing

lessons.title: Finding a flat (and avoiding rental scams)

scenes.text: Sneha, 23, moves to Hyderabad for her first job. She finds a beautiful 1BHK online at a surprisingly low rent.
The ‘owner’ says he is abroad and asks for ₹15,000 ‘token advance’ on UPI before she can see the flat.
Her colleague Farhan says: never pay before you see the flat and meet the owner. They check — the photos are copied from another listing.
She finds a real flat through a verified visit, with a checklist, and negotiates the rent.

steps.title: Set your budget first
steps.body:
A common guideline: keep rent around **25–30% of take-home pay** (it may be higher in expensive cities, then cut elsewhere). Add the hidden costs:
- Security deposit (often 2–3 months in many cities; in some cities more)
- Brokerage (often around one month’s rent if you use a broker; negotiate)
- Maintenance charges, electricity, water, internet, gas, furniture
- Moving costs and the first month’s rent.

steps.title: The visit checklist
steps.body:
- **Water**: pressure, timing, hard/soft water, any tanker dependence.
- **Walls/ceiling**: seepage, damp patches, cracks (check corners and under sinks).
- **Electricity**: number of sockets, earthing, meter type, power backup.
- **Light and air**: does sunlight reach? Cross-ventilation?
- **Mobile network** inside the flat.
- **Safety**: door locks, grills, guard, CCTV, fire exits, lighting in the lane at night.
- **Distance**: commute time at peak hours; hospital, market.
- **Rules**: society rules about guests, pets, food, bachelors, parking.

steps.title: Rental scam red flags
steps.body:
- Rent far below the area’s typical rent.
- ‘I’m abroad / in the army, pay token and I’ll courier keys.’
- Pressure: ‘three people want it, pay in one hour.’
- No visit allowed; owner won’t video-call from the flat.
- Documents that don’t match (name on electricity bill vs owner).
Never pay before visiting and seeing ownership proof (e.g., property tax receipt or sale deed copy plus ID). Pay deposits by bank transfer to the owner’s account with a written receipt.

steps.title: Negotiating
steps.body: Ask politely for: lower deposit, fixing issues before move-in (written), a smaller yearly increase, inclusion of existing furniture, or a waived painting charge. Visiting several flats gives you a fair sense of the market and confidence to negotiate.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Compute your maximum rent (30% of take-home) and the total cash needed to move in (deposit + brokerage + first rent + moving).

activity.prompt: Flat visit checklist — tick when checked
items: Turned on taps and checked water pressure
Looked for damp patches and seepage
Tested a few sockets and switches
Checked door lock and window grills
Saw owner ID and proof of ownership
Asked total maintenance and utility costs

quiz.q: A common guideline for rent is…
quiz.why: A common guideline is that rent should be around 25–30% of take-home pay, leaving room for other needs and savings. 80% would leave too little for living costs.

quiz.q: An ‘owner’ abroad asks for token money before any visit. This is…
quiz.why: An 'owner' abroad who asks for token money before any visit is a common rental scam. Never pay before seeing the property and getting proof of ownership.

quiz.q: Best way to pay a security deposit?
options: Bank transfer to the owner’s account with written receipt
quiz.why: Pay a deposit by bank transfer to the owner's account with a written receipt, which creates proof. Cash without receipt, crypto or gift cards leave no reliable record.

quiz.q: Damp patches on walls suggest…
quiz.why: Damp patches on walls suggest seepage or leakage, which can mean mould and health problems. They are not a sign of good ventilation.

sources: Consumer awareness on rental fraud (police cyber cell advisories)

lessons.title: The rent agreement: what it must say

scenes.text: Joseph in Chennai signs a one-page agreement without reading. When he leaves, the landlord keeps his whole deposit for ‘painting and cleaning’.
His friend Meenakshi’s agreement lists the deposit, refund timeline, notice period and a move-in inventory with photos.
When she leaves, deductions are limited to a broken fan regulator, as agreed.
Joseph learns: the agreement is your protection — read and negotiate before signing.

steps.title: Essential clauses
steps.body:
- Names and addresses of landlord and tenant(s); property address.
- **Rent** amount, due date, payment mode; late-payment terms.
- **Security deposit** amount and **refund timeline and conditions**.
- **Term** (start and end date), **renewal** and **yearly increase** (e.g., 5%).
- **Lock-in period** (if any) and **notice period** for both sides.
- Who pays **maintenance, electricity, water, property tax**.
- **Repairs**: which are tenant’s (minor) and landlord’s (structural, major).
- Use (residential only), subletting rules, guests/pets if relevant.
- **Inventory** of fixtures and furniture (annexure).

steps.title: Why many agreements are 11 months
steps.body: Under the **Registration Act 1908**, a lease of immovable property for **one year or more** must be registered. Many people therefore use **11-month** agreements on stamp paper (or e-stamp), which are often not registered, to avoid registration fees and procedures. However, **stamp duty** rules and registration practices vary by state, and some states (for example, Maharashtra) require registration of leave-and-licence agreements regardless of period. A registered agreement is stronger evidence in a dispute. Check your state’s rules — many states offer online e-registration.

steps.title: The Model Tenancy Act 2021
steps.body: The central government released a **Model Tenancy Act** in 2021 as a template for states. It applies only where a state adopts its own law based on it. It proposes written agreements reported to a Rent Authority, a cap on residential security deposits (two months’ rent), clear repair duties and a faster dispute process. Old **Rent Control Acts** still apply in many states. So rules depend on where you live.

steps.title: Read before you sign
steps.body:
- Blank spaces → fill or strike out.
- Vague clause: ‘deductions as per owner’s discretion’ → ask for specific terms.
- Very long lock-in (you pay penalty if you leave early).
- Clauses allowing entry anytime without notice.
- Keep a signed copy with all pages initialled; both parties and two witnesses usually sign.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Laws and stamp duty differ by state and change over time; for high-value or unusual arrangements, consult a lawyer or your state’s registration department.

statements.s: In India, a lease of one year or more generally must be registered under the Registration Act.
statements.why: That’s why 11-month agreements are popular.

statements.s: The Model Tenancy Act 2021 automatically applies in every state.
statements.why: It is a model; states must adopt their own law.

statements.s: An agreement should state the security deposit and how and when it will be refunded.
statements.why: Clear terms prevent disputes later.

statements.s: Stamp duty on rent agreements is the same in every state.
statements.why: Stamp duty is set by each state.

statements.s: Initialling every page and keeping a signed copy is a good habit.
statements.why: Prevents page substitution and gives you proof.

quiz.q: Why are many rent agreements for 11 months?
options: Leases of one year or more generally need registration
quiz.why: Leases of one year or more generally need to be registered, which costs time and money, so many agreements are for 11 months. It is a legal and cost reason, not tradition.

quiz.q: A notice period clause tells you…
options: How early either side must inform before ending the agreement
quiz.why: A notice period clause says how early either side must inform the other before ending the agreement. It is not about Wi-Fi, rent due dates or police details.

quiz.q: The Model Tenancy Act proposes a residential deposit cap of…
quiz.why: The Model Tenancy Act proposes a residential security deposit cap of two months' rent, where a state adopts it. It is not ten months or a full year.

quiz.q: ‘Deductions at owner’s discretion’ is…
quiz.why: 'Deductions at owner's discretion' is vague and invites disputes, so negotiate specific terms for what can be deducted. It is neither clear nor required by law.

sources: Model Tenancy Act 2021 (Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs)

lessons.title: Moving in: inventory, verification and rent receipts

scenes.text: On move-in day in Bengaluru, Ishaan records a slow video of every room, the scratched kitchen counter and a cracked bathroom tile.
He emails it to his landlord with the date and meter readings.
The landlord reminds him to complete police tenant verification, which the city requires.
Two years later, the landlord tries to charge for the cracked tile. Ishaan forwards the old email. Problem solved.

steps.title: Move-in documentation
steps.body:
1. **Inventory list**: every fan, light, geyser, AC, furniture item, curtain rod, key — with condition.
2. **Dated photos/video** of every wall, floor, fixture and existing damage.
3. **Meter readings**: electricity, water, gas.
4. Email or message all of it to the landlord the same day and ask for acknowledgement.
5. Count and label keys.

steps.title: Police tenant verification
steps.body: Many Indian cities and states require landlords to get **tenant verification** done with the local police; it is usually the landlord’s responsibility, often with the tenant’s ID details and photo. Many state police websites or apps allow online submission. It protects both sides. Keep a copy.

steps.title: Rent receipts and HRA
steps.body: Pay rent through bank transfer/UPI and keep **rent receipts** (signed, with landlord name, address, amount, period). Salaried employees claiming **HRA exemption** (available in the old tax regime) usually need rent receipts, and employers typically ask for the **landlord’s PAN when annual rent exceeds ₹1 lakh**. Never make fake rent receipts — the tax department can verify.

steps.title: First-week setup
steps.body:
- Change or re-key locks if allowed (agree in writing).
- Update your address: bank, Aadhaar (address update), employer, delivery apps.
- Save numbers: landlord, society office, plumber, electrician, nearest hospital, police station.
- Check smoke and gas safety; know the fire exit.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make an inventory template in your notes app now: Room → Item → Condition → Photo taken (Y/N).

activity.prompt: Put the move-in steps in a sensible order.
items: Sign and keep a copy of the agreement
Pay deposit by bank transfer and get a receipt
Walk through with landlord and record a dated video
Note meter readings and make an inventory
Email photos, inventory and readings to the landlord
Complete police tenant verification as required
Update your address with bank and other services

quiz.q: Why email move-in photos to the landlord?
options: Creates dated proof of the flat’s condition
quiz.why: Emailing move-in photos creates dated proof of the flat's condition, which prevents unfair deductions later. It does not give discounts or Wi-Fi.

quiz.q: Police tenant verification is mainly…
options: A safety registration required in many cities
quiz.why: Police tenant verification is a safety registration required in many cities. It is not a tax or an electricity bill, and is not optional everywhere.

quiz.q: Employers usually ask for the landlord’s PAN for HRA when yearly rent exceeds…
quiz.why: Employers usually require the landlord's PAN for HRA when annual rent exceeds ₹1 lakh. Below that, it is generally not needed.

quiz.q: Best way to pay rent?
quiz.why: Pay rent by bank transfer or UPI and keep receipts, since a traceable payment is proof. Cash without receipts, vouchers or payment through a friend leave no clear record.

sources: Income Tax Department guidance on HRA

lessons.title: Problems, moving out and getting your deposit back

scenes.text: After two years in Ahmedabad, Kavya gives two months’ notice in writing as her agreement requires.
The landlord says he will deduct full repainting, a deep clean and ‘wear and tear’ — almost the entire deposit.
Kavya replies calmly with her move-in video, the agreement clause and quotes for the actual broken items.
They agree on a fair deduction for one broken window latch. Her deposit returns within the agreed 30 days.

steps.title: Wear and tear vs damage
steps.body: **Normal wear and tear** is the natural ageing from ordinary living: slightly faded paint, minor scuffs, loose hinges from use. **Damage** is harm beyond normal use: holes in walls, broken tiles, burnt counters, stained mattresses. Fair deductions usually cover **damage** and **unpaid dues**, not ordinary ageing — but your agreement’s specific clauses (for example, an agreed painting charge) matter.

steps.title: Moving-out steps
steps.body:
1. Give **written notice** (email/WhatsApp + letter) as per notice period.
2. Pay final bills; take final meter readings and photos.
3. Repair what you broke; clean the flat.
4. Do a joint inspection; compare with move-in inventory.
5. Return all keys against a written acknowledgement.
6. Ask for the deposit refund with an itemised list of any deductions, by bank transfer.

steps.title: Handling disputes calmly
steps.body:
- Keep everything **in writing**; be polite and factual.
- Offer evidence: agreement clause, move-in video, receipts, quotes for repair costs.
- Propose a fair compromise.
- If it fails: send a formal letter, then a lawyer’s legal notice. Depending on the state, you may approach the **Rent Controller / Rent Authority** (where applicable) or a **civil court**. Free legal aid is available through **Legal Services Authorities** for eligible people.

steps.title: During the tenancy
steps.body:
- Don’t stop paying rent to ‘punish’ the landlord over repairs — it weakens your position. Write and keep records.
- Landlords generally should give **reasonable notice** before visiting, as per your agreement.
- Don’t sublet without written permission.
- Report any illegal eviction attempt (cutting water/electricity, changing locks) to police and seek legal help.
This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Around the world
steps.body: In England and Wales, for most assured shorthold tenancies, deposits must be placed in a government-approved deposit protection scheme. Many countries have similar rules. In India protections depend on state law and your agreement — which is why documentation is your best friend.

a.text: Moving out, your landlord says: ‘I’m keeping ₹40,000 of your ₹50,000 deposit for painting and general wear.’ Your agreement says only damage beyond normal wear will be deducted.

choices.label: Shout and refuse to return keys
choices.feedback: Withholding keys can put you in the wrong and escalates the dispute.

choices.label: Reply in writing with the clause, move-in video, and ask for an itemised list
choices.feedback: Calm, documented and specific.

b.text: He sends a list: repainting ₹30,000 (walls only faded), broken latch ₹1,000, cleaning ₹2,000.

choices.label: Accept the latch and cleaning, dispute the painting with evidence and suggest a settlement
choices.feedback: Fair and well-supported.

choices.label: Accept everything to avoid conflict
choices.feedback: You may lose money you’re fairly owed.

bad.text: The dispute worsens. Return keys against acknowledgement and restart with written, evidence-based communication.

meh.text: Peaceful but costly. Next time, document and negotiate — fairness is not the same as conflict.

good.text: He agrees to deduct ₹3,000. You get ₹47,000 back by bank transfer. Documentation wins.

quiz.q: Which is normal wear and tear?
options: Slightly faded paint after two years
quiz.why: Slightly faded paint after two years is normal wear and tear from ordinary living. A hole in a wall, a broken window or a burnt counter is damage the tenant may pay for.

quiz.q: How should you give notice when moving out?
options: In writing, as per the notice period
quiz.why: Give notice in writing, as per the notice period in the agreement, because written notice is proof. Verbal notice or a message through a neighbour is hard to prove.

quiz.q: If a deposit dispute can’t be settled, a next step can be…
options: Legal notice, then rent authority/court depending on state
quiz.why: If a deposit dispute cannot be settled, send a legal notice and then go to the rent authority or court, depending on the state. Use formal, lawful channels, not shaming or damaging the flat.

quiz.q: Stopping rent because repairs are delayed is…
options: Risky — it can weaken your position; document and communicate instead
quiz.why: Withholding rent over delayed repairs is risky because it can put you in breach and weaken your position. Keep paying, document the problem, send written requests and use lawful remedies.

questions.q: Before paying any money for a flat you should…
options: Visit it and verify the owner
questions.why: Before paying anything, visit the flat and verify that the person is the real owner. Photos and pressure to pay quickly or in cash are typical of rental fraud.

questions.q: Move-in photos should be…
options: Dated and shared with the landlord
questions.why: Dated move-in photos shared with the landlord are proof of the flat's initial condition, which protects your deposit later. Deleting them or taking them after a year defeats the purpose.

questions.q: A rent of ₹12,000 with take-home ₹40,000 is…
questions.why: Rent share = 12,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.30, which is 30% of take-home pay. That is at the upper end of the usual 25–30% guideline.

questions.q: Lock-in period means…
options: You can’t leave before it ends without penalty (as agreed)
questions.why: A lock-in period is a minimum commitment: you cannot leave before it ends without the penalty agreed in the contract. It has nothing to do with door locks or deposit refunds.

questions.q: Which is the landlord’s typical responsibility?
questions.why: Structural and major repairs, such as serious seepage, usually fall on the landlord. Tenants normally pay for their own groceries and internet and for damage they cause, like a bulb they broke.

questions.q: Agreements of one year or more generally require…
questions.why: Agreements of one year or more generally need registration under the Registration Act 1908, which is why many are for 11 months. Police approval or a passport is not the requirement.

questions.q: Which document helps claim HRA exemption?
questions.why: Rent receipts are the proof employers require to allow an HRA exemption. Movie tickets, a gas bill or a meter photo do not show rent paid.

questions.q: Model Tenancy Act 2021 is…
options: A model law states may adopt
questions.why: The Model Tenancy Act 2021 is a model law that states may adopt or adapt by enacting their own versions. It is not automatically mandatory, nor limited to shops.

questions.q: Total move-in cash: rent ₹15,000, deposit 2 months, brokerage 1 month, plus first month’s rent. How much?
questions.why: Deposit of 2 months = 2 × 15,000 = 30,000; brokerage 1 month = 15,000; first month's rent = 15,000. Total = 30,000 + 15,000 + 15,000 = ₹60,000.

questions.q: Landlord cuts electricity to force you out mid-tenancy. Best response?
options: Document, write to him, report to police and seek legal help
questions.why: Cutting essential services to force a tenant out is an illegal eviction tactic. Document it, write to the landlord, report to police and seek legal help; retaliating or stopping rent weakens your case.

questions.q: Which clause is most likely to cause a deposit dispute?
options: Refund within 30 days by bank transfer
Itemised deductions for damage beyond normal wear
questions.why: 'Deductions at owner's sole discretion' has no objective limits, so it is the likeliest to cause a dispute. Joint inspection, itemised deductions and a refund deadline give clarity.

questions.q: Strongest evidence package in a deposit dispute?
options: Signed agreement, dated move-in video/inventory, written notice, final readings, key handover acknowledgement
questions.why: The strongest package is documents and dated media: the signed agreement, move-in video or inventory, written notice, final readings and key handover acknowledgement. Memory, posts or opinions carry little weight.

questions.q: A friend in Maharashtra plans an unregistered 11-month leave-and-licence agreement. Best advice?
options: Check state rules — Maharashtra requires registration of leave-and-licence agreements; online registration is available
questions.why: Rules differ by state, and Maharashtra requires leave-and-licence agreements to be registered, with online registration available. A verbal or unregistered agreement leaves the friend with little proof.

life-money.title: Money that makes sense
life-money.description: Budgeting, saving, safe UPI, credit cards and CIBIL, loans and EMIs, investing basics (FD, PPF, EPF, NPS, mutual funds, SIP, index funds), insurance and Indian income tax — explained from zero with worked examples.

courses.title: Budgeting, saving & safe UPI
courses.summary: Learn where money goes, build a simple monthly budget, create an emergency fund, use UPI without getting cheated and shop smartly using unit prices.
outcomes: Learners can split take-home income into needs, wants and savings
Learners can calculate a target emergency fund
Learners can explain exactly when a UPI PIN is and is not needed
Learners can compare products using price per unit
Learners know what to do in the first hour after a payment fraud

lessons.title: Where does my money go? Building your first budget

scenes.text: Meera, 22, starts her first job in Pune. Her offer letter says ₹4.2 lakh a year, but her first credit is only about ₹28,000.
By the 20th of the month her account shows ₹1,900. She has no idea where it went: food delivery, a new phone cover, a weekend trip, rent, auto rides.
Her aunt, a school accountant, tells her: ‘Money you don’t plan is money you don’t control. Write it down for one month.’
Three months later Meera has a budget, saves ₹5,600 a month automatically and still enjoys a movie every weekend.

steps.title: Income, take-home pay and expenses
steps.body:
Your **gross salary** (or CTC, cost to company) is not what reaches your bank. Deductions such as provident fund (EPF), professional tax and income tax (TDS) are taken out first. What lands in your account is **take-home pay** or **net income**. Always budget with take-home pay.

An **expense** is anything money leaves your account for. Expenses come in three shapes:
- **Fixed**: same every month (rent, phone plan, EMI, fees)
- **Variable**: changes month to month (groceries, fuel, electricity)
- **Occasional**: once or twice a year (insurance premium, festival gifts, school admission, vehicle service). These are the ones people forget.

steps.title: Worked example: the 50/30/20 split
steps.body:
A popular starting rule: **50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings**.

Meera’s take-home is ₹28,000.
- Needs (50%): ₹14,000 — rent share ₹8,000, groceries ₹3,000, travel ₹1,500, phone & internet ₹500, utilities ₹1,000
- Wants (30%): ₹8,400 — eating out, movies, shopping, trips
- Savings (20%): ₹5,600 — emergency fund first, then investments

It is a guide, not a law. In a costly city rent alone may be 40%; then cut wants to 20% and keep savings at least 10–20%. Someone living with family may save 40% or more.

steps.title: Turn occasional costs into monthly ones
steps.body: Add up all yearly costs and divide by 12. Example: insurance ₹9,000 + Diwali gifts ₹6,000 + bike service ₹3,000 = ₹18,000 a year = **₹1,500 a month**. Move ₹1,500 every month into a separate ‘sinking fund’. When the bill comes, the money is already waiting and your budget does not break.

steps.title: Common budgeting mistakes
steps.body:
- **Saving what is left** at month-end (usually nothing). Instead save first, on salary day, with an automatic transfer.
- **Lifestyle creep**: every raise disappears into bigger spending. Save at least half of every raise.
- **Ignoring small daily spends**: ₹150 a day on snacks and coffee is about ₹4,500 a month — ₹54,000 a year.
- **A budget so strict you quit in two weeks**. Keep some guilt-free fun money.
- **Forgetting UPI spends**: small scans add up; check your UPI app history weekly.

steps.title: Try this: the 30-day money diary
steps.body: For the next 30 days, write every rupee you spend (notebook, notes app or spreadsheet). At the end, group spends into needs, wants and savings. Most people are surprised by one category. Then set next month’s plan and open the **Budget simulator** lab to test it.

activity.prompt: Sort Meera’s spends into the right bucket.

items.text: Monthly SIP in an index fund
Food delivery on a lazy Sunday

quiz.q: Which number should you build your budget on?
options: Take-home pay that reaches your bank
quiz.why: Deductions like EPF and TDS are removed before pay reaches you, so only take-home pay can actually be spent or saved.

quiz.q: With ₹40,000 take-home, what does the 50/30/20 rule suggest for savings?
quiz.why: The 50/30/20 rule puts 20% of take-home pay into savings: 20% of ₹40,000 = 0.20 × 40,000 = ₹8,000.

quiz.q: A ₹12,000 yearly insurance premium should be planned as…
options: Paid using a credit card minimum due
quiz.why: A yearly bill is easiest to handle by saving a fixed amount monthly: ₹12,000 ÷ 12 = ₹1,000. Using a card minimum due would add interest and a surprise bill would strain the budget.

quiz.q: What is the best time to move money into savings?
options: At the end of the month from what is left
Only when you get a bonus
quiz.why: ‘Pay yourself first’ — saving on salary day before spending is far more reliable.

quiz.q: ‘Lifestyle creep’ means…
options: Spending rises every time income rises, so savings never grow
quiz.why: When every raise is fully spent, you earn more but are no richer. Save part of each raise.

lessons.title: The emergency fund: your financial airbag

scenes.text: Arjun, 29, a technician in Chennai, earns well but spends everything. One Monday his company shuts its local office.
The same month his father needs a hospital stay that insurance only partly covers.
With no savings, Arjun swipes credit cards and takes an instant app loan at a huge interest rate. Within six months he owes ₹2.3 lakh.
His colleague Lakshmi faced a similar month calmly — she had six months of expenses parked in a savings account and a sweep-in FD.

steps.title: What an emergency fund is
steps.body:
An **emergency fund** is money kept only for real emergencies: job loss, medical bills, urgent repairs, urgent travel for family. It is not for a sale, a phone upgrade or a holiday.

Common guideline: **3 to 6 months of essential expenses**. Choose closer to 6 (or more) if your income is irregular (freelancer, business, commission), you have dependants, or your job is less secure. Essential means needs only: rent, food, EMIs, insurance, utilities, school fees, medicines.

steps.title: Worked example: how big and how long
steps.body:
Lakshmi’s essential expenses are ₹18,000 a month.
- Target: ₹18,000 × 6 = **₹1,08,000**
- If she saves ₹5,000 a month, she needs ₹1,08,000 ÷ 5,000 ≈ **22 months**.
- If she adds her ₹20,000 Diwali bonus, she needs (1,08,000 − 20,000) ÷ 5,000 ≈ 18 months.

Start with a **mini goal** of one month (₹18,000). Reaching a first milestone keeps you motivated.

steps.title: Where to keep it
steps.body:
The fund must be **safe** and **quickly available**, even if the return is modest:
- A **savings account** (ideally a separate one so you are not tempted)
- A **fixed deposit with sweep-in** or an FD you can break early (small penalty is acceptable)
- Some people keep part in a **liquid mutual fund**, which usually allows withdrawal in about a working day.

Bank deposits in India are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank (principal and interest together). Do **not** keep the emergency fund in shares, crypto or long lock-in products like PPF.

steps.title: Mistakes that empty the airbag
steps.body:
- Using it for wants (‘It’s a sale, technically an emergency’).
- Investing it in stocks — markets can fall exactly when you lose your job.
- Not refilling it after use. After an emergency, rebuild it before restarting other goals.
- Lending it to friends without thinking whether you can afford to lose it.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: List your essential monthly expenses and multiply by 6. Write that number on a sticky note. Then set an automatic transfer on salary day — even ₹1,000 — to a separate account named ‘Airbag’.

activity.prompt: Ravi’s essential expenses are ₹15,000 a month. He wants a 6-month emergency fund. How much does he need (in ₹)?

quiz.q: Which is a genuine use of an emergency fund?
quiz.why: Emergency funds are for unexpected, essential needs like losing income or urgent medical bills.

quiz.q: Why should a freelancer usually keep a bigger emergency fund?
options: Income is irregular, so gaps between payments are likely
quiz.why: Irregular income makes gaps more likely, so a larger cushion (6+ months) is wiser.

quiz.q: Which is the WORST place for an emergency fund?
options: Shares of a single small company
quiz.why: A single stock can fall sharply exactly when you need the money. Emergency money must be safe and available.

quiz.q: Up to what amount are bank deposits insured by DICGC per depositor per bank?
quiz.why: DICGC insurance covers up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, principal and interest together.

lessons.title: UPI without fear: how scams really work

scenes.text: Ravi in Lucknow lists his old sofa online for ₹6,000. Within minutes a ‘buyer’ says he is an army officer posted far away and will pay in advance.
The buyer sends a UPI ‘request’ and says: ‘Just enter your PIN to receive the ₹6,000.’
Ravi remembers his sister’s rule: ‘A PIN is a key that opens your money to go OUT. Nobody needs your key to put money IN.’
He declines, blocks the number and reports it. A neighbour who entered the PIN in a similar trick lost ₹18,000.

steps.title: The golden rule of UPI
steps.body:
**You never need your UPI PIN, OTP, card CVV or to scan a QR code to RECEIVE money.** Money comes in when someone else sends it to your UPI ID or number.

You use your PIN only to **send** money or **approve a debit**. So:
- A **collect request** (‘request money’) that asks for your PIN = money will leave your account.
- **Scanning a QR code** and entering your PIN = paying, not receiving.
- If a message says ‘enter PIN to get refund/prize/cashback’, it is a scam.

steps.title: The most common tricks
steps.body:
- **Fake buyer**: sends a collect request or QR ‘to pay you’.
- **Fake customer care**: you search ‘XYZ helpline’ online, call a fake number, and they ask you to install a **screen-sharing app** (they can then see your OTPs).
- **Wrong transfer**: ‘I sent ₹5,000 to you by mistake, please return it’ — with a fake SMS. Check your actual bank balance, not the SMS.
- **KYC expiry**: ‘Your account will be blocked today, click this link.’ Banks do not block accounts by a random SMS link.
- **Electricity bill** threats: ‘Power will be cut tonight, call this number.’
All of them use **urgency** and **fear** or **greed**.

steps.title: Safe UPI habits
steps.body:
- Set a daily transaction limit in your app that suits you.
- Keep a separate low-balance account linked to UPI for daily spends.
- Lock your phone and UPI app; never share your screen with strangers.
- Read the screen before entering a PIN: does it say **Pay** or **Debit**? To whom?
- Use only official apps from the official app store; take helpline numbers only from the app or the bank’s official website.

steps.title: If money is stolen: act in the first hour
steps.body:
1. Call the **National Cyber Crime Helpline 1930** immediately, or report at the national cybercrime reporting portal (cybercrime.gov.in). Quick reports give the best chance of freezing the money.
2. Call your bank’s official helpline and block UPI/cards; ask for a complaint reference number.
3. Keep screenshots: transaction ID (UTR), time, the scammer’s number/UPI ID.

Under RBI rules on unauthorised electronic transactions, reporting quickly (within three working days) can protect you from liability when the fault is a third-party breach and not your own negligence like sharing your PIN. Delays increase your risk.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Open your UPI app now. Find: (1) where to see transaction history, (2) how to set a transaction limit, (3) how to raise a complaint or dispute. Write down 1930 in your phone contacts as ‘Cyber Fraud Helpline’.

a.text: You are selling a cycle online. A buyer messages: ‘I’ll pay ₹4,000 now. I’ve sent a request on UPI — please approve with your PIN to receive.’ What do you do?

choices.label: Enter the PIN to receive the money
choices.feedback: A PIN approves money going OUT. You just paid the scammer.

choices.label: Decline the request and ask him to send money to your UPI ID
choices.feedback: Correct. Receiving needs no PIN.

b.text: He sends a screenshot ‘₹40,000 paid by mistake, please return ₹36,000!’ Your bank app balance has not changed.

choices.label: Refund ₹36,000 quickly, he seems upset
choices.feedback: Screenshots and SMS can be faked. Always check your real balance.

choices.label: Check your bank balance, ignore the pressure, block and report
choices.feedback: Exactly. No money arrived, so there is nothing to return.

lost.text: You lost money. Call 1930 and your bank right now, keep the transaction ID and screenshots, and report on cybercrime.gov.in. Speed matters.

win.text: You stayed safe. Rule to remember: no PIN, no QR scan, no OTP is ever needed to receive money.

quiz.q: When do you need to enter your UPI PIN?
options: To send money or approve a debit
quiz.why: The PIN authorises money leaving your account. Receiving needs nothing from you.

quiz.q: A ‘customer care’ caller asks you to install a screen-sharing app to fix a refund. This is…
options: A common scam to watch your OTPs and PIN
Safe if the caller is polite
quiz.why: A caller asking you to install a screen-sharing app lets scammers see your OTPs and PIN, so it is a common scam. Politeness does not make it safe, and RBI or banks do not require it.

quiz.q: Which number should you call first after a cyber/UPI fraud in India?
quiz.why: 1930 is the National Cyber Crime Helpline; it can help freeze money quickly. Also inform your bank.

quiz.q: Someone says they sent you money by mistake and shows an SMS. What should you check?
quiz.why: Fake SMS messages and screenshots are easy to make, so only your actual bank balance or statement proves whether money arrived. Do not refund before checking it.

quiz.q: Which feeling do almost all scams try to create?
quiz.why: Scammers rush you so you don’t stop to think. Slowing down is your best defence.

sources: RBI customer protection circular on unauthorised electronic transactions (2017)

lessons.title: Smart shopping: unit prices, MRP and the 24-hour rule

scenes.text: Fatima in Hyderabad sees a ‘Big Value Pack’ of detergent and a smaller pack. She assumes big is always cheaper.
Her son checks the price per kg on his phone: the big pack is actually ₹10 a kg more expensive.
In Manchester, Tom, a student, sees headphones ‘70% off — today only’. He buys them and later finds the same price every week.
Both learn two habits: compare price per unit, and wait 24 hours before any unplanned want.

steps.title: Price per unit is the real price
steps.body:
Packs come in different sizes so you can’t compare the printed price directly. Convert everything to the **same unit**: price per kg, per litre, per 100 g, per piece or per wash.

Formula: **unit price = price ÷ quantity**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Detergent A: 1 kg for ₹120 → ₹120 per kg.
Detergent B: 500 g for ₹65 → 0.5 kg, so ₹65 ÷ 0.5 = **₹130 per kg**.
A is cheaper per kg by ₹10.

But also ask: Will I use the big pack before it expires? Do I have space? Cheap per unit is wasteful if half gets thrown away (common with food).

steps.title: MRP and labels in India
steps.body:
Packaged goods in India must show the **MRP (maximum retail price), inclusive of all taxes**, net quantity, manufacturer details and date of manufacture/packing. A shop cannot charge **above** MRP — you can complain to the National Consumer Helpline (1915) if it does. Shops may sell below MRP; always compare.

For food, ‘use by’ is about safety and ‘best before’ is about quality.

steps.title: Tricks that make you overspend
steps.body:
- **Anchoring**: a crossed-out ‘original’ price makes the sale price look tiny.
- **Fake urgency**: countdown timers and ‘only 2 left’.
- **Buy 2 get 1**: great only if you needed three.
- **‘No-cost EMI’** and Buy-Now-Pay-Later: the cost may be hidden in the price or fees, and missed payments hurt your credit score.
- **Shopping hungry or bored**: you buy more.

steps.title: The 24-hour rule and a list
steps.body: For any unplanned **want** over a set amount (say ₹1,000), wait 24 hours. If you still want it tomorrow and it fits your wants budget, buy it guilt-free. For groceries, shop with a **list** made after checking your kitchen. Play the **Market Day** game to practise quick price comparisons.

activity.prompt: Oil: 1 litre costs ₹180; a 5-litre can costs ₹850. What is the price per litre of the 5-litre can (in ₹)?

quiz.q: 500 g of tea costs ₹260 and 250 g costs ₹140. Which is cheaper per kg?
quiz.why: Compare per kg: ₹260 ÷ 0.5 = ₹520/kg for the 500 g pack, while ₹140 ÷ 0.25 = ₹560/kg for the 250 g pack. The 500 g pack is cheaper.

quiz.q: MRP printed on a pack in India is…
options: Inclusive of all taxes, and the maximum a shop may charge
quiz.why: MRP is the maximum retail price, inclusive of all taxes, and a shop may not charge more than it. It is not a minimum price and applies in shops as well as online.

quiz.q: Which is a good defence against impulse buying?
quiz.why: The 24-hour rule lets the urge pass; if you still want the item and can afford it, buy it calmly. Countdown timers, EMIs and shopping hungry push you to impulse buy.

quiz.q: A big pack is cheaper per unit but half will expire before use. It is…
options: Possibly worse value because of waste
quiz.why: A bigger pack is a better buy only if you use it; if half expires, the real cost per unit used is higher. Value depends on what you use, not only the unit price.

questions.q: Which part of income should a budget be based on?
questions.why: Base a budget on take-home pay, because it is the money you can actually spend or save. CTC, gross pay and uncertain bonuses include amounts you will not receive.

questions.q: Which of these is a ‘need’?
questions.why: An electricity bill is a need because utilities are essential. A designer bag, concert ticket and gaming skin are wants.

questions.q: To receive money on UPI you must…
options: Do nothing except share your UPI ID or number
questions.why: To receive money on UPI you only share your UPI ID, number or QR; no PIN, OTP or scanning is needed. Anyone asking for a PIN to 'send' you money is trying to take it.

questions.q: Take-home ₹30,000. Under 50/30/20, how much for wants?
questions.why: Under 50/30/20, wants get 30% of take-home: 0.30 × 30,000 = ₹9,000.

questions.q: Yearly costs of ₹24,000 should be saved monthly as…
questions.why: Spread a yearly cost across 12 months: ₹24,000 ÷ 12 = ₹2,000 per month.

questions.q: What is the usual emergency fund guideline?
questions.why: A usual emergency fund guideline is 3–6 months of essential expenses, more if income is irregular. A week or leftovers would not cover a job loss.

questions.q: Essentials ₹20,000/month; target 6 months; saving ₹8,000/month. About how many months to build it?
Rice: 5 kg for ₹340 or 10 kg for ₹700. Cheaper per kg?
questions.why: Per kg, 5 kg for ₹340 is 340 ÷ 5 = ₹68, while 10 kg for ₹700 is 700 ÷ 10 = ₹70. So the 5 kg pack is cheaper.

questions.q: Why is a single company’s shares a poor place for an emergency fund?
options: Value can fall sharply exactly when you need cash
questions.why: Emergency money must be stable and quickly available. One company's shares can fall sharply just when you need cash, so they are a poor home for it, though they can be sold.

questions.q: A caller asks you to install a remote screen-sharing app to process a refund. Best action?
options: Refuse, hang up, contact the company only through its official app or website
questions.why: Refuse, hang up and contact the company only through its official app or website. Remote screen-sharing exposes OTPs and PINs, and genuine refunds never need it.

questions.q: After a UPI fraud, which combination gives the best chance of recovery?
options: Only post about it on social media
Call 1930 and your bank immediately, save the transaction ID, report on the cybercrime portal
questions.why: Speed and evidence help authorities and banks freeze funds; RBI rules favour quick reporting.

questions.q: Your take-home rises from ₹30,000 to ₹40,000. Which plan best avoids lifestyle creep?
options: Save at least half of the raise automatically
questions.why: Saving at least half of a raise automatically builds wealth while still letting you enjoy a better lifestyle. Spending all the extra ₹10,000, borrowing more or stopping the emergency fund is lifestyle creep.

questions.q: A ‘no-cost EMI’ offer is best evaluated by…
options: Comparing the total amount paid (price + fees) with the best one-time price elsewhere
questions.why: A 'no-cost EMI' can hide costs in a higher price or processing fees. Compare the total amount paid with the best one-time price elsewhere instead of trusting the label.

questions.q: Which statement about the 50/30/20 rule is most accurate?
options: It is a law in India
It is a flexible starting guide; adjust percentages to your city and goals while protecting savings
questions.why: The 50/30/20 rule is a flexible starting guide, not a law. Adjust the shares to your city and goals while protecting savings; needs are not fixed at 80% and savings need not be exactly 20%.

courses.title: Credit cards, CIBIL score & loans
courses.summary: How credit cards really charge you, what a CIBIL/credit score is and how to build one, how EMIs are calculated, and how to avoid debt traps and illegal loan apps.
outcomes: Learners can explain billing cycle, due date, minimum due and interest-free period
Learners can name the factors that build or damage a credit score
Learners can calculate an EMI and the total interest on a loan
Learners can recognise flat-rate and illegal digital-lending traps
Learners can choose a debt-repayment strategy

lessons.title: How a credit card really works

scenes.text: Kabir, 24, in Bengaluru gets his first credit card with a ₹1,00,000 limit. It feels like a second salary.
He spends ₹60,000 in a month on a phone and gifts. The statement says ‘Minimum amount due: ₹3,000’. He pays just that.
Next month he is charged interest of over ₹2,000 on the unpaid balance, and new purchases also start attracting interest.
His manager Anita explains: ‘A card is a 50-day loan that is free only if you pay the full statement every month.’ Kabir sets an auto-debit for the total amount due.

steps.title: The vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Credit limit**: the maximum you may owe.
- **Billing cycle**: about a month of spends collected into one **statement**.
- **Statement date**: the day the bill is made.
- **Due date**: usually around 15–20 days after the statement date.
- **Total amount due**: everything you owe for that statement.
- **Minimum amount due**: a small part (often around 5% of dues plus some charges). Paying it avoids a late fee, **not interest**.
- **Interest-free period**: if you pay the total by the due date, purchases cost no interest. Depending on when you spend in the cycle, this is often up to about 45–50 days.

steps.title: Worked example: the minimum-due trap
steps.body:
Kabir owes ₹60,000 and pays the ₹3,000 minimum. ₹57,000 is **revolving credit**. Card interest is commonly around 3–3.75% a month (roughly 36–45% a year — check your card’s terms).

At 3.5% a month: ₹57,000 × 0.035 ≈ **₹1,995** for one month, plus GST on the interest. In many cards, once you revolve, even new purchases lose their interest-free period until you clear the full balance. Paying only the minimum can stretch a ₹60,000 bill over years and cost tens of thousands in interest.

steps.title: Expensive habits
steps.body:
- **Cash withdrawal** from a credit card: fee plus interest usually from day one.
- **Late payment**: late fee + interest + damage to your credit score.
- **Using more than about 30% of your limit** regularly can lower your score (high ‘utilisation’).
- **Converting everything to EMI** without checking processing fee and interest.
- Sharing card number, CVV or OTP with anyone who calls.

steps.title: Using a card well
steps.body: Used carefully, a card builds credit history, gives purchase protection and rewards. Rules: spend only what is already in your budget, set **auto-debit for total amount due**, keep utilisation low, and review the statement every month for unknown charges. If you cannot pay in full, stop using the card and make a repayment plan.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find on a real or sample statement: statement date, due date, total due, minimum due and the monthly interest rate (often in the ‘Most Important Terms and Conditions’). Write them down.

statements.s: Paying the minimum amount due avoids all interest.
statements.why: It only avoids the late fee. Interest is charged on the unpaid balance.

statements.s: Paying the total amount due by the due date means purchases cost no interest.
statements.why: That is the interest-free period.

statements.s: Withdrawing cash on a credit card is usually interest-free for 50 days.
statements.why: Cash advances usually attract a fee and interest from the day of withdrawal.

statements.s: Using a small part of your limit and paying on time helps build a credit score.
statements.why: Low utilisation and on-time payments are strong positive factors.

statements.s: A bank official may ask for your CVV and OTP on a phone call to ‘upgrade’ your card.
statements.why: Banks never ask for OTP/CVV on calls. It is a scam.

quiz.q: What does paying only the ‘minimum amount due’ protect you from?
quiz.why: Paying the minimum due avoids the late payment fee, but interest still applies on the remaining balance. It does not stop interest, the annual fee or GST.

quiz.q: Roughly what yearly interest do many Indian credit cards charge on revolving balances?
quiz.why: Monthly rates of about 3–3.75% add up to roughly 36–45% a year. Check your card’s terms.

quiz.q: Which keeps your credit utilisation healthy?
options: Keeping usage to roughly 30% or less of the limit
quiz.why: Keep credit utilisation to roughly 30% or less of your limit, which shows you are not dependent on credit. Using 90% or maxing out the card hurts your score.

quiz.q: Best single habit with a credit card?
options: Auto-debit for the total amount due
Pay only when the bank calls
quiz.why: Auto-debit for the total amount due ensures the full bill is paid on time, which avoids interest and builds your score. Paying only the minimum or at random leaves interest and late fees.

sources: RBI Master Direction on Credit Card and Debit Card (2022)

lessons.title: Your credit score (CIBIL) — what builds it, what breaks it

story.title: Priya and Sam apply for loans

scenes.text: Priya, 27, in Delhi, applies for a car loan. The bank checks her credit report and offers her a lower interest rate because of her score of 790.
Her friend Sam has never had a loan or card. He is not ‘bad’ — but he has no history, so lenders know nothing about him.
Her cousin Rohan is rejected: two missed EMIs on a phone loan and a ‘settled’ credit card account appear in his report.
All three learn what lenders see — and how to improve it.

steps.title: What a credit score is
steps.body:
A **credit score** is a three-digit number that summarises how you have handled borrowed money. In India the score ranges from **300 to 900**; higher is better. Many lenders treat roughly **750 and above** as good, but each lender has its own policy.

Scores are made by **credit bureaus** (credit information companies) licensed by RBI: **TransUnion CIBIL, Experian, Equifax and CRIF High Mark**. People say ‘CIBIL score’ the way they say ‘Xerox’ for photocopy, but there are four bureaus and your scores can differ slightly.

steps.title: What affects the score
steps.body:
- **Payment history** (biggest factor): paying EMIs and card bills on time, every time.
- **Credit utilisation**: how much of your card limits you use.
- **Credit mix**: a mix of secured (home, car) and unsecured (card, personal) loans handled well.
- **Length of history**: older well-handled accounts help.
- **New credit enquiries**: many loan applications in a short time look ‘credit hungry’.
- **Negative remarks**: ‘written off’ or ‘settled’ (paid less than owed) hurt for years. Being a **guarantor** or **joint borrower** also makes you responsible if the other person misses payments.

steps.title: Building and repairing
steps.body:
No history? Start small: a basic credit card (or a card against a fixed deposit), use a little, pay in full. Missed payments? Clear overdue amounts, then make every future payment on time — recent behaviour matters most, and scores improve over months. Avoid applying for many loans at once.

Checking **your own** score is a ‘soft’ enquiry and does not lower it. RBI requires each bureau to give you one free full credit report a year.

steps.title: Errors and myths
steps.body:
- **Myth**: checking your own score lowers it. False.
- **Myth**: income decides your score. Income is not part of the score; repayment behaviour is.
- **Myth**: paid agents can ‘wipe’ your bad history for a fee. Real negative records can’t be erased; only **errors** can be corrected.
- **Errors happen**: a loan that isn’t yours, a closed loan shown as open. Raise a dispute with the bureau online; the lender must verify and correct. Unknown loans in your name may mean identity theft — report it.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Download your free credit report from one bureau’s official site. Check that every account listed is yours, that closed loans show ‘closed’, and that your name, PAN and address are correct.

activity.prompt: Match each action to its effect on your score.
pairs: Applying to 6 lenders in one month
‘Settling’ a card by paying less than owed

quiz.q: The credit score range used by Indian bureaus is…
quiz.why: Credit scores in India run from 300 to 900, with higher being better. The other ranges are not used by the bureaus.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a credit bureau in India?
quiz.why: SEBI regulates securities markets and is not a credit bureau. Experian, CRIF High Mark and TransUnion CIBIL are credit bureaus.

quiz.q: Does checking your own credit score lower it?
options: No, it is a soft enquiry
quiz.why: Checking your own score is a soft enquiry and does not lower it. Only hard enquiries from lenders when you apply for credit can affect it.

quiz.q: The single biggest factor in a credit score is usually…
quiz.why: Payment history is usually the biggest factor in a credit score, because on-time repayment shows reliability. Salary, city and bank brand are not scored.

quiz.q: You find a loan in your report that you never took. You should…
options: Raise a dispute with the bureau and inform the lender; consider identity theft reporting
quiz.why: A loan you never took may be fraud in your name, so dispute it with the bureau, inform the lender and consider reporting identity theft. Ignoring or paying it leaves the record and the risk.

sources: RBI — Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act 2005 and RBI directions

lessons.title: Loans and EMI: the maths banks use

scenes.text: Nisha, 31, in Jaipur, needs ₹5 lakh for her sister’s higher studies. Offer A: ‘only 7% flat’. Offer B: 12% per year on reducing balance.
7% sounds cheaper. Her friend Joseph, a loan officer in Kochi, asks her to compare the EMI and total interest instead of the headline rate.
They calculate: the ‘7% flat’ loan actually costs about the same as roughly 12–13% reducing.
Nisha also learns that a shorter tenure means a higher EMI but much less total interest.

steps.title: Principal, rate, tenure, EMI
steps.body:
- **Principal (P)**: the amount borrowed.
- **Interest rate**: the yearly price of borrowing.
- **Tenure (n)**: number of monthly instalments.
- **EMI** (equated monthly instalment): the fixed monthly payment that covers interest and part of the principal.

In a **reducing-balance** loan (the normal method for bank home, car and personal loans) interest is charged only on what you still owe. Early EMIs are mostly interest; later EMIs are mostly principal.

steps.title: Worked example: calculating an EMI
steps.body:
Formula: **EMI = P × r × (1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1)**, where r = yearly rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100.

P = ₹5,00,000, 12% a year, 5 years.
- r = 12 ÷ 12 ÷ 100 = 0.01
- n = 60, (1.01)^60 ≈ 1.8167
- EMI = 5,00,000 × 0.01 × 1.8167 ÷ 0.8167 ≈ **₹11,122**
- Total paid ≈ 11,122 × 60 = ₹6,67,320
- Total interest ≈ **₹1,67,320**

You don’t need to do this by hand every time — bank websites have EMI calculators — but knowing the formula helps you check offers.

steps.title: The ‘flat rate’ trap
steps.body:
A **flat rate** charges interest on the full original amount for the whole tenure, even though you repay every month.

₹5,00,000 at 7% flat for 5 years: interest = 5,00,000 × 7% × 5 = ₹1,75,000. EMI = 6,75,000 ÷ 60 = **₹11,250** — higher than the 12% reducing loan’s ₹11,122! Always compare **EMI, total cost, processing fees** and the **APR** (annual percentage rate including fees). RBI rules require lenders to give a Key Fact Statement showing the APR for many retail loans.

steps.title: Tenure, prepayment and floating rates
steps.body:
Longer tenure → smaller EMI → **much more total interest**. On a 20-year home loan, total interest can be close to or more than the original loan.

**Floating rate** loans change with the bank’s benchmark rate; **fixed rate** stay the same for a period. Under RBI rules, banks and NBFCs cannot charge foreclosure or prepayment penalties on floating-rate term loans taken by individuals for non-business purposes. Prepaying even small amounts early in a loan saves a lot of interest.

steps.title: A healthy limit
steps.body: A common guideline is to keep **all EMIs together under about 30–40% of take-home pay**. Borrow for things that grow value or are essential (education, a home you can afford) rather than for holidays and gadgets.

activity.prompt: A loan has an EMI of ₹11,122 for 60 months on a principal of ₹5,00,000. What is the total interest paid (in ₹)?

quiz.q: In a reducing-balance loan, interest is charged on…
quiz.why: In a reducing-balance loan, interest is charged on the outstanding balance, so it falls as you repay principal. Flat-rate loans charge on the original amount.

quiz.q: Two loans have the same rate. One is 3 years, one is 7 years. The 7-year loan has…
quiz.why: At the same rate, a longer 7-year loan has a lower EMI but costs more total interest because you owe money for longer. The 3-year loan has the higher EMI and less interest.

quiz.q: Why is ‘7% flat’ misleading?
options: Interest is on the full original amount, so the effective rate is much higher
quiz.why: A flat rate charges interest on the full original amount for the whole term, even as you repay, so the effective rate is much higher; 7% flat over 5 years is roughly 12–13% reducing. Flat rates are legal but misleading.

quiz.q: For r in the EMI formula with 9% yearly interest, you use…
quiz.why: The monthly rate in the EMI formula is annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100, so 9% gives 9 ÷ 12 ÷ 100 = 0.0075.

quiz.q: Can a bank charge a prepayment penalty on an individual’s floating-rate home loan (non-business)?
options: Only if prepaid in the first month
quiz.why: RBI rules bar foreclosure or prepayment charges on floating-rate loans to individuals that are not for business. So the bank cannot charge a penalty, whether in the first month or later.

sources: RBI circulars on Key Fact Statement and foreclosure charges

lessons.title: Debt traps, loan apps and getting out of debt

scenes.text: Sunita, 34, in Nagpur, needs ₹8,000 for school fees. An app promises a loan in 5 minutes, ‘no documents’.
It asks for access to her contacts and photos. She gets only ₹5,600 after ‘fees’ and must repay ₹8,000 in 7 days.
When she is a day late, agents call her relatives and send threatening messages.
Her brother helps her report the app at 1930 and on the cybercrime portal, checks RBI’s list of regulated lenders, and they make a plan to clear her other debts.

steps.title: What a debt trap looks like
steps.body:
A **debt trap** is when you borrow to pay old loans, and the total keeps growing. Warning signs:
- You pay only minimum dues on cards.
- EMIs take more than about 40–50% of take-home pay.
- You use one loan or card to pay another.
- You hide bills from your family.
The earlier you act, the easier it is to escape.

steps.title: Illegal loan apps: red flags
steps.body:
- Lender is not a bank or an **RBI-registered NBFC** (or the app doesn’t clearly name the regulated lender behind it).
- Asks for access to **contacts, photos, gallery**.
- Deducts big ‘fees’ upfront; very short tenure (7–15 days).
- No clear **Key Fact Statement** with the APR.
- Threats, morphed photos, calls to your contacts.

RBI’s digital lending rules require loans to be disbursed into the borrower’s own bank account by the regulated lender and costs to be disclosed. Harassment is a crime: report at **1930** / cybercrime.gov.in and to the police. You can report unauthorised lenders on RBI’s **Sachet** portal.

steps.title: Two ways to pay off many debts
steps.body:
Sunita owes: card A ₹20,000 at 42%, phone loan ₹15,000 at 24%, friend ₹5,000 at 0%.
- **Avalanche**: pay minimums on all, then put every extra rupee on the **highest interest** (card A). Saves the most money.
- **Snowball**: clear the **smallest balance** first (friend ₹5,000) for a quick win, then the next. Builds motivation.
Both work if you stop adding new debt. Avalanche is cheaper; snowball is easier for many people to stick to.

steps.title: Getting help
steps.body:
- Talk to your bank before you miss payments; ask about restructuring or a lower-interest loan to replace costly card debt (debt consolidation).
- Sell unused things; pause wants for a few months.
- Tell one trusted family member — shame keeps people stuck.
- Under RBI’s fair practices code, recovery agents must not harass, threaten or call at odd hours. Complain to the lender and, if unresolved, to the **RBI Ombudsman** (Integrated Ombudsman Scheme).

steps.title: Around the world
steps.body: Payday loans in the UK and USA, and loan sharks everywhere, use the same trick: fast cash, tiny amount, huge effective interest. In many countries, free non-profit debt counselling exists. The rule is universal: if a loan feels too easy, read the total cost.

a.text: You need ₹10,000 urgently. An app offers instant cash but asks for contact and gallery access. What now?

choices.label: Allow access — it’s fast
choices.feedback: Contact access is a classic tool for harassment. Legitimate lenders don’t need your gallery.

choices.label: Check if the lender is a bank/RBI-registered NBFC and look for the Key Fact Statement
choices.feedback: Good. Verifying the regulated lender is the first step.

b.text: You can’t find any regulated lender named. Alternatives?

choices.label: Ask your bank about a small personal loan or overdraft, or ask family for a short-term loan with a written plan
choices.feedback: Regulated, transparent options are far safer.

choices.label: Try three more instant apps
choices.feedback: Multiple unregulated loans multiply the trap.

bad.text: The app harasses your contacts. Don’t pay extra under threat: save evidence, report at 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in, file a police complaint and tell your contacts it’s a scam.

good.text: You borrowed safely and know the full cost. Make a repayment date in your calendar.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag for an illegal loan app?
options: Money sent to your bank account
Asks for access to your contacts and photos
quiz.why: Asking for access to your contacts and photos is a red flag for an illegal loan app, because that access is used for harassment. A clear Key Fact Statement and an RBI-regulated lender are good signs.

quiz.q: The avalanche method pays extra first on…
quiz.why: The avalanche method pays extra on the loan with the highest interest rate first, which saves the most interest. The smallest balance first is the snowball method.

quiz.q: Recovery agents calling your relatives with threats is…
quiz.why: Recovery agents threatening you or your relatives are not allowed, because harassment violates RBI rules and can be a crime. Report it; it is not normal or required by law.

quiz.q: If a bank does not resolve your complaint, you can approach…
quiz.why: The RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme handles complaints against regulated entities.

questions.q: What does EMI stand for?
questions.why: EMI stands for Equated Monthly Instalment, a fixed monthly payment covering principal and interest. The other expansions are not real terms.

questions.q: Higher credit scores are…
questions.why: Higher credit scores are better because they show reliable repayment, which helps you get loans on better terms.

questions.q: Paying a credit card’s total amount due by the due date means…
questions.why: Paying the total amount due by the due date means you pay no interest on purchases, because you are within the interest-free period.

questions.q: Which hurts a credit score the most?
options: Keeping old cards open and unused
questions.why: Missing payments hurts a score most because payment history is the biggest factor. Keeping old cards open, having a savings account or checking your own score does not hurt.

questions.q: Credit card limit ₹50,000. Using about how much keeps utilisation near 30%?
questions.why: Utilisation near 30% means 30% of the limit: 0.30 × 50,000 = ₹15,000.

questions.q: Cash withdrawn using a credit card usually…
options: Attracts a fee and interest from day one
questions.why: Cash withdrawn on a credit card attracts a fee and interest from day one, with no interest-free period. It is among the most expensive ways to use a card.

questions.q: For 6% yearly interest, the monthly rate r in the EMI formula is…
questions.why: Monthly rate = annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100, so 6% gives 6 ÷ 12 ÷ 100 = 0.005.

questions.q: ₹2,00,000 at 10% flat for 2 years. Total interest?
questions.why: Flat interest is on the full amount for each year: 2,00,000 × 10% × 2 = ₹40,000.

questions.q: Which statement about credit bureaus in India is correct?
options: There are four RBI-licensed bureaus and scores can differ slightly
questions.why: India has four RBI-licensed bureaus (CIBIL, Experian, Equifax, CRIF High Mark), and scores can differ slightly. They only supply reports; lenders decide approvals, and SEBI does not run them.

questions.q: Becoming a guarantor for a friend’s loan means…
options: If they miss payments you are liable and your credit report can be affected
questions.why: A guarantor is legally responsible if the borrower defaults, and the loan can show on the guarantor's credit report. It carries real risk and pays no interest.

questions.q: Owes card 42%, personal loan 14%, car loan 9%. With ₹5,000 extra each month, the avalanche method targets…
questions.why: The avalanche method targets the highest interest rate first, and the credit card at 42% is the costliest. Extra payments there save the most interest while you pay minimums on the others.

questions.q: Which number best compares two loans with different fees?
questions.why: APR or total cost including fees is the best way to compare loans because it includes fees and the interest method. A headline flat rate hides costs, and a logo or advert tells you nothing.

questions.q: A loan of ₹1,00,000 at 12% reducing over 12 months has an EMI of about ₹8,885. Total interest is about…
questions.why: Total paid = 8,885 × 12 = ₹1,06,620, so interest = 1,06,620 − 1,00,000 ≈ ₹6,620. A flat 12% would charge ₹12,000, so reducing balance is cheaper.

questions.q: Someone pays only minimum dues on ₹80,000 card debt and plans to open two new cards. Best advice?
options: Stop new spending, pay highest-interest debt aggressively or consolidate at a lower rate, and avoid new credit applications
Ignore it, it will settle itself
questions.why: Stopping new debt and reducing high-interest balances breaks the trap; new applications and app loans worsen it.

courses.title: Grow your money: FD, PPF, EPF, NPS, mutual funds & SIP
courses.summary: Compounding and inflation, safe options (FD, RD, PPF), retirement options (EPF, NPS), mutual funds, SIPs and index funds, and how to avoid investment scams.
outcomes: Learners can compute compound growth and use the rule of 72
Learners can explain why inflation makes ‘safe’ money lose value
Learners can compare FD, PPF, EPF and NPS on safety, lock-in and purpose
Learners can explain NAV, SIP, expense ratio and index funds
Learners can spot ‘guaranteed high return’ scams

lessons.title: Compounding and inflation: time is your superpower

scenes.text: Ananya starts investing ₹3,000 a month at 25. Her friend Vikram waits until 35, thinking he’ll ‘catch up later’.
Both stop adding at 60. Assuming the same yearly return, Ananya ends up with far more — even though Vikram later invests bigger amounts.
Meanwhile their grandmother notices milk that cost far less in her youth now costs many times more. Money kept idle buys less each year.
The two forces every investor must understand: compounding (friend) and inflation (enemy).

steps.title: Simple vs compound interest
steps.body:
**Simple interest** is paid only on the original amount. **Compound interest** is paid on the original amount *and* on interest already earned — interest earns interest.

Formula: **A = P × (1 + r)^t**, where P = starting amount, r = yearly rate as a decimal, t = years (yearly compounding).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
₹1,00,000 at 8% a year for 10 years:
- Simple: interest = 1,00,000 × 0.08 × 10 = ₹80,000 → **₹1,80,000**
- Compound: 1,00,000 × (1.08)^10 ≈ 1,00,000 × 2.1589 = **₹2,15,892**
After 20 years compound: × 4.661 ≈ ₹4,66,096; after 30 years: × 10.06 ≈ ₹10,06,266. The growth speeds up with time — that’s why starting early matters more than starting big.

steps.title: The rule of 72
steps.body:
Quick mental maths: **years to double ≈ 72 ÷ yearly return %**.
- 6% → about 12 years
- 8% → about 9 years
- 12% → about 6 years
It also works for inflation: at 6% inflation, prices roughly **double in 12 years**, so the same money buys about half.

steps.title: Real return = return − inflation (roughly)
steps.body: If your savings earn 3% while inflation is 6%, your money **loses about 3% of buying power** each year, even though the number in your account grows. The **real return** is roughly return minus inflation. Safe options protect capital; growth options (like equity) aim to beat inflation over long periods but go up and down along the way. A good plan uses both, depending on when you need the money.

steps.title: Try this in the lab
steps.body: Open the **Compound interest** lab. Put ₹10,000 at 8% for 10, 20 and 30 years. Then compare starting 10 years later. Note how much of the final amount is interest.

activity.label: Yearly return (%) — see how long money takes to double

bands.text: Doubling takes about 24–72 years. Savings-account style returns often fail to beat inflation.
About 12–18 years to double. Typical of fixed deposits / small savings; roughly keeps pace with inflation.
About 8–12 years to double. Long-term mixed portfolios aim here, with some ups and downs.
About 6–8 years to double. Long-term equity has achieved such returns in some periods, with big swings. Not guaranteed.
About 5 years to double. Anyone ‘guaranteeing’ this every year is a red flag for a scam.

quiz.q: ₹10,000 at 10% compound for 2 years becomes…
quiz.why: Compound growth: 10,000 × 1.1 = 11,000 after year 1, then 11,000 × 1.1 = ₹12,100. Simple interest would give only ₹12,000.

quiz.q: By the rule of 72, money at 9% doubles in about…
quiz.why: Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate = 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years.

quiz.q: Savings earn 4%, inflation is 6%. Real return is about…
quiz.why: Real return ≈ interest rate − inflation = 4% − 6% = −2%, so your buying power falls even though the balance grows.

quiz.q: Why does starting early matter so much?
options: Interest rates are higher for the young
Compounding needs time; growth accelerates in later years
quiz.why: Starting early matters because compounding needs time, and growth accelerates in later years as interest earns interest. Banks do not give young people higher rates.

lessons.title: Safe and retirement options: FD, RD, PPF, EPF, NPS

scenes.text: Rekha, 38, a teacher in Bhopal, has money scattered: a savings account, an FD her father opened, EPF from her school and a PPF account she forgot.
Her son Aman, a commerce student, makes a table: what each product is for, how safe it is and when the money can be taken out.
Rekha realises: FD for goals in 1–3 years, PPF and EPF for long-term and retirement, and she starts NPS for extra retirement savings.

steps.title: Fixed deposit (FD) and recurring deposit (RD)
steps.body:
- **FD**: lump sum locked for a chosen period (7 days to 10 years) at a fixed rate. Breaking early usually means a small penalty.
- **RD**: deposit a fixed amount every month for a period; good for building a goal amount.
- Interest is **taxable** at your income-tax slab; banks deduct TDS above certain limits.
- Bank deposits are insured by **DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank**.
Best for: short-term goals and parts of an emergency fund.

steps.title: PPF — Public Provident Fund
steps.body:
- Government-backed small-savings scheme, open at a post office or bank.
- **15-year** term, extendable in blocks of 5 years. Partial withdrawals and loans are allowed after some years under the rules.
- Deposit **₹500 to ₹1.5 lakh per financial year**.
- Interest rate is set by the government each quarter.
- Interest and maturity are tax-free, and deposits qualify for deduction under the old tax regime.
Best for: safe, long-term savings (children’s future, retirement).

steps.title: EPF — Employees’ Provident Fund
steps.body: For many salaried employees, **12% of basic pay + DA** is deducted for EPF, and the employer also contributes (part goes to the Employees’ Pension Scheme). Managed by **EPFO**. Your **UAN** (Universal Account Number) stays the same when you change jobs — transfer old accounts instead of withdrawing, so compounding continues. You can check your passbook on the EPFO portal or UMANG app. Withdrawing EPF for small wants is one of the most common retirement mistakes.

steps.title: NPS — National Pension System
steps.body: A voluntary, **market-linked** retirement scheme regulated by **PFRDA**. You choose a fund manager and a mix of equity, corporate bonds and government securities (or an automatic age-based mix). **Tier I** is the main retirement account with withdrawal restrictions until retirement; **Tier II** is an optional flexible account. At retirement, part of the corpus can be withdrawn and part must be used to buy an **annuity** (a regular pension). Withdrawal rules and percentages have been revised over time — check the current PFRDA rules before deciding.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Locking emergency money in PPF or NPS.
- Forgetting nominations — always add a **nominee** to every account.
- Withdrawing EPF on every job change.
- Assuming ‘safe’ means ‘enough’: safe products may barely beat inflation; long goals may need some equity too.

activity.prompt: Match each product to its best description.
pairs: Lump sum at a fixed rate for a chosen term
Fixed monthly deposits towards a goal
Salary-linked provident fund managed by EPFO
Market-linked retirement scheme regulated by PFRDA
Insures bank deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank

quiz.q: What is the basic term of a PPF account?
quiz.why: A PPF account has a basic term of 15 years, and it can be extended in blocks of 5 years.

quiz.q: Maximum PPF deposit per financial year?
