quiz.why: The maximum PPF deposit is ₹1.5 lakh per financial year (minimum ₹500). There is a limit.

quiz.q: Your UAN is linked to…
quiz.why: The UAN is the single Universal Account Number for your EPF that stays with you across employers. It is not linked to credit cards or passports.

quiz.q: Which product is market-linked?
quiz.why: NPS invests in equity and bonds, so its returns vary with markets. PPF, FD and RD have fixed or government-set rates.

quiz.q: Best home for money needed in 18 months for a course fee?
quiz.why: Money needed in 18 months should be safe with a fixed date, so FD or RD fits. NPS Tier I is locked for retirement, PPF is long-term and small-cap shares can fall right before the fee is due.

sources: Ministry of Finance — PPF Scheme rules

lessons.title: Mutual funds, SIP and index funds explained simply

scenes.text: Imran, 26, runs a small café in Srinagar. He wants to invest but has no time to study companies.
His friend Grace from Shillong explains a mutual fund as a big basket: thousands of people put money in, and a professional manager buys many shares or bonds.
He starts a ₹2,000 monthly SIP in a Nifty 50 index fund. In month three the market falls and he panics.
Grace shows him that his ₹2,000 bought more units that month. He stays invested.

steps.title: What a mutual fund is
steps.body:
A **mutual fund** pools money from many investors and invests it in shares (equity), bonds (debt) or both (hybrid), as per its stated objective. It is run by an **AMC** (asset management company) and regulated by **SEBI**.

You own **units**. The price of one unit is the **NAV** (net asset value), calculated each business day. If the fund’s investments rise, NAV rises. Mutual fund returns are **not guaranteed**: ‘Mutual fund investments are subject to market risks.’

steps.title: Key words
steps.body:
- **Equity funds**: mainly shares; higher ups and downs; for goals 5+ years away.
- **Debt funds**: bonds and money-market; lower volatility, but not risk-free.
- **Index fund**: copies an index like the **Nifty 50** or **Sensex** instead of a manager picking stocks. Usually low cost.
- **Expense ratio**: yearly fee as a % of your money. Small differences compound over decades.
- **Direct plan** vs **regular plan**: same fund; regular includes distributor commission so its expense ratio is higher.
- **Exit load**: a fee if you sell too soon (check the fund document).

steps.title: Worked example: SIP and rupee cost averaging
steps.body:
A **SIP** (systematic investment plan) invests a fixed amount every month.
Imran invests ₹1,000 monthly:
- Month 1 NAV ₹10 → 100 units
- Month 2 NAV ₹8 → 125 units
- Month 3 NAV ₹12.50 → 80 units
Total ₹3,000 for 305 units → average cost ≈ **₹9.84 per unit**, lower than the simple average NAV of ₹10.17. Falls let you buy more units. This is **rupee cost averaging**. It reduces timing stress; it does not guarantee profit.

steps.title: Mistakes beginners make
steps.body:
- Stopping SIPs when markets fall (that’s when units are cheap).
- Choosing funds only by last year’s return.
- Owning 12 similar funds (no real diversification, more confusion).
- Ignoring the expense ratio.
- Investing money needed within 1–3 years in equity.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find one Nifty 50 index fund’s factsheet. Note: NAV, expense ratio (direct plan), exit load and benchmark. Compare with one other index fund tracking the same index — which has lower cost?

activity.prompt: Complete the sentences.
activity.text: The price of one mutual fund unit is called the ___. A fixed monthly investment is called a ___. A fund that copies the Nifty 50 is an ___ fund. The yearly fee charged by a fund is its expense ___.

quiz.q: Who regulates mutual funds in India?
quiz.why: SEBI regulates mutual funds and the securities markets. PFRDA regulates pensions, RBI banks and IRDAI insurance.

quiz.q: An index fund…
options: Copies a market index like Nifty 50
quiz.why: An index fund copies a market index like Nifty 50 instead of picking stocks. It still carries market risk and promises no fixed return.

quiz.q: Why is a direct plan usually cheaper than a regular plan?
options: It has no distributor commission, so a lower expense ratio
quiz.why: A direct plan has no distributor commission, so its expense ratio is lower. The portfolio is the same as in a regular plan, which includes the commission.

quiz.q: In a SIP, when NAV falls, your fixed amount buys…
quiz.why: When the NAV falls, the same fixed SIP amount buys more units because each unit costs less.

quiz.q: Equity funds suit goals that are…
quiz.why: Equity funds suit goals usually 5+ years away because they need time to recover from market falls. Goals within a year need safer options.

lessons.title: Risk, goals, diversification — and investment scams

scenes.text: Harish, 45, in Surat, joins a Telegram group promising ‘3% daily profit’ from ‘expert trading’.
He invests ₹50,000 and sees fake profits on a dashboard. He adds ₹4 lakh. When he asks to withdraw, they demand a ‘tax fee’.
The group disappears. His niece Zoya, who invests through a plain SIP, helps him report it at 1930.
Together they learn how real investing works: goals, time, diversification — and no guarantees.

steps.title: Order of steps (the money ladder)
steps.body:
1. Budget and stop high-interest debt.
2. Emergency fund (3–6 months).
3. Adequate **health and term life insurance** if others depend on you.
4. Then invest for goals.
Skipping steps is how people end up selling investments at a loss in an emergency.

steps.title: Match the product to the goal’s time
steps.body:
- **Under 3 years** (bike, course fee): FD, RD, high-quality debt options.
- **3–5 years** (car, wedding): a mix — mostly safe, some equity.
- **5+ years** (child’s higher education, retirement): equity index funds/diversified equity, plus PPF/EPF/NPS.
Example: Zoya, 28, has ₹10,000 a month for investing: ₹6,000 in a Nifty 50 index fund SIP for retirement, ₹2,000 in PPF, ₹2,000 in an RD for a laptop next year.

steps.title: Diversification
steps.body: **Don’t put all eggs in one basket.** Spread across many companies (a fund does this), across asset types (equity, debt, gold), and across time (SIP). Diversification doesn’t remove risk but reduces the chance that one bad event ruins you. A higher potential return always comes with higher risk — there is no free lunch.

steps.title: Scam checklist
steps.body:
- **Guaranteed** high returns (‘2% a day’, ‘double in 6 months’).
- Pressure to bring friends (Ponzi/pyramid pattern).
- Tips on WhatsApp/Telegram from ‘experts’ or fake celebrity videos.
- Paying into a personal bank account or UPI ID.
- ‘Pay a fee/tax to withdraw your profits’.
- Unregulated ‘advisers’: check SEBI registration of investment advisers and research analysts on SEBI’s website; brokers must be SEBI-registered.
Report at 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in and SEBI’s SCORES portal for complaints against regulated entities.

steps.title: Calm investor habits
steps.body: Automate SIPs, review once or twice a year, rebalance if your mix drifts far from plan, and avoid checking prices daily. Always add nominees. If you take advice, prefer a SEBI-registered investment adviser who charges a transparent fee.

a.text: A WhatsApp group admin says: ‘Join our VIP stock group, 5% weekly guaranteed. Pay ₹10,000 to my UPI to start.’

choices.label: Pay — guaranteed is safe
choices.feedback: No legitimate investment guarantees 5% weekly. Paying to a personal UPI is a big red flag.

choices.label: Ask for their SEBI registration number and check it on SEBI’s website
choices.feedback: Good move.

b.text: They send a registration number, but SEBI’s site shows a different name. They push: ‘Offer closes in 1 hour!’

choices.label: Leave the group and report the number
choices.feedback: Correct — mismatched details plus urgency = scam.

choices.label: Pay half to test
choices.feedback: ‘Small test’ payments are how they hook people.

bad.text: The money is gone and they ask for ‘withdrawal tax’. Don’t pay more. Report at 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in immediately.

good.text: Safe. Real investing is boring: diversified funds, time and patience.

quiz.q: Which should come before investing in equity?
options: Emergency fund and clearing high-interest debt
quiz.why: Before investing in equity, build an emergency fund and clear high-interest debt. That safe base prevents forced selling when you need cash.

quiz.q: ‘Guaranteed 3% per day’ indicates…
quiz.why: No genuine investment can guarantee 3% per day, so such claims are likely a scam. FDs and government bonds offer modest, fixed returns.

quiz.q: Diversification means…
options: Putting all money in one hot stock
Spreading money across companies, asset types and time
quiz.why: Diversification means spreading money across companies, asset types and time, so one failure does less damage. Putting everything in one hot stock does the opposite.

quiz.q: Where can you check if an investment adviser is genuine in India?
quiz.why: Check SEBI's list of registered intermediaries, which publishes registered advisers and research analysts. An adviser's own Telegram, a random SMS or a comment is not a verification.

questions.q: Compound interest means…
options: Interest only on the original amount
Interest also earned on past interest
questions.why: Compound interest means you earn interest on past interest as well as on the original amount. Interest only on the original amount is simple interest.

questions.q: SIP stands for…
questions.why: SIP stands for Systematic Investment Plan, where a fixed amount is invested regularly, for example monthly.

questions.q: Who regulates NPS?
questions.why: PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority) regulates the NPS. SEBI regulates markets, IRDAI insurance and EPFO runs the EPF.

questions.q: Rule of 72 at 6% return: years to double?
questions.why: Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years.

questions.q: NAV is…
options: The price of one unit of a mutual fund
questions.why: NAV (net asset value) is the price of one unit of a mutual fund. It is not a bank charge or a tax.

questions.q: ₹50,000 at 10% compounded yearly for 3 years?
questions.why: Compounding for 3 years: 50,000 × 1.1³ = 50,000 × 1.331 = ₹66,550. Simple interest would give ₹65,000.

questions.q: Which is true of PPF?
questions.why: PPF has a 15-year term with government-set interest and a yearly deposit cap of ₹1.5 lakh. It is not market-linked and not fully withdrawable at any time.

questions.q: Two index funds track Nifty 50: expense ratios 0.2% and 1.0%. Long-term, the 0.2% fund…
options: Is likely to give higher net returns
questions.why: Both track the same index, so gross returns are similar and the 0.2% fund keeps more for you after lower fees. Over the long term this is likely to give higher net returns, with the same risk.

questions.q: Inflation 6%, FD 7% before tax. If tax takes 30% of interest, the real return is about…
questions.why: After tax the FD earns 7% × 0.7 = 4.9%. Real return ≈ 4.9 − 6 = −1.1%, so buying power falls.

questions.q: SIP ₹1,000 at NAVs ₹20, ₹25, ₹20. Total units?
questions.why: Units = amount ÷ NAV each time: 1,000 ÷ 20 = 50, 1,000 ÷ 25 = 40 and 1,000 ÷ 20 = 50. Total = 50 + 40 + 50 = 140 units.

questions.q: Changing jobs, the best thing to do with EPF is usually…
options: Transfer it under the same UAN
Move it to a credit card
questions.why: When changing jobs, transfer your EPF under the same UAN so it keeps compounding and your retirement savings stay intact. Withdrawing and spending it loses that growth.

questions.q: A 30-year-old saving for retirement and a child’s school fees due in 1 year. Best mix?
options: Retirement: equity index SIP/EPF/NPS; school fees: FD/RD
questions.why: Match risk to time horizon: retirement is decades away so equity index SIPs, EPF and NPS suit, while school fees due in 1 year need safe FD or RD. Small-cap stocks or crypto could fall before the fees are due.

questions.q: Which statement about rupee cost averaging is accurate?
options: It lowers average cost when prices fluctuate but cannot prevent losses if markets fall long-term
It means buying once a year
questions.why: Rupee cost averaging smooths the average purchase cost when prices fluctuate, but it is not a guarantee and cannot prevent losses if markets keep falling. It is not limited to FDs or yearly buying.

courses.title: Insurance & income tax basics in India
courses.summary: Term life, health and motor insurance without jargon; income tax basics — PAN, TDS, Form 16, AIS, old vs new regime — and how to file an ITR.
outcomes: Learners can explain why term insurance is for dependants
Learners can read key health-policy terms: sum insured, waiting period, co-pay, room-rent limit
Learners can explain FY vs AY, TDS, Form 16 and AIS
Learners can describe old vs new tax regime in general terms and where to check current slabs
Learners can list the steps of filing and verifying an ITR

lessons.title: Insurance basics: what to buy and what to skip

scenes.text: Deepa, 35, in Kolkata, is the main earner for her daughter and mother. An agent offers a policy that ‘gives money back’.
Her colleague Martin explains the difference between protection (insurance) and investment.
Deepa buys a pure term plan with a large cover for a modest premium, a family health policy, and invests the rest separately.
She tells her mother where the policy papers are and adds nominees — the step most people forget.

steps.title: How insurance works
steps.body:
Insurance is **pooling risk**: many people pay a small **premium**, and the few who suffer a covered loss get paid. You buy it for events that would be financially devastating (death of an earner, major illness, accident, big liability), not for small costs you can handle yourself.

Key words: **premium** (what you pay), **sum assured / sum insured** (the cover), **policy term**, **nominee** (who receives the claim), **exclusions** (what is not covered), **claim**.

steps.title: Term life insurance
steps.body:
A **term plan** pays the nominee if the insured person dies during the term. If you survive, nothing is paid back — that’s why it’s cheap for a large cover. You need it only if someone **depends on your income** (children, spouse, parents) or you have big loans.

A common rule of thumb for cover: about **10–15 times annual income**, plus outstanding loans, minus existing savings. Disclose health facts and habits like smoking honestly — non-disclosure can lead to claim rejection.

steps.title: Mixing insurance and investment
steps.body: Many traditional plans (endowment, money-back) combine small life cover with savings. They are often costlier than buying a term plan and investing separately, and returns are typically modest. Before buying any plan, ask: What is the sum assured? What is the return if I survive (ask for the illustration)? What are the surrender charges? Under IRDAI rules you have a **free-look period** to cancel a new policy if you are not satisfied — check the period in your policy document.

steps.title: Other insurance
steps.body:
- **Health insurance**: covered in the next lesson; essential for every family.
- **Motor insurance**: **third-party insurance is compulsory** under the Motor Vehicles Act for vehicles on public roads. ‘Comprehensive’ also covers damage to your own vehicle.
- **Personal accident** and **home** insurance: affordable add-ons worth considering.
Buy from IRDAI-registered insurers; verify the agent or app.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make a one-page ‘family folder’: policy numbers, insurer helplines, nominees, where papers are kept. Share it with one trusted family member.

activity.prompt: Does this person need a term life plan now?

items.text: Earner with a big home loan and a spouse
Retired person with no dependants and enough savings

quiz.q: A term plan pays out when…
options: The insured dies during the term
quiz.why: A term plan is pure protection and pays out only if the insured dies during the term. It pays nothing on survival and is not linked to markets or retirement.

quiz.q: Who most needs term insurance?
options: Someone with no dependants and no loans
quiz.why: Term insurance replaces income, so it matters most for someone whose income supports dependants. With no dependants and no loans, there is little need.

quiz.q: Which motor cover is compulsory in India?
quiz.why: Third-party motor cover is compulsory under the Motor Vehicles Act. Comprehensive and zero depreciation are optional extras.

quiz.q: Hiding a smoking habit when buying a policy can lead to…
quiz.why: Hiding a smoking habit is material non-disclosure, which can lead to claim rejection. Insurers can void a claim if important facts were concealed.

sources: IRDAI consumer education (Bima Bharosa / policyholder handbooks)

lessons.title: Health insurance: reading the fine print

scenes.text: Mr. Kulkarni, 58, in Nashik, is admitted for surgery. His policy has a sum insured of ₹5 lakh, so he feels safe.
The final bill is ₹3.2 lakh, but the insurer pays only part. His room cost more than the policy’s room-rent limit, so other charges were reduced in proportion.
His daughter Shalini, a nurse, sits with him to read the policy wording: co-pay, room-rent limit, waiting periods.
At renewal they move to a plan without a room-rent cap and keep an emergency fund for the gaps.

steps.title: Core terms
steps.body:
- **Sum insured**: maximum the insurer pays in a policy year.
- **Family floater**: one sum insured shared by the family.
- **Cashless**: at a **network hospital**, the insurer pays the hospital directly (after approval). **Reimbursement**: you pay and claim later with bills.
- **Pre- and post-hospitalisation**: costs before and after admission covered for a set number of days.
- **Day-care procedures**: treatments needing less than 24 hours (e.g., cataract).

steps.title: Fine print that reduces claims
steps.body:
- **Waiting periods**: an initial period (often 30 days, except accidents), specific-illness waiting periods and a longer waiting period for **pre-existing diseases**. Check exact durations in your policy.
- **Co-pay**: you pay a fixed % of every claim (e.g., 20%).
- **Room-rent limit**: if you take a costlier room, many policies reduce other charges proportionately.
- **Sub-limits** on specific treatments.
- **Exclusions**: e.g., cosmetic treatment.
Always read the **policy wording** and the **customer information sheet**, not just the brochure.

steps.title: Worked example: co-pay
steps.body: Claim ₹2,00,000 with 20% co-pay: you pay ₹40,000; the insurer pays ₹1,60,000 (if everything else is covered). A lower premium with high co-pay can cost much more when you actually fall ill.

steps.title: Good practices
steps.body:
- Buy early while healthy — premiums and waiting periods hurt less.
- Don’t rely only on employer cover: it usually ends when you leave the job.
- Disclose all existing illnesses honestly.
- Keep the insurer’s/TPA’s helpline and e-card on your phone.
- **Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY** provides cover of up to ₹5 lakh per family per year for eligible families at empanelled hospitals; check eligibility officially.
- Complaints: insurer’s grievance cell first, then IRDAI’s Bima Bharosa system or the **Insurance Ombudsman**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take your family’s policy and find: sum insured, co-pay, room-rent limit, pre-existing disease waiting period, and the cashless helpline. If any is unclear, call the insurer and write down the answer.

cards.back: The maximum the insurer will pay in a policy year.
At a network hospital, the insurer settles the bill directly after approval.
The fixed percentage of each claim that you pay yourself.
Time after buying when certain illnesses (especially pre-existing ones) are not covered.
A cap on room charges; exceeding it can cut other charges proportionately.
A free forum for policyholder complaints not resolved by the insurer.

quiz.q: Claim ₹1,00,000 with 10% co-pay. You pay…
quiz.why: Co-pay is the share you pay: 10% of ₹1,00,000 = ₹10,000, and the insurer pays the remaining ₹90,000.

quiz.q: Cashless treatment is usually available at…
quiz.why: Cashless treatment is available at network hospitals, which have tie-ups with the insurer. Pharmacies and ordinary shops are not part of the network.

quiz.q: Why shouldn’t you rely only on employer health cover?
options: It usually ends when you leave the job
quiz.why: Employer cover usually ends when you leave the job, which could leave you uninsured when you are older and costlier to insure. So keep your own policy too.

quiz.q: Which document gives the exact coverage rules?
quiz.why: The policy wording is the legal contract and gives the exact coverage rules. An agent's chat, an advertisement or a hospital menu is not binding.

sources: IRDAI Health Insurance Regulations and consumer handbooks

lessons.title: Income tax basics: PAN, TDS, Form 16, AIS and the two regimes

scenes.text: Rahul, 23, starts work in Gurugram. His salary slip shows ‘TDS’ and HR asks him to choose ‘old or new regime’.
He thinks: ‘Tax is already deducted, so I don’t need to do anything.’
His uncle, a chartered accountant, explains: TDS is an advance; the return (ITR) is where you settle the final tax and report all income, including FD interest.
They compare both regimes on the official calculator and Rahul picks the one with lower tax for his situation.

steps.title: The basic vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Financial year (FY)**: 1 April to 31 March, the year you earn.
- **Assessment year (AY)**: the next year, when that income is assessed and the return filed. Income of FY 2025–26 is filed in AY 2026–27.
- **PAN**: 10-character permanent account number; needed for filing and many financial transactions.
- **TDS**: tax deducted at source by the payer (employer, bank) and deposited against your PAN.
- **Form 16**: certificate from your employer showing salary and TDS.
- **Form 26AS** and **AIS** (Annual Information Statement): on the income-tax portal, they show TDS and many transactions reported about you (interest, dividends, large purchases). Match them before filing.

steps.title: Slab system
steps.body: India taxes individuals in **slabs**: income up to a basic exemption limit is not taxed, and higher portions are taxed at rising rates. Only the part of income inside each slab is taxed at that slab’s rate — moving into a higher slab does **not** make all your income taxed at the higher rate. Rebates can make tax zero up to a certain income. Slabs, rebates and standard deduction change in Union Budgets, so **always check current slabs on the official Income Tax Department website (incometax.gov.in)**.

steps.title: Old regime vs new regime (in general)
steps.body:
- **New regime**: lower slab rates and higher rebate limits, but most deductions and exemptions are **not** allowed (for example most of 80C, 80D and HRA). It is the **default** regime.
- **Old regime**: higher slab rates, but you can claim deductions and exemptions such as 80C investments (PPF, EPF, ELSS, life premium, up to the 80C limit), 80D health premium, HRA and home-loan interest, subject to rules.

Which is better depends on how many deductions you genuinely have. Salaried people without business income can generally choose each year when filing; people with business income have restrictions on switching. Use the official tax calculator to compare.

steps.title: How to compare (method, not slabs)
steps.body:
1. Write gross income (salary + interest + other income).
2. **New regime**: subtract only the deductions allowed there (such as the standard deduction for salaried people), then apply new slabs.
3. **Old regime**: subtract standard deduction and all eligible deductions (80C, 80D, HRA exemption, etc.), then apply old slabs.
4. Add cess, apply any rebate, compare.
Rule of thumb: if your genuine deductions are small, the new regime often wins; with large deductions (home loan interest + full 80C + HRA), the old one may win. Don’t buy products only to save tax.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting **FD/savings interest** — it is taxable and appears in AIS.
- Not checking Form 26AS/AIS vs Form 16.
- Thinking ‘no tax due’ means ‘no need to file’ — filing may still be required or useful (refunds, loans, visas, carrying forward losses).
- Falling for ‘tax refund’ SMS links — the department communicates through the official portal; never share OTPs.

activity.prompt: Old regime or new regime? Sort the general features.

items.text: Allows 80C deductions like PPF and ELSS
Applies automatically if you don’t opt for the other
Most exemptions like HRA not available

quiz.q: Income earned in FY 2025–26 is filed in…
quiz.why: Income earned in FY 2025–26 is assessed in the next year, AY 2026–27, and the return is filed then. The assessment year follows the financial year.

quiz.q: TDS is…
options: Tax deducted at source as an advance against your final tax
quiz.why: TDS is tax deducted at source as an advance against your final tax. It is credited to your PAN and adjusted when you file your return.

quiz.q: Moving into a higher slab means…
options: All income taxed at the higher rate
Only the income in that slab is taxed at the higher rate
quiz.why: Tax slabs are marginal, so moving into a higher slab taxes only the income inside that slab at the higher rate, not all your income.

quiz.q: Which regime is the default?
quiz.why: The new tax regime is the default and applies unless you opt for the old regime where permitted.

quiz.q: Where should you check current slab rates?
quiz.why: Slab rates change in budgets, so check the official Income Tax Department website for current ones. Old textbooks, shopping sites and forwarded images may be outdated or fake.

sources: Income Tax Department of India — taxpayer services and tax calculator
Income-tax Act (as amended by Finance Acts)

lessons.title: Filing your ITR step by step

scenes.text: Shabnam, 27, a lab analyst in Vadodara, has salary and some FD interest. She has always paid an agent ₹1,500 to file.
This year she logs into the e-filing portal with her PAN, downloads AIS, and finds most details pre-filled.
She notices the FD interest in AIS that the agent had missed last year, and adds it.
She submits, e-verifies with an Aadhaar OTP, and gets her refund a few weeks later.

steps.title: Which form?
steps.body: The department publishes several ITR forms. **ITR-1 (Sahaj)** is for resident individuals with simpler income (salary/pension, one house property, other sources like interest) within the income limit and conditions set for that year. Other forms cover capital gains, business income, foreign assets and so on. The portal guides you; read the eligibility notes each year.

steps.title: Due dates and verification
steps.body:
For most individuals who don’t need a tax audit, the usual due date is **31 July** after the end of the financial year (the government sometimes extends it — check the official portal). Late filing can attract a fee and loss of some benefits.

After submitting, you must **verify** the return within the allowed time (currently 30 days) — e-verify via Aadhaar OTP, net banking or other methods. **An unverified return is treated as not filed.**

steps.title: Step by step
steps.body:
1. Collect: Form 16, bank interest certificates, AIS/Form 26AS, rent receipts or investment proofs (if old regime).
2. Log in at the official e-filing portal using PAN (link Aadhaar with PAN).
3. Choose assessment year, form and regime.
4. Check pre-filled data; add missing income (interest, freelancing).
5. Claim eligible deductions; compute tax; pay any balance (self-assessment tax) first.
6. Submit and e-verify. Download the acknowledgement.
7. Track refund status; ensure your bank account is pre-validated on the portal.

steps.title: Avoid trouble
steps.body:
- Don’t claim deductions you don’t have — the department matches data and can send notices.
- Respond to genuine notices on the portal (check them under your login), not via links in SMS.
- Keep records for several years.
- If income is complex (capital gains, business, foreign income), consider a qualified professional.

steps.title: After filing
steps.body: Save the ITR-V acknowledgement PDF. Many banks, visa offices and lenders ask for 2–3 years of ITRs as proof of income. Filing on time each year — even with modest income — builds a clean financial record.

activity.prompt: Your ITR readiness checklist
items: AIS and Form 26AS downloaded and checked
Regime compared on the official calculator
Return submitted before the due date

quiz.q: An ITR submitted but not verified is…
quiz.why: An ITR that is submitted but not verified is treated as not filed, because verification completes the filing.

quiz.q: The usual due date for non-audit individuals is…
quiz.why: The usual due date for non-audit individuals is 31 July, unless extended, so check the portal for extensions. It is not 31 March or flexible.

quiz.q: Which document shows many transactions reported about you, like interest and dividends?
quiz.why: The Annual Information Statement (AIS) lists many reported transactions, such as interest and dividends. A ration card, voter ID or passport does not.

quiz.q: You get an SMS: ‘Claim your tax refund, click here and enter card details.’ You should…
options: Ignore it; check refund status only by logging into the official portal
quiz.why: Ignore such SMS messages and check refund status only by logging into the official portal. Refunds go to your pre-validated bank account, so no card details are ever needed.

sources: Income Tax Department e-filing portal help

questions.q: The amount you pay for insurance is called…
questions.why: The amount you pay for insurance cover is the premium. A nominee gets the payout, a claim is a request for payment and the sum insured is the cover amount.

questions.q: PAN has how many characters?
questions.why: A PAN is a 10-character alphanumeric number. Aadhaar has 12 digits.

questions.q: India’s financial year runs…
questions.why: India's financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March, not the calendar year.

questions.q: Term insurance gives money back if you survive. True?
questions.why: False. A pure term plan pays only on death within the term and gives nothing back if you survive.

questions.q: Employer certificate showing salary and TDS is…
questions.why: Form 16 is the certificate an employer issues showing salary paid and TDS. Form 49A is the PAN application and Form 60 is used when you have no PAN.

questions.q: A health policy with 20% co-pay and a ₹50,000 claim — insurer pays…
questions.why: With 20% co-pay you pay 20% of ₹50,000 = ₹10,000, so the insurer pays 50,000 − 10,000 = ₹40,000.

questions.q: Which motor insurance is mandatory for vehicles on public roads in India?
questions.why: Third-party insurance is mandatory for vehicles on public roads in India. Zero depreciation, engine protect and comprehensive are optional.

questions.q: Which is usually NOT allowed in the new tax regime?
questions.why: Most deductions such as Section 80C (including PPF) are not available in the new regime. The standard deduction for salaried people, filing an ITR and paying tax online remain.

questions.q: Exceeding a policy’s room-rent limit often leads to…
questions.why: Exceeding a policy's room-rent limit often leads to a proportionate reduction of other charges, so the claim is scaled down. It does not raise cover or give an upgrade.

questions.q: A rule-of-thumb term cover for someone earning ₹8 lakh a year with no loans?
questions.why: A common rule of thumb is 10–15 times annual income, so for ₹8 lakh that is about ₹80 lakh to ₹1.2 crore. ₹8 lakh is too low and ₹5 crore 'always' ignores individual need.

questions.q: FD interest is missing from your Form 16. When filing you should…
options: Report it under income from other sources (it appears in AIS)
questions.why: All income must be reported, so add the FD interest under income from other sources; it will appear in the AIS anyway. Hiding or ignoring it risks notices and penalties.

questions.q: Someone with large genuine deductions (home-loan interest, full 80C, HRA) should…
options: Buy more insurance to save tax
Compute tax under both regimes and pick the lower
questions.why: With large genuine deductions, compute tax under both regimes and pick the lower, because the better regime depends on your deductions. Buying more insurance just to save tax is not the logic.

questions.q: An agent says, ‘This plan gives life cover, high returns, and tax savings — no need to see the illustration.’ The best response is…
options: Ask for the sum assured, benefit illustration, surrender charges and compare with term + separate investment
questions.why: Understanding cover, returns and costs prevents mis-selling; free-look period also helps.

questions.q: Rahul crosses into a higher tax slab by ₹10,000. What happens?
options: His whole income is taxed at the higher rate
Only the ₹10,000 above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate (before any rebate effects)
questions.why: Tax slabs are marginal, so only the ₹10,000 above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate, not his whole income. The employer does not pay it and tax is not zero.

life-relationships-family.title: Family & relationships
life-relationships-family.description: Talking to parents, sibling fights, career decisions with family, marriage expectations, in-laws, couple conflict, recognising abuse, caring for elders, and loss and grief.

courses.title: Talking with family: parents, siblings and big decisions
courses.summary: How to talk to parents so they actually listen, handle sibling conflict fairly, discuss career choices with family, set respectful boundaries and repair after a fight.
outcomes: Learners can choose the right time and use ‘I’ statements with parents
Learners can tell fair from unfair fighting and calm sibling conflicts
Learners can present a big decision (like a career choice) with a plan
Learners can give a sincere apology and set a respectful boundary

lessons.title: Talking to parents so they listen

scenes.text: Ishita, 14, in Lucknow wants to go on a 3-day school trip to Nainital. Last year she asked while her father was rushing to work, and the answer was a sharp ‘No’.
This time she waits until Sunday evening tea, when he’s relaxed.
She shows the school letter, teacher’s phone number, itinerary and cost, and says: ‘I know you worry about safety. Here’s how the school handles it.’
Her father asks questions, calls the teacher, and agrees — with a daily check-in call.

steps.title: Why parents say no
steps.body: Most parents’ ‘no’ comes from **worry** (safety, money, studies, what relatives will say) or from **not having enough information**. Many parents grew up in a different world and are protecting you the way they know. Seeing their fear behind the anger helps you respond calmly instead of fighting.

steps.title: The 4-step conversation
steps.body:
1. **Pick the moment**: not when they’re tired, rushing, angry or in front of guests.
2. **Start with their concern**: ‘I know you worry about…’
3. **Use ‘I’ statements**: ‘I feel left out when I can’t join my friends’ instead of ‘You never let me do anything!’
4. **Bring a plan**: facts, costs, safety steps, a compromise (‘I’ll call every night’, ‘I’ll finish my project first’).
Then **listen** to their answer fully, even if it’s not what you want.

steps.title: Words that help and words that hurt
steps.body:
Helpful: ‘Can we talk about something important?’ · ‘What would make you comfortable?’ · ‘I understand.’ · ‘Can I explain my side?’
Hurtful: ‘You don’t understand anything!’ · ‘Everyone else’s parents allow it.’ · Silent treatment, door slamming, sarcasm.
Tone matters as much as words. If you get too upset, say ‘Can we continue this later?’ and come back.

steps.title: When you can’t talk to your parents
steps.body: Some topics feel impossible to raise, or a parent may be unsafe (violence, abuse, addiction). Talk to another trusted adult: relative, teacher, school counsellor. If you are being harmed, call **Childline 1098** or **112** in an emergency. Asking for help is a sign of strength.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of one request you want to make. Write: (1) their likely worry, (2) your ‘I’ statement, (3) your plan and a compromise. Practise it once in front of a mirror.

a.text: You want to join a weekend coding club that ends at 7 pm. Your mother is cooking dinner after a long workday. When do you ask?

choices.label: Right now, loudly, while she’s cooking
choices.feedback: She’s tired and busy — not the best moment.

choices.label: After dinner when she’s relaxed: ‘Can I talk to you about something?’
choices.feedback: Good timing makes listening easier.

choices.label: ‘You never listen to me!’ and slam the door
choices.feedback: This turns a request into a fight.

choices.label: ‘Okay, sorry. Can we talk after dinner?’
choices.feedback: Nice recovery.

b2.text: She says: ‘7 pm is late. How will you get home?’

choices.label: ‘I’ll share my location, come back with Riya whose father picks us up, and call when I leave.’
choices.feedback: You addressed her real worry with a plan.

choices.label: ‘Stop worrying, I’m not a baby.’
choices.feedback: Dismissing her concern makes ‘no’ more likely.

bad.text: The conversation ends badly. Wait, calm down, apologise for your tone and try again with a plan.

good.text: She agrees to try it for a month. You built trust — next requests will be easier.

quiz.q: Which is an ‘I’ statement?
options: ‘I feel left out when I can’t join my friends.’
quiz.why: An 'I' statement shares your feeling without blaming, as in 'I feel left out when I can't join my friends.' Phrases with 'you never' or 'everyone else' blame or exaggerate.

quiz.q: Most parental ‘no’s come from…
quiz.why: Most parental refusals come from worry or lack of information, not from wanting you unhappy. So answering their worry with facts helps.

quiz.q: Best time to ask for something important?
options: When they’re relaxed and have time
quiz.why: Ask when they are relaxed and have time, because they can listen properly. During a fight, while rushing or in front of guests, they are less likely to hear you.

quiz.q: If home isn’t safe, a child in India can call…
quiz.why: If home is not safe, a child in India can call Childline 1098. 1915 is consumer help, 1906 is LPG and 155260 is for cyber fraud.

sources: UNICEF parenting and adolescent communication resources

lessons.title: Sibling conflict: fighting fair

scenes.text: Brothers Aman, 13, and Kabir, 10, in Kolkata fight every evening over the TV and the shared phone.
Their mother keeps saying, ‘Why can’t you be like your brother?’ — to both of them. The fights get worse.
Their aunt, a teacher, helps them make a weekly screen schedule and a ‘cool-down corner’ rule.
A month later they still argue sometimes — but now they also team up in games.

steps.title: Why siblings fight
steps.body: Sibling conflict is **normal** — siblings share space, things, parents’ attention and different personalities. Fights increase with **comparison** (‘your sister is so neat’), **unfairness** (real or felt), **boredom**, **tiredness** and **stress** at home. Learning to handle sibling conflict teaches skills you’ll use with friends, colleagues and partners.

steps.title: Fair fighting rules
steps.body:
- **Talk about the problem, not the person** (‘You took my charger without asking’ not ‘You’re a thief’).
- **No hitting, no name-calling, no breaking things**.
- **Take a break** when angry: 10–20 minutes to cool down, then come back.
- **Each person speaks without interruption**; then repeat back what you heard.
- **Find a win-win**: schedules, turns, ‘you choose today, I choose tomorrow’, ask before borrowing.
- **Don’t drag old fights** into new ones.

steps.title: For parents and elders
steps.body:
- **Avoid comparisons and labels** (‘the clever one’, ‘the naughty one’).
- Spend some **one-on-one time** with each child.
- Treat children **fairly, not identically** — needs differ by age.
- Teach problem-solving instead of always being the judge.
- Step in immediately for physical harm or bullying.

steps.title: When it’s more than ‘normal fighting’
steps.body: If one sibling repeatedly hurts, threatens, humiliates or controls another, or touches them in ways that feel wrong, it is **not normal sibling rivalry** — it is harm. Tell a parent or trusted adult. Children can call **1098**. Every child has a right to feel safe at home.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With your sibling, write a simple agreement for your most common fight (TV, phone, room, chores). Stick it somewhere both of you can see.

activity.prompt: Fair or unfair fighting move?

items.text: ‘I get upset when you use my things without asking.’
Taking a 15-minute break to calm down
Agreeing to take turns with the TV

quiz.q: Sibling conflict is…
options: Normal, and can teach life skills
Always a sign of bad parenting
quiz.why: Sibling conflict is normal and can teach life skills like negotiating and compromise. What matters is how it is handled, and it is not a sign of bad parenting.

quiz.q: Which makes sibling fights worse?
quiz.why: Constant comparisons breed resentment and make sibling fights worse. Fair rules, schedules and one-on-one time reduce conflict.

quiz.q: ‘Fair, not identical’ means…
options: Everyone gets the exact same thing always
Treatment fits each child’s needs and age
quiz.why: 'Fair, not identical' means treatment fits each child's needs and age, because needs differ. Giving everyone the exact same thing always is not truly fair.

quiz.q: A sibling repeatedly hurts and threatens you. You should…
options: Tell a trusted adult or call 1098
quiz.why: Repeated hurting and threatening is not normal rivalry, so tell a trusted adult or call Childline 1098. Hitting back or keeping quiet keeps you unsafe.

sources: American Academy of Pediatrics — sibling rivalry guidance

lessons.title: Big decisions with family: career, college, city

scenes.text: Rohan, 17, in Hyderabad loves design. His parents and relatives expect him to do engineering ‘for a safe future’.
Every dinner discussion becomes a fight; Rohan stops talking.
His school counsellor helps him research design courses, entrance exams, fees, job roles and salaries, and talk to two working designers.
He presents a plan to his parents. They agree he’ll prepare for a design entrance exam, with a backup option, and review after results.

steps.title: Understand what your family fears
steps.body: Family pressure about careers usually comes from **love + fear**: fear of financial insecurity, of you struggling, of ‘what people will say’, or of a field they don’t understand. Many parents made sacrifices for your education. Respecting that while explaining your choice works better than rebellion or silent surrender.

steps.title: Build a decision file
steps.body:
1. **Interest & strengths**: what you enjoy, what you’re good at (marks, projects, feedback).
2. **Research**: courses, entrance exams, colleges, fees, duration.
3. **Career reality**: job roles, starting salaries, growth, real people you can talk to.
4. **Risks and backup**: what if it doesn’t work out? (another course, a skill, a gap-year plan)
5. **Ask for a trial**: an internship, a short course, a portfolio by a date.
Presenting this calmly shows maturity — and helps you check your own choice honestly.

steps.title: Bring in helpers
steps.body: A **school counsellor**, a respected relative or teacher, or a professional in the field can talk to your parents. Sometimes parents hear the same thing better from another adult. Aptitude and interest assessments with a qualified counsellor can also give neutral information.

steps.title: When pressure becomes too much
steps.body: If pressure makes you feel hopeless, unable to sleep or eat, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, tell someone today — a trusted adult or **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7), or **112** in an emergency. No exam or career is worth your life, and there are always more paths than it seems.

steps.title: Around the world
steps.body: Career conflicts with family happen everywhere — in Lagos, Seoul and Toronto too. Research across cultures finds that young people do best when they have both **autonomy** (some choice) and **family support**. Aim for a decision your family can live with and you can commit to.

activity.prompt: Write your decision file for one big choice: your interest, your research so far, your family’s worries, and one compromise or trial you could propose.
activity.hint: Be honest about risks — it makes your case stronger, not weaker.

quiz.q: Family career pressure usually comes from…
options: Love mixed with fear of insecurity
quiz.why: Family career pressure usually comes from love mixed with fear of insecurity. Understanding that fear helps you have a calmer conversation.

quiz.q: Which makes your case strongest?
options: A researched plan with a backup
quiz.why: A researched plan with a backup shows maturity and answers your family's worries. Silence, threats or shouting do not.

quiz.q: A ‘trial’ in this context means…
options: A short course or internship to test the choice
quiz.why: A 'trial' is a short course or internship to test the choice, which lowers risk and fear. It is not an exam, a court case or running away.

quiz.q: If career pressure leads to thoughts of self-harm, call…
quiz.why: If career pressure leads to thoughts of self-harm, call Tele-MANAS 14416 or 112; help is available 24×7. Staying silent is not safe, and 1906 and 1915 are for other services.

lessons.title: Apologies, boundaries and repair

scenes.text: During an argument in Indore, Neha, 16, tells her mother, ‘You’ve ruined my life.’ Her mother goes silent and cries in the kitchen.
Neha feels terrible but doesn’t know how to fix it. ‘Sorry’ feels too small.
That night she says: ‘Ma, I’m sorry I said that. It was cruel and not true. I was upset about the phone rule. Next time I’ll ask for a break instead of yelling.’
Her mother hugs her. They later agree on a phone rule together. Neha also learns to say ‘Please knock before entering’ calmly.

steps.title: A real apology has five parts
steps.body:
1. **Say sorry clearly**: ‘I’m sorry.’
2. **Name what you did**: ‘…for shouting and saying you ruined my life.’
3. **Show you understand the impact**: ‘That must have really hurt.’
4. **No excuses or ‘but’**: avoid ‘I’m sorry, but you…’
5. **Repair and change**: ‘Next time I’ll ask for a break.’ Then actually do it.
A fake apology — ‘Sorry if you felt hurt’ — blames the other person’s feelings.

steps.title: Boundaries with family
steps.body: A **boundary** is a respectful limit that protects your wellbeing: ‘Please knock before coming into my room’, ‘I don’t want to discuss my weight at family gatherings’, ‘I can’t lend money this month.’ Boundaries are not disrespect. Say them **calmly, briefly and kindly**, and repeat if needed. Adults can set boundaries with parents and relatives too — about privacy, money, marriage questions or advice.

steps.title: Scripts you can use
steps.body:
- ‘I love you and I need some privacy — please knock.’
- ‘I appreciate your concern; I’d rather not talk about this today.’
- ‘I can help on Saturday, not on weekdays.’
- ‘When you joke about my marks in front of relatives, I feel embarrassed. Could you stop?’

steps.title: Repair isn’t possible alone
steps.body: Repair needs both sides. If someone repeatedly humiliates, threatens or hurts you, apologies alone don’t fix it — protecting yourself and getting help from a trusted adult or helpline (1098 for children, 181 for women in many states, 112 in emergencies) comes first.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of one unresolved hurt in your family where you were wrong. Write a five-part apology. Deliver it when the time is right.

activity.prompt: Put the parts of a sincere apology in order.
items: Say what you will do differently, then do it

quiz.q: Which is a sincere apology?
options: ‘I’m sorry I shouted. It hurt you. I’ll take a break next time.’
quiz.why: A sincere apology is specific, owns the impact and commits to change, as in 'I'm sorry I shouted. It hurt you. I'll take a break next time.' 'Sorry, but…' and 'sorry if you felt hurt' shift blame.

quiz.q: A boundary is…
options: A respectful limit protecting your wellbeing
quiz.why: A boundary is a respectful limit that protects your wellbeing, and it supports healthy relationships. It is not a wall, punishment or disrespect.

quiz.q: Best way to state a boundary?
options: Calmly, briefly and kindly, repeating if needed
quiz.why: State a boundary calmly, briefly and kindly, and repeat it if needed. Shouting, saying nothing or using someone else is less effective.

quiz.q: Why avoid ‘sorry, but…’?
options: It cancels the apology by adding an excuse
quiz.why: Avoid 'sorry, but…' because the 'but' adds an excuse that cancels the apology and shifts blame.

questions.q: Which is an ‘I’ statement?
options: ‘I feel hurt when plans change suddenly.’
questions.why: An 'I' statement shares your feeling without blaming, as in 'I feel hurt when plans change suddenly.' 'You always' and 'everyone hates you' attack the other person.

questions.q: Is sibling conflict normal?
questions.why: Yes, sibling conflict is common in most families and often normal.

questions.q: Childline number?
questions.why: The Childline number is 1098, for children in need. 101 is fire, 1930 is cyber fraud and 1915 is consumer help.

questions.q: Best time to ask parents for something important?
questions.why: Ask when parents are relaxed, so they can listen. Anger, guests or traffic make a good hearing unlikely.

questions.q: A fair fighting rule is…
options: Talk about the problem, not the person
questions.why: A fair fighting rule is to talk about the problem, not the person. Name-calling, bringing up old fights and refusing breaks make conflict worse.

questions.q: Which phrase sets a boundary politely?
questions.why: 'Please knock before entering my room' is clear and kind, so it sets a boundary politely. Saying 'I hate you', shouting or giving the silent treatment do not.

questions.q: Parents comparing siblings usually…
questions.why: Comparing siblings usually increases rivalry, because comparison breeds resentment. It does not improve grades or stop fights.

questions.q: ‘Sorry if you were offended’ is…
questions.why: 'Sorry if you were offended' is a non-apology that shifts responsibility, because it does not own what you did. A full apology names your action and its impact.

questions.q: Key elements of a strong career discussion with family?
options: Research, realistic plan, backup, possible trial
questions.why: A strong career discussion uses research, a realistic plan, a backup and possibly a trial, which answer your family's fears with facts. Ultimatums, silence or just copying friends do not.

questions.q: Your parent says no because of safety worries. Most effective response?
options: Acknowledge the worry and propose specific safety steps
questions.why: Acknowledge the worry and propose specific safety steps, which addresses the real concern. Sneaking out, accusing them or going silent shuts down the talk.

questions.q: Siblings: one repeatedly threatens and humiliates the other. This is…
questions.why: Repeated threats and humiliation are harm, not normal rivalry, and need adult intervention. It is not character building.

questions.q: Which best describes ‘fair, not identical’ parenting?
options: Rules and support suited to each child’s age and needs, applied consistently
questions.why: 'Fair, not identical' means rules and support suited to each child's age and needs, applied consistently. The same bedtime for a 6- and 16-year-old ignores their needs, and favouritism is unfair.

questions.q: A teen feels hopeless after career fights and mentions not wanting to live. Best action by a friend?
options: Take it seriously, stay with them, involve a trusted adult, call 14416 or 112 if in immediate danger
questions.why: Take it seriously, stay with them, involve a trusted adult and call 14416 or 112 if there is immediate danger. Keeping it secret or telling them to toughen up could cost a life.

questions.q: Which repair plan after a big family fight is most likely to work?
options: Calm down, give a specific apology, listen to their side, agree a new rule together, follow through
questions.why: Calm down, give a specific apology, listen to their side, agree a new rule together and follow through. Ownership plus changed behaviour rebuilds trust, but gifts, waiting or blaming do not.

courses.title: Marriage, in-laws and partnership
courses.summary: What to discuss before marriage, India’s legal basics (age, consent, dowry, registration), living with in-laws and joint families, communicating through conflict, and recognising and escaping domestic abuse.
outcomes: Learners can list key topics couples should discuss before marriage
Learners know India’s legal basics: marriage age, dowry prohibition, registration
Learners can handle in-law expectations as a team with boundaries
Learners can spot the ‘four horsemen’ in conflict and use their antidotes
Learners can recognise domestic violence and know the protections and helplines
courses.guardianNote: For adults. Covers marriage expectations, family conflict and domestic violence factually and non-graphically, with Indian laws and helplines.

lessons.title: Before marriage: expectations and conversations

scenes.text: Priyanka and Vivek in Pune met through families and liked each other. They talked about movies, food and travel — but not much else.
After marriage they discover big differences: she plans to keep working and move cities for her career; his family expects her to stay home; he wants children soon, she wants to wait three years.
Their cousins Fatima and Jacob, married for ten years, had spent months discussing money, careers, children and chores before their wedding.
Priyanka and Vivek start couples counselling and finally have the conversations they skipped. It takes time, but they find a shared plan.

steps.title: Marriage is a choice and a partnership
steps.body: Whether arranged, introduced or chosen yourselves, a healthy marriage starts with **free and full consent** of both people. Love and attraction matter, but daily life runs on **shared values, communication and practical agreements**. Many conflicts after marriage come from **expectations never spoken aloud**.

steps.title: Conversations to have before marriage
steps.body:
- **Money**: incomes, debts, saving, spending style, who manages what, supporting parents.
- **Careers**: will both work? Relocation? Further study?
- **Children**: whether, when, how many; parenting values.
- **Home**: where to live (with parents or separately), chores, cooking — who does what.
- **Families**: expectations of each side, festivals, visits, involvement in decisions.
- **Religion, food, lifestyle**: practices, drinking, smoking.
- **Health**: physical and mental health conditions, openness about medical history.
- **Conflict**: how each of you handles anger and disagreement.
- **Intimacy and consent**: respect, comfort and that consent matters within marriage too.

steps.title: Legal basics in India
steps.body:
- **Minimum marriage age**: **21 for men and 18 for women** under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 and personal laws. Child marriage is an offence.
- **Dowry** — giving, taking or demanding it — is **illegal** under the **Dowry Prohibition Act 1961**. Dowry-related cruelty is a serious crime under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
- **Registering your marriage** (under the relevant personal law or the **Special Marriage Act 1954**) gives clear legal proof needed for passports, visas, insurance, inheritance and protection of rights. Many states make registration compulsory.
- The Special Marriage Act allows marriage between people of any religion as a civil marriage, with a notice period.
This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Red flags before marriage
steps.body:
- Pressure to marry against your wishes or in a hurry
- Dowry or ‘gift’ demands, direct or hinted
- Controlling behaviour: checking your phone, limiting your friends, deciding your clothes
- Lies about job, income, health or previous marriage
- Contempt or explosive anger, even ‘only once’
It is far easier to step back before marriage than after. Help is available if you are being forced: **112**, women’s helpline **181** (many states), or local police and protection officers.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Use the checklist with your partner or someone you’re considering. Note topics where you disagree — they aren’t necessarily deal-breakers, but they need a plan.

activity.prompt: Pre-marriage conversation checklist
items: Money: incomes, debts, saving and support for parents
Where we’ll live and how chores are shared
How we handle anger and disagreement
Agreed: no dowry, and we’ll register the marriage

quiz.q: Minimum legal marriage age in India is…
quiz.why: The legal minimum marriage age in India is 21 for men and 18 for women, under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 and personal laws.

quiz.q: Is dowry legal if both families agree?
options: No — giving, taking or demanding dowry is illegal
quiz.why: No. Giving, taking or demanding dowry is illegal under the Dowry Prohibition Act 1961, even if both families agree.

quiz.q: Why register a marriage?
options: Legal proof for visas, insurance, inheritance and rights
quiz.why: Registering a marriage gives legal proof for visas, insurance, inheritance and rights, protecting both spouses. It is not just a formality and is not banned.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag before marriage?
options: Checking your phone and controlling your friends
quiz.why: Checking your phone and controlling your friends is a red flag, because controlling behaviour often escalates. Discussing money, chores and health openly are healthy signs.

lessons.title: In-laws and joint families: a team approach

scenes.text: Ananya moves into her husband Karthik’s family home in Chennai. Every Sunday her mother-in-law comments on her cooking in front of relatives.
Ananya complains to Karthik; he says, ‘That’s just how Amma is.’ Ananya feels alone.
In a calm talk, she explains how it feels. Karthik agrees they are a team. He speaks privately and respectfully to his mother; Ananya also asks her mother-in-law to teach her a family recipe.
The comments reduce. A month later, they cook sambar together. It isn’t perfect, but it’s much better.

steps.title: Why in-law tensions happen
steps.body: A marriage joins two families with different habits, food, rules and expectations. Parents may feel they are ‘losing’ a child or that their ways are being rejected. The new spouse may feel judged or like a guest. Many joint and nuclear families in India manage this well — usually because the couple acts as a **team** and everyone shows **respect**.

steps.title: The couple as a team
steps.body:
- Agree on **key decisions together first** (finances, children, moving out, festivals), then share with families.
- Each spouse usually handles **their own parents** in difficult conversations — it lands more gently.
- **Never mock** your spouse’s family, and don’t complain about your spouse to your family for every small issue.
- **Back each other in public**, discuss disagreements in private.

steps.title: Respectful scripts
steps.body:
- To a parent (by their own child): ‘Amma, I know you mean well. When you comment on Ananya’s cooking in front of others, it hurts her. Could you tell her privately or teach her?’
- To in-laws: ‘I’d love to learn how you make this. Could you show me on Saturday?’
- Boundary: ‘We’ve decided to handle our finances ourselves, but we’ll always ask your advice on big things.’
- Saying no: ‘We won’t be able to come this weekend; we’ll visit next Sunday.’

steps.title: Building goodwill
steps.body: Small regular gestures matter: asking about health, remembering birthdays, sharing chores, involving grandparents with children, appreciating their help. Expect differences and choose your battles — not every comment needs a response.

steps.title: When it crosses a line
steps.body: Constant insults, threats, restricting someone’s movement or money, dowry demands, or violence by a spouse or in-laws is **not ‘family adjustment’** — it’s abuse, and the law protects against it (next lessons). Seek help early.

a.text: Your mother-in-law insists you give your salary to the family account. You and your spouse haven’t discussed this. What first?

choices.label: Argue with your mother-in-law immediately
choices.feedback: Conflict before a couple-plan usually escalates.

choices.label: Talk privately with your spouse first and agree a plan together
choices.feedback: Team first.

b1.text: The argument gets heated; your spouse feels caught in the middle.

choices.label: Pause, apologise for the tone, and plan with your spouse
choices.feedback: Good recovery.

choices.label: Tell your spouse to choose between you and their mother
choices.feedback: Ultimatums deepen the divide.

b2.text: You both agree to contribute a fixed amount to household expenses and manage the rest yourselves. Who explains it?

choices.label: Your spouse explains it respectfully to their parent, with you present
choices.feedback: Often the gentlest route.

choices.label: You announce it at a family dinner without warning
choices.feedback: Public surprises cause embarrassment and resistance.

bad.text: Tension rises. Step back, reconnect with your spouse privately, and approach the family together and respectfully.

good.text: Your mother-in-law isn’t thrilled but accepts. Your contribution is appreciated, and your financial independence is respected.

quiz.q: What’s usually the best first step in an in-law disagreement?
options: Agree a plan with your spouse privately
quiz.why: First agree a plan with your spouse privately, so you act as a team. Confronting the in-law publicly, ignoring your spouse or posting about it escalates the problem.

quiz.q: Who should usually raise a sensitive issue with a parent?
quiz.why: A sensitive issue with a parent should usually be raised by their own child, your spouse, because it lands more gently. An outsider may offend.

quiz.q: Which builds goodwill with in-laws?
options: Small regular gestures and asking to learn from them
quiz.why: Small regular gestures and asking to learn from them build goodwill through respect and involvement. Public complaints, mocking or never visiting harm the relationship.

quiz.q: Repeated dowry demands from in-laws are…
options: Illegal and a form of abuse
quiz.why: Repeated dowry demands are illegal and a form of abuse, because dowry and related cruelty are crimes. They are not a tradition or just a money matter.

sources: Family therapy literature on couple boundaries

lessons.title: Fighting fair as a couple

scenes.text: Every night Sana and Arif in Lucknow argue about dishes. It starts with ‘You never help!’ and ends with Arif walking out.
Soon they argue about everything — and stop talking for days.
A counsellor teaches them gentle start-ups, taking 20-minute breaks, and listing all household tasks — including the ‘invisible’ planning work.
They split tasks fairly and agree a signal for ‘I need a break’. Arguments still happen, but they don’t spiral.

steps.title: Conflict is normal; contempt is dangerous
steps.body: All couples disagree. Psychologist **John Gottman**’s long-term research with couples found that **how** couples argue predicts relationship trouble more than **whether** they argue. He described four especially harmful patterns, the ‘**Four Horsemen**’: **criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling** — with contempt the most damaging.

steps.title: The four horsemen and their antidotes
steps.body:
- **Criticism** (attacking character: ‘You’re so lazy’) → **Gentle start-up**: ‘I feel overwhelmed with the dishes. Could you do them on weekdays?’
- **Contempt** (eye-rolling, mocking, insults) → **Build appreciation**: notice and say what you value in your partner.
- **Defensiveness** (‘It’s not my fault, you…’) → **Take responsibility** for your part, even a small part.
- **Stonewalling** (shutting down, silent treatment) → **Self-soothe**: take a 20–30 minute break, calm your body, then come back.

steps.title: Housework and the mental load
steps.body: Arguments about chores are often about **fairness and feeling valued**. Besides visible tasks (cooking, cleaning), there’s **invisible work**: planning meals, remembering bills, school forms, doctor visits, gifts. Write **all** tasks down, including planning, then share both **doing** and **remembering**. Fair doesn’t always mean 50:50 every day; it means both agree it’s fair overall.

steps.title: Repair attempts
steps.body: During a heated moment, small gestures — a joke, a touch, ‘I’m sorry, let me try again’, ‘Can we pause?’ — help bring things back. Accepting your partner’s repair attempt matters as much as making one. Some problems are long-lasting (differences in personality); aim to talk about them with understanding rather than ‘winning’.

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: If arguments regularly involve fear, threats, intimidation, or any violence, it is not a ‘communication problem’ — it is abuse (next lesson). For ongoing non-violent conflict, couples counselling with a qualified professional can help a lot; it’s a sign of commitment, not failure.

activity.prompt: Match each harmful pattern to its antidote.
pairs: Take a break and self-soothe, then return

quiz.q: Which of the ‘four horsemen’ is considered most damaging?
quiz.why: Of the 'four horsemen' of conflict, contempt is considered most damaging because it signals disgust and superiority. Criticism, defensiveness and stonewalling also hurt but less.

quiz.q: ‘You’re so lazy’ is an example of…
quiz.why: 'You're so lazy' attacks character rather than a specific behaviour, so it is criticism. A gentle start-up would name the issue without blame.

quiz.q: The antidote to stonewalling is…
options: Taking a calming break and returning to talk
quiz.why: The antidote to stonewalling is taking a calming break and returning to talk, because calm bodies talk better. Yelling, leaving forever or mocking make it worse.

quiz.q: ‘Mental load’ means…
quiz.why: 'Mental load' is the invisible work of planning and remembering things for a household. It is real work that needs sharing.

sources: Gottman, J. — research on marital stability

lessons.title: When it’s not okay: recognising domestic abuse

scenes.text: Meena, 29, in Jaipur makes excuses for missing family events. Her husband controls her salary, checks her phone and has hit her ‘only when he’s angry’.
Her in-laws tell her to ‘adjust’ for the family’s honour.
Her school friend Rehana notices bruises and quietly gives her the women’s helpline number and the name of the district Protection Officer.
With support, Meena gets a protection order and stays in a safe place. She says: ‘I thought it was my fault. It wasn’t.’

steps.title: Forms of domestic abuse
steps.body:
Domestic violence is a **pattern of power and control** by a partner or family member. India’s **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (PWDVA)** recognises:
- **Physical**: hitting, pushing, choking, burning
- **Emotional/verbal**: insults, humiliation, threats, isolating from friends and family
- **Sexual**: forced or coerced sexual acts, degrading behaviour
- **Economic**: taking salary, denying money for necessities, stopping someone from working, dowry demands
Abuse often starts small and increases over time. **It is never the victim’s fault.**

steps.title: Legal protection (India)
steps.body:
- Under the **PWDVA 2005**, a woman can approach a **Protection Officer**, a registered service provider, the police or a **Magistrate** for: **protection orders**, **residence orders** (right to live in the shared household), **monetary relief**, **custody orders** and **compensation**.
- Cruelty by a husband or his relatives, and dowry-related offences, are crimes under the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** (which replaced IPC provisions such as section 498A). Dowry is prohibited under the **Dowry Prohibition Act 1961**.
- Free legal aid: Legal Services Authorities (**15100**).
This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: A safety plan
steps.body:
- Save helplines: **112** (emergency), **181** (women’s helpline in many states), the National Commission for Women’s helpline, **One Stop Centres** (Sakhi) in districts offering shelter, medical, legal and counselling support.
- Keep copies of IDs, bank details, medicines, phone charger and some cash in a safe place or with a trusted person.
- Agree a **code word** with a trusted friend to signal danger.
- Know the safest exit and where you can go.
- Keep evidence safely: photos of injuries, medical records, messages.
- In immediate danger, leave if you can and call 112.

steps.title: Helping someone else
steps.body: Listen without judging; believe them; don’t pressure them to leave immediately (leaving can be the most dangerous time and needs planning); share helplines; offer practical help (a phone, a place to stay, going with them). Respect their decisions while keeping the door open. Men and LGBTQ+ people can also experience abuse — they deserve the same support; counsellors, legal aid and police can help.

steps.title: Children in the home
steps.body: Children who witness domestic violence are also harmed. If a child is being hurt or is in danger, call **1098** or **112**.

activity.prompt: Hard questions about abuse, answered calmly

items.q: He only hits me when he’s drunk or stressed. Is that abuse?
items.a: Yes. Alcohol or stress may be triggers but are not excuses. Violence is a choice and a crime. You deserve safety.

items.q: He never hits me but controls all my money and phone. Is that abuse?
items.a: It can be. Economic and emotional control are recognised forms of domestic abuse under the PWDVA.

items.q: If I complain, will I lose my home?
items.a: The PWDVA provides for residence orders protecting a woman’s right to live in the shared household. A Protection Officer or legal aid lawyer can explain options.

items.q: My family says ‘adjust’ for honour. What do I do?
items.a: Your safety matters more than appearances. Reach out to a trusted person, a One Stop Centre, 181 or 112.

items.q: Can men be victims of domestic abuse?
items.a: Yes. Anyone can experience abuse. Men can seek counselling, legal advice and police help for threats or violence.

quiz.q: Which law gives protection orders for women facing domestic violence?
quiz.why: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (PWDVA) gives protection orders to women facing domestic violence. The other laws deal with consumers, information or vehicles.

quiz.q: Taking a partner’s salary and denying money for necessities is…
quiz.why: Taking a partner's salary and denying money for necessities is economic abuse, which the PWDVA recognises. It is not normal budgeting or a legal duty.

quiz.q: When helping a friend in an abusive relationship, you should…
options: Listen, believe, share helplines and offer practical help
quiz.why: Listen, believe, share helplines and offer practical help, which supports safety planning. Confronting the abuser alone, forcing a decision or telling everyone can raise the danger.

quiz.q: One Stop Centres provide…
options: Shelter, medical, legal and counselling support
quiz.why: One Stop Centres provide shelter, medical, legal and counselling support in one place for women affected by violence. They do not handle driving tests or passports.

sources: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
Ministry of Women and Child Development — One Stop Centres
WHO violence against women fact sheet

questions.q: Minimum marriage age for women in India?
questions.why: The minimum marriage age for women in India is 18, and for men it is 21.

questions.q: Is dowry legal in India?
questions.why: No. Dowry is prohibited in India, since the Dowry Prohibition Act of 1961.

questions.q: Emergency number if someone is in danger at home?
questions.why: 112 is the emergency number to call if someone is in danger at home. 155260 is for cyber fraud, 1906 for LPG and 1915 for consumer help.

questions.q: Which should couples discuss before marriage?
questions.why: Couples should discuss money, careers, children, chores and families before marriage, because unspoken expectations cause conflict later. Horoscopes or the menu alone are not enough.

questions.q: ‘You’re useless’ is an example of…
questions.why: 'You're useless' attacks the person's character, so it is criticism or contempt. A gentle start-up or appreciation would not.

questions.q: Which law allows civil marriage between people of different religions?
questions.why: The Special Marriage Act 1954 is the civil marriage law that allows marriage between people of different religions. The Companies Act, RTI Act and Motor Vehicles Act are unrelated.

questions.q: In-law conflict: the couple should usually…
options: Act as a team and agree plans privately first
questions.why: In in-law conflict the couple should usually act as a team and agree on plans privately first. Taking opposite sides publicly, ignoring each other or moving cities does not solve it.

questions.q: Antidote to defensiveness?
questions.why: The antidote to defensiveness is taking responsibility for your part, which lowers tension. Counter-attacking, silence or leaving escalate the conflict.

questions.q: PWDVA recognises which forms of abuse?
questions.why: The PWDVA recognises physical, emotional/verbal, sexual and economic abuse, a broad definition. It is not limited to dowry, in-laws or only physical harm.

questions.q: Why is registering a marriage important?
options: Proof for legal rights, visas, insurance and inheritance
questions.why: Registering a marriage gives proof for legal rights, visas, insurance and inheritance, so it brings legal certainty. It is not for avoiding tax or getting a driving licence.

questions.q: A friend says her husband controls her phone and money and has slapped her twice. Best first response?
options: Believe her, listen, share 181/112/One Stop Centre info, help with a safety plan
Tell her parents without her consent immediately
questions.why: Believe her, listen, share 181, 112 and One Stop Centre information, and help with a safety plan. Controlling her phone and money and slapping her is abuse; calling him or telling parents without consent may increase risk.

questions.q: Which statement about the ‘mental load’ is accurate?
options: Planning and remembering household tasks is real work that should be shared
It only applies at the office
questions.why: The mental load is the planning and remembering of household tasks, which is real work that should be shared. If unequal, the invisible work causes resentment.

questions.q: Under the PWDVA, a residence order can…
options: Protect a woman’s right to live in the shared household
questions.why: Under the PWDVA, a residence order protects a woman's right to live in the shared household. It does not cancel the marriage, give a passport or transfer property to neighbours.

questions.q: Which combination best predicts a stable marriage, according to long-term couple research?
options: Disagreeing with gentle start-ups, appreciation, responsibility-taking and successful repair attempts
questions.why: Long-term couple research finds stable marriages disagree with gentle start-ups, appreciation, responsibility-taking and successful repair attempts. How couples handle conflict matters most; avoiding it or winning every argument does not help.

courses.title: Caring for elders, and living with loss
courses.summary: Practical care for ageing parents (medicines, falls, memory changes, legal rights), avoiding caregiver burnout, understanding grief, and supporting grieving adults and children.
outcomes: Learners can organise medicines and make a home safer from falls
Learners can recognise memory-loss warning signs and seek assessment
Learners know elders’ legal rights and Elderline 14567
Learners can spot caregiver burnout and build support
Learners can explain common grief reactions and support grieving adults and children
courses.guardianNote: For adults. Discusses ageing, illness, death and grief gently and factually, with where to get help (Elderline 14567, Tele-MANAS 14416).

lessons.title: Caring for ageing parents: health, safety and rights

scenes.text: Mr. Subramanian, 78, lives alone in Coimbatore. His daughter Lakshmi works in Bengaluru and calls every evening.
One morning he slips in the bathroom and lies on the floor for two hours before a neighbour hears him.
Lakshmi visits and makes changes: grab bars, a non-slip mat, night lights, a pill organiser, a medical alert button and a weekly doctor tele-consult.
She also saves Elderline 14567 and arranges a neighbour check-in every morning.

steps.title: Medicines without mistakes
steps.body:
- Make a **single updated list**: medicine name, dose, time, purpose, prescribing doctor. Carry it to every doctor visit.
- Use a **weekly pill organiser** with morning/afternoon/night slots.
- Set **phone alarms** or a family reminder system.
- Ask the doctor periodically whether all medicines are still needed — older adults often take many medicines, which raises the risk of side effects and interactions.
- Watch for side effects like dizziness, confusion or falls, and report them.
- Never stop or change doses without asking the doctor.

steps.title: Preventing falls
steps.body:
Falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults.
- **Bathroom**: grab bars, non-slip mats, a shower chair, no-step entry if possible.
- **Lighting**: night lights from bedroom to toilet.
- **Floors**: remove loose rugs and clutter; fix wobbly steps; handrails on stairs.
- **Footwear**: well-fitting, non-slip slippers.
- **Health**: regular eye checks, review of medicines, and gentle strength and balance exercise (as advised by a doctor or physiotherapist).
- A **phone or alert button** within reach.

steps.title: Memory changes: when to see a doctor
steps.body: Occasional forgetfulness is common with age. Get a medical assessment if you notice: repeatedly asking the same questions, getting lost in familiar places, trouble managing money or daily tasks, confusion about time or place, personality changes, or poor judgement. Some causes (like vitamin deficiencies, thyroid problems, depression, medicine side effects) are treatable. Early assessment for dementia also helps families plan.

steps.title: Elders’ rights and support in India
steps.body:
- The **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007** obliges children (and certain relatives) to maintain parents and senior citizens who can’t maintain themselves; claims go to a **Maintenance Tribunal**. It also addresses abandonment.
- **Elderline 14567**: national helpline for information, guidance, emotional support and help in cases of abuse.
- Many banks offer doorstep banking for senior citizens; hospitals and railways may have senior-citizen facilities.
- Help elders keep **nominations**, a **will** and important papers in order; consider a **power of attorney** if they want help managing affairs.
This is general education, not legal or medical advice.

steps.title: Respect and independence
