choices.feedback: That’s your right under the Good Samaritan provisions.

choices.label: Leave without informing anyone
choices.feedback: You may leave, but informing staff about what happened helps the victim’s treatment.

bad.text: That increased risk. Remember: secure the scene, call 112, don’t move the injured unless there’s danger, control bleeding.

good.text: You helped save a life within the golden hour — and the law protects you.

quiz.q: First step at a road accident scene?
options: Move the injured to your car immediately
quiz.why: First make the scene safe, for example by warning traffic, to prevent further crashes. Moving the injured, removing helmets or filming comes later or is wrong.

quiz.q: Can police force a Good Samaritan to give personal details?
quiz.why: No, disclosure is voluntary for a Good Samaritan, under the Good Samaritan guidelines. Police cannot force a helper to give personal details.

quiz.q: Which section of the Motor Vehicles Act protects Good Samaritans?
quiz.why: Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act, inserted in 2019, protects Good Samaritans. 302 and 420 are IPC sections and 1A is not relevant.

quiz.q: Why not remove an injured rider’s helmet routinely?
options: It may worsen a neck/spine injury
quiz.why: Do not routinely remove an injured rider's helmet because it may worsen a neck or spine injury. Remove it only if needed to open the airway.

quiz.q: The ‘golden hour’ refers to…
options: The period after injury when prompt care most improves survival
quiz.why: The 'golden hour' is the period after injury when prompt care most improves survival. It has nothing to do with sunset, lunch or traffic.

sources: Motor Vehicles Act 1988, sections 2(12A) and 134A (2019 amendment)
Supreme Court — Save Life Foundation v. Union of India (2016)

lessons.title: Phones, drinking, tiredness — and after a minor crash

scenes.text: Driving home in Jaipur, Akash glances at a WhatsApp message for ‘just two seconds’.
He rear-ends a scooter at a signal. Luckily the rider is only shaken.
They move to the side, take photos, exchange details and insurance information, and Akash apologises.
Akash now keeps his phone in the glovebox — ‘Do Not Disturb while driving’ is permanently on.

steps.title: Distraction
steps.body: At 60 km/h a car moves about 17 metres every second. A 2-second glance at a phone = 33 metres driven blind. Using a handheld phone while driving is an offence in India. Hands-free calls still distract the mind. Use ‘Do Not Disturb while driving’, set navigation before starting, and pull over safely if you must use the phone.

steps.title: Alcohol and drugs
steps.body: In India the legal limit is **30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood** for drivers; drink-driving carries heavy fines and possible imprisonment, and penalties increase for repeat offences. Even small amounts slow reaction time and judgement. Some medicines (for allergies, sleep, pain) cause drowsiness — read the label. Plan ahead: designated sober driver, cab, or stay over. Never ride with a drunk driver.

steps.title: Tiredness kills
steps.body: Drowsy driving causes many highway crashes, especially between midnight and dawn and after lunch. Warning signs: yawning, heavy eyelids, drifting lanes, missing exits. Coffee and open windows don’t fix it. **Stop safely and rest**; take a break about every 2 hours on long drives; share driving.

steps.title: After a minor crash
steps.body:
1. Stop safely; hazard lights on; check for injuries; call 112 if anyone is hurt.
2. Stay calm; don’t argue or admit fault in anger.
3. Take **photos**: vehicles, number plates, positions, road, damage.
4. Exchange names, phone numbers, vehicle registration and insurance details.
5. Inform your **insurer promptly** (many have a time limit).
6. If someone is injured, there is a dispute, or for certain claims, report to the police; an FIR or police report may be needed.
7. Keep repair bills and medical records.

steps.title: Keep your papers ready
steps.body: Carry (or keep in DigiLocker / mParivahan) your driving licence, registration certificate, valid insurance and PUC certificate. Digital documents from these official apps are accepted by traffic authorities.

activity.prompt: A car moves at 54 km/h. The driver looks at a phone for 3 seconds. How many metres does the car travel ‘blind’? (54 km/h = 15 m/s)

quiz.q: Legal blood-alcohol limit for drivers in India?
quiz.why: The legal blood-alcohol limit for drivers in India is 30 mg per 100 ml of blood. 80 mg is the limit in some other countries.

quiz.q: Best cure for drowsiness while driving?
quiz.why: The only cure for drowsiness is to stop safely and rest, since only sleep fixes sleepiness. An open window or loud music gives a brief lift, and driving faster adds risk.

quiz.q: After a minor crash, first check…
quiz.why: After a minor crash, first check whether anyone is injured, because people come before cars or phones.

quiz.q: Digital driving licence and RC in DigiLocker/mParivahan are…
quiz.why: Digital driving licences and RCs in DigiLocker or mParivahan are official documents and are accepted by traffic authorities. They are valid in India, not illegal.

questions.q: Helmet rule for pillion riders in India?
questions.why: Both the rider and the pillion must wear helmets. It is not optional or limited to night or highways.

questions.q: When crossing in India, look first…
questions.why: Traffic nearest you comes from the right because India drives on the left, so look right first.

questions.q: At an accident, dial…
questions.why: At an accident, dial 112, the all-emergency number. 155260 and 1930 are cyber fraud lines and 1906 is LPG.

questions.q: A child under the safe age to judge traffic should…
questions.why: A young child should hold an adult's hand because children cannot judge speed and distance well. Crossing alone, running or using earphones is unsafe.

questions.q: Do rear-seat car passengers need seatbelts?
questions.why: Yes, rear-seat passengers need seatbelts too; it is required and life-saving. Unbelted rear passengers can be thrown forward and injure themselves and others.

questions.q: Good Samaritans in India are protected under MV Act section…
questions.why: Good Samaritans are protected under Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act. The other numbers are unrelated.

questions.q: Stopping distance includes…
questions.why: Stopping distance is reaction distance (while you notice and respond) plus braking distance. Both add up.

questions.q: Why stay a door’s width from parked cars when cycling?
questions.why: Keep a door's width from parked cars so you are not hit by a suddenly opened door; 'dooring' crashes are common.

questions.q: A conscious crash victim has neck pain. You should…
questions.why: A conscious crash victim with neck pain may have a spine injury, so keep them still and call 112. Walking, sitting up or giving water could worsen it.

questions.q: At 90 km/h, a 2-second glance covers about…
questions.why: 90 km/h = 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 m/s, so in 2 seconds you travel 25 × 2 = 50 m.

questions.q: Hospital refuses to treat an accident victim until the helper pays a deposit. Under Good Samaritan guidelines…
options: Helpers shouldn’t be made to pay or be detained; emergency care shouldn’t be delayed
questions.why: Under Good Samaritan guidelines, helpers should not be made to pay or be detained, and emergency care should not be delayed. The guidelines protect helpers and the victim's access to care.

questions.q: If braking distance at 40 km/h is about 8 m, at 80 km/h it is roughly…
questions.why: Braking distance grows with the square of speed, so doubling from 40 to 80 km/h makes it about 4 times: 8 × 4 = 32 m.

questions.q: Which plan for a party night is safest?
options: Designated sober driver or cab; never ride with a drunk driver
questions.why: Only zero alcohol before driving is safe, so use a designated sober driver or a cab and never ride with a drunk driver. Coffee, open windows or driving slowly do not remove impairment.

questions.q: Correct priority at a highway crash with fuel leaking and one unresponsive victim not breathing?
options: Wait for police before touching anything
Light a flare near the fuel
Secure scene/warn traffic, call 112, if fire risk move victim only as needed for safety, start CPR
questions.why: Danger comes first: secure the scene and warn traffic, call 112, move the victim only if there is an immediate fire risk, and start CPR if they are not breathing. Do not light a flare near fuel, film or wait while someone is not breathing.
